description:

text:
Asia-Pacific medical technology (MedTech) demand is expected to reach US$132 billion (S$170.9 billion) by 2030, growing at 6.9 per cent annually — outpacing the global market growth rate of 5.5 per cent over the same period1. Capturing this opportunity requires clinical evidence, capital, clear regulatory pathways and manufacturing partners.

Singapore has built an ecosystem that brings these critical enablers together, helping MedTech companies scale and succeed. We are home to the world’s top 30 MedTech companies, with the sector generating over S$20 billion in manufacturing output and employing more than 17,000 people.

Here is how Singapore's ecosystem helps companies innovate and scale globally.

1. Research and clinical partnerships that speed up product development

WHY IT MATTERS: Building a globally competitive MedTech product rarely follows a straight line from lab to market. As then Minister-in-Charge of Energy and Science & Technology, Dr Tan See Leng noted at the Singapore Medical Device Venture Showcase in June 2026, a commercially viable MedTech business needs more than good science – other factors like regulatory clarity, patient capital, manufacturing capabilities, industry partnerships and talent matter, too."2

HOW SINGAPORE HELPS:

Productisation support: MedTech Catapult, a S$38 million national platform under the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), helps MedTech companies bridge the gap between research and market adoption. It brings together engineering and prototyping capabilities with quality assurance, clinical, regulatory and business development expertise to de-risk product development and accelerate commercialisation.

Connections with research and clinical partners: Global companies can work with hospitals, universities and research institutes on product development and clinical research. Agilent, for example, established the US$29 million (S$38.6 million) National University of Singapore-Agilent Hub for Translation & Capture to develop new ways of translating clinical research into diagnostics. Singapore also offers sustained public investment in biomedical and translational research under the S$37 billion Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE) 2030 plan.

Growing access to capital and venture support: Investors and venture-building platforms including ClavystBio, Santé Accel Singapore, and SG Growth Capital provide healthcare ventures with capital, mentorship and global networks.

PROOF IN PRACTICE:

EssilorLuxottica: Its Singapore Centre for Innovation & Technologies Asia helped conceptualise the Stellest® lens with the company’s other R&D hubs globally, manufactured prototypes for clinical trials in the United States and China, and led clinical studies and programme coordination. In 2025, the US Food and Drug Administration authorised Stellest® as the first spectacle lens to slow myopia progression in children.

Bypass Solutions: Working with MedTech Catapult and local contract manufacturers, it has completed key preclinical studies for its peripheral artery disease treatment and is moving towards a first-in-human trial in Singapore.

2.Regulatory credibility that can cut time to market

WHY IT MATTERS: Asia is a high-growth but fragmented market. Each jurisdiction retains approval authority, so repeated regulatory reviews consume time and capital.

At the LSI Asia Emerging MedTech Summit 2026, Adjunct Professor (Dr) Raymond Chua, Chief Executive Officer of Singapore's Health Sciences Authority (HSA), pointed to HSA's growing network of regulatory reliance arrangements as a way to reduce duplication — making Singapore an increasingly practical entry point for companies looking to move efficiently from one approval to many across the region.

name: Microsoft
title: British watchdog seeks tougher terms around Microsoft's dominance of business software
description:
The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is opening a consultation on whether to tag the Redmond software giant with strategic market status in respect of its portfolio of business software applications.
Its proposal document notes Microsoft has been by far the largest provider of business software in the UK for decades.
Rivals back licensing scrutiny Cloud providers previously complained that Microsoft's licensing terms make it more costly for companies to deploy Windows Server instances and services such as SQL Server on non-Microsoft clouds.
The proposed SMS designation grew out of the CMA’s investigations into whether the big global players were having a negative impact on the cloud services market in the UK.
In a statement sent to The Register, Microsoft said it does not share the CMA’s views in its proposed decision on business software solutions.
text:
The UK's competition watchdog wants to designate Microsoft with strategic market status (SMS) in business software, allowing the regulator it to intervene to level the playing field, and says it is considering other areas for investigation.

Regulators around the world are watching to see what the UK decides in this case, with bodies such as the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and the European Commission mulling similar actions.

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) is opening a consultation on whether to tag the Redmond software giant with strategic market status in respect of its portfolio of business software applications.

This follows an investigation the regulator started back in May into Microsoft’s software portfolio including Word, Excel, Outlook, PowerPoint and Teams, plus its security, server and operating systems. The watchdog is also probing whether Microsoft enjoys a position of “substantial and entrenched market power” through the suite of software that could be seen as stifling competition and harming buyer choice.

It lays out its proposed decision in a document [PDF] and is inviting comments that must be submitted by November 13. The CMA will make its final decision by February 13, 2027.

Bargain spotter

The CMA makes it clear the company holds a strong position in each of the five areas it investigated (personal computer operating systems, productivity software suites, security software, server operating systems and relational database management systems), and that customers face barriers when switching providers – limiting their choice and weakening the ability of other software developers to offer rival products.

Its proposal document notes Microsoft has been by far the largest provider of business software in the UK for decades. It finds that many customers view Microsoft's portfolio as a unified software environment, forming an end-to-end, integrated stack which makes for easier technical integration between products, with discounted pricing for buying whole bundles of applications together.

This makes customers less likely to adopt products from alternative providers that may offer similar or superior functionality, as doing so would duplicate licensing costs for products already in their Microsoft bundle, the CMA says.

“Organizations should be able to choose the products that work best for them, switch provider when they want to and combine services from different suppliers. We want to ensure businesses have the freedom to choose how they use Microsoft’s products alongside alternatives,” said CMA chief exec Sarah Cardell.

Finding that the criteria for SMS designation are met would not imply or assume wrongdoing on Microsoft’s part, the regulator stresses.

A separate document [PDF] spells out the potential interventions that the CMA could make. These include ensuring that Microsoft’s technical design choices do not restrict the ability to use other providers; that commercial arrangements (like bundling) do not limit effective competition; and preventing Microsoft from using its market power in business software to distort competition in adjacent activities, such as cloud services.

Rivals back licensing scrutiny

Cloud providers previously complained that Microsoft's licensing terms make it more costly for companies to deploy Windows Server instances and services such as SQL Server on non-Microsoft clouds.

The proposed SMS designation grew out of the CMA’s investigations into whether the big global players were having a negative impact on the cloud services market in the UK. This largely fizzled out with the watchdog securing undertakings from Microsoft and Amazon Web Services (AWS) that they would work to reduce barriers to switching between clouds and operating multi-cloud deployments.

In an update, the CMA says that more can be done to address barriers to switching between cloud providers and using multiple cloud services, and it will continue to work with AWS and Microsoft to address them.

It also says it its looking into whether customers can freely choose the best AI tools, and whether alternative AI providers have a level playing field to compete against Copilot.

In a statement sent to The Register, Microsoft said it does not share the CMA’s views in its proposed decision on business software solutions.

“All our products - including Copilot - are open and interoperable, giving customers the ability to use them alongside competing services and choose solutions that work best for them at attractive prices. We will continue engaging constructively to ensure UK customers and businesses carry on benefiting from robust competition,” a spokesperson told us.

However, some pressure groups were quick to signal their approval. The Browser Choice Alliance said it welcomes the CMA’s proposed decision, adding that: “BCA members have long experienced how Microsoft leverages its market power from Windows and productivity software to push users towards its Edge browser, even where they’re trying to use an alternative.”

The Open Cloud Coalition, which counts Google as a member, said: “Microsoft’s restrictive software licensing practices distort competition in the cloud, harm choice, and increase costs. This once-in-a-generation opportunity to end these practices can strengthen competition and lower customer costs, if the CMA acts quickly and decisively.” ®

At Microsoft and GitHub, I watched senior leaders get 60 to 70 pages of status updates every week. Nobody reads that. Leaders skim for problems, and the real ones get buried under update after update that says “on track” followed by three paragraphs explaining everything that’s going on. And don't get me started about "watermelon status" updates. So I built an AI skill that turns the context from people's day-to-day work into a rollup a leader can read in under a minute. It was inspired by a workflow in Agentic Beyond Code, and it sorts every piece of work into four buckets: 🚨 Needs help: health dropped, dates slipped, or it’s off track 👋 Needs a nudge: nobody has updated it in over a week 🎉 Worth celebrating: shipped this week or on track for weeks straight ✅ Everything else: one line with a count The pattern works with any tool that tracks status and history. I built this version in Productboard Spark and scheduled it to run every Monday, so leaders get it without anyone writing it. If you want the skill, reach out and I’ll send it your way. Would love to hear if other leaders have flipped status updates from pushing lots of paper to pulling what they need to enforce the values of the org.

Transcript

Hi, I'm Chris Butler and I'm a product evangelist for product board. One of the things I dealt with a lot whenever I would help senior leaders in a product OPS role was to help them understand what was going on inside their teams and where they could potentially intervene or help out. And when I was working at Microsoft and GitHub, one of the biggest problems for a senior vice president was that they might get something like 60 or 70 pages worth of these types of updates every week from the all the teams that they had reporting into them. And so I started to think about like, how might we make it easier to go from a push of status to these? Leaders to them, being able to pull it out of the environment. Using product board Spark, I created a skill to be able to get a leader a weekly rollup of things that they should take action on. And for this weekly rollup I want to get some information about initiative that is happening right now. And so the skill is now going to grab everything that's associated with this initiative, look for changes in status, look for comments, and then start to build a roll up for me. And so now the report is coming back with some key information. It's trying to show me where I might need to intervene or kind of pre escalate before the team asks for help. Maybe some places where something hasn't been updated for a while that need me to give it a nudge. And then one of the things I think is most important actually for building kind of cultural values within an organization is really finding places where you can celebrate people and the work they've done. And then of course, it tries to hide anything that is not actually that valuable for me to get update about. And now the great thing about this is that I can take the skill and create some type of schedule, say I want to be able to do this on some weekly basis, say every Monday after people have filled out their status on Fridays. And so with that, if you're interested in the skill and want to check it out, either go to the Makers community or I will be posting this. As the new CFO, Long jumps headfirst into the fray.
text:
Mark Long, 59, replaced Weigand as CFO on Wednesday—“effective immediately,” according to Supermicro—and he brings with him a stack of bona fides. He previously served as CFO and chief strategy officer at $130 billion data storage company Western Digital, and he runs an investment and advisory firm, Prime Impact Capital. Long also served a stint as co-CEO and CFO of a SPAC he cofounded that raised $300 million before it merged in 2023 with a Beijing-based auto insurance technology platform, Cheche Technology.

He joins Supermicro at an incredibly complex moment for the hardware maker with deep ties to Nvidia and its CEO, Jensen Huang, and Musk’s xAI, which was folded into SpaceX. Long’s record as a veteran executive and tech investor is likely intended to help clear the cloud that has hovered over Supermicro for the past two years and to burnish its credibility with skeptical investors.

In March, the Department of Justice and FBI indicted and arrested Supermicro cofounder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw in a shocking smuggling case allegedly involving $2.5 billion of Supermicro hardware loaded with Nvidia’s export-controlled chips being illegally routed to China. Liaw, along with two others associated with Supermicro, was alleged to have gone to extreme lengths to deceive officials, including using hair dryers to remove and replace sticky labels and staging thousands of dummy servers that were nonworking physical replicas of actual Supermicro servers—because the real servers had already been diverted to China.

Supermicro is not named as a defendant in the case, and has said it is cooperating with law enforcement. Liaw has pleaded not guilty. His March arrest, however, kicked off another board-led internal investigation—separate from the previous probe that led to the CFO search—that Supermicro said in August found no evidence that current members of senior management knew about the smuggling scheme.

Until he resigned after being arrested and charged in the smuggling case, Liaw had served on the Supermicro board and had a long history with fellow cofounders Charles Liang and Sara Liu. (Liu and Liang are married and both serve on the Supermicro board.) Liaw had previously left Supermicro in the midst of an internal audit committee investigation just before a 2018 SEC probe charged Supermicro and its then-CFO with improper revenue recognition practices. Supermicro settled the SEC’s charges and paid a $17.5 million settlement in 2020. Liaw returned to Supermicro as a consultant in May 2021 and eventually became a full-time employee before rejoining the board in December 2023.

The prior probe, which led the company to commit to replacing Weigand with a more experienced CFO, was spurred by the abrupt resignation of auditor EY and investigated export controls and rehiring of employees who had resigned in 2017 after the earlier accounting investigation. As CFO and chief compliance officer, Weigand was held responsible for process lapses the investigation turned up, which included a consulting arrangement with the former CFO that EY wasn’t informed about, the company disclosed in 2024.

Since Liaw’s March 2026 arrest, Supermicro has since disclosed that it got hit with a grand jury subpoena from the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York related to both Liaw’s indictment and the company’s compliance program and internal controls. It also got subpoenas and inquiries from foreign authorities, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and the Bureau of Industry and Security, the national security and enforcement arms of the U.S. Department of Commerce that polices trade compliance and violations. In Liaw’s case, his lawyer informed the judge the documents Supermicro would give the government could be material to his defense, and his trial was pushed back from November 2026 to March 2027.

Since then, one of the workers who was indicted with Liaw and worked as a contractor for Supermicro, has pleaded guilty, according to court records in the case. Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun pleaded guilty last week to four counts, including conspiracy to smuggle goods and violate export rules and obstruction of justice.

The last count is new, according to Sun’s superseding information document, and shows that Sun pleaded guilty to a charge that he deleted an encrypted messaging app on his phone on March 19, 2026, the day of the arrests. His sentencing is set for September 2027, and he’s facing a maximum of 20 years for the obstruction and conspiracy charges. Sun is also required to give up any of the proceeds from the export offenses. His lawyers did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and it isn’t specified in his court records whether he has a cooperation agreement with the government.

As the new CFO, Long jumps headfirst into the fray. The board recently added Intel’s former IT CTO, Shesha Krishnapura, and another board member, Judy Lin, retired. Lin was previously vice president at Western Digital from 2007 to September 2012, leaving after Long began consulting for Western Digital in March 2012, before he officially joined the company as chief strategy officer in January 2013.

For the role, Long will get a base salary of $725,000 plus a signing bonus of $500,000 and a guaranteed annual cash bonus of $500,000. He’ll be eligible to get additional cash bonuses and an annual equity grant based on company performance and his individual achievement. As for equity, Long got an initial equity grant valued at about $4.1 million based on Thursday’s stock price, and options on 150,000 shares.

Supermicro declined to make Long available for interviews. In a statement CEO Charles Liang welcomed Long and thanked Weigand. Liang said Long would have “an immediate positive impact” in strengthening the company’s financial execution.

Weigand will stay to assist in the CFO transition. A Supermicro spokesperson said further details about his role would be shared at a later date.

text:
On its third quarter of 2026 earnings call, held on Oct. 13, 2026, Johnson & Johnson(NYSE:JNJ) raised its full-year sales outlook after operational revenue grew 6%. Strong pharmaceutical demand helped the healthcare giant absorb legal costs and medical device headwinds outside the U.S. Three takeaways from the call stand out for long-term investors.

1. Annual Sales Are On Track To Cross a $100 Billion Milestone

The company's Innovative Medicine division, which develops prescription drugs, powered performance with 7.9% operational growth. Cancer treatments led the gains, while Tremfya, an injectable therapy for inflammatory diseases, expanded its market share. This momentum keeps the company on pace to breach a historic sales threshold this year.

With sales in the quarter of more than $25 billion we are on track to meet our guidance and exceed $100 billion in annual revenue for the first time in our company's 140 year history.

-- Joaquin Duato, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer

2. Medical Technology Leadership Is Addressing Temporary Global Growth Headwinds

Operational growth in MedTech, the company's medical device segment, slowed to 2.5% due to disruptions in the Middle East, volume-based procurement, a government bulk-buying program in China, and delays in the adoption of Abiomed heart pumps. Management plans to restore double-digit growth through new product rollouts, including OTTAVA, its soft-tissue robotic surgery system.

Simply put, we can do better, and we absolutely will. And right now, we are focused solely on the actions needed to deliver stronger results in the fourth quarter and beyond.

-- Timothy Schmid, Executive Vice President, Worldwide Chairman, MedTech

3. Portfolio Refinement Favors Spinning Off Orthopedics Over Major Acquisitions

Management clarified that double-digit growth targets rely on internal investments rather than large corporate acquisitions. To streamline operations, the business is leaning toward a tax-free spinoff for DePuy Synthes, its orthopedics subsidiary, by mid-2027.

Given the way DePuy Synthes is performing and the momentum Nimesh Nana and his team are generating, we are leaning toward a spin as being the best option to create long term value for Johnson & Johnson shareholders.

-- Joseph J. Wolk, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer

Looking Ahead

Operational momentum is accelerating into late 2026, and leadership expects further progress next year. High-margin oncology treatments and surgical device rollouts provide durable structural advantages across global markets. Management is watching regulatory timelines for VARIPULSE Pro, an electrophysiology catheter, and commercial preparation for OTTAVA, its soft-tissue robotic surgery platform.

That is why we have the confidence to say that we will finish 2026 strong and that 2027 will be an even better year for Johnson & Johnson.

-- Joaquin Duato, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer

Commercial execution across prescription drugs and medical devices continues to support long-term compounding.

The depth of our portfolio, momentum from new product launches, and upcoming pipeline catalysts further reinforce our conviction in achieving double digit growth by the end of this decade with sustainable growth beyond.

-- Joseph J. Wolk, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer

text:
From Insulin Maker to Obesity Juggernaut

Ten years ago, Eli Lilly (NYSE:LLY | LLY Price Prediction) was a steady Indianapolis drugmaker known for insulin and a dependable dividend. In its 150th year, it now carries a market cap of roughly $1.117 trillion. The incretin era rewrote the company.

Tirzepatide drove most of that change. Lilly sells it as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes and as Zepbound for obesity, which launched in late 2023. In Q2 2026 the pair generated $14.9 billion in revenue, and Lilly wrote roughly 6 out of 10 U.S. obesity prescriptions.

Lilly also kept building. The FDA approved its oral GLP-1 pill Foundayo in Q1 2026, and the company announced new plants from Indiana to Texas. Adding Mounjaro to China’s reimbursement list helped drive 172% international growth for the drug. FY2025 revenue reached $65.18 billion, up 44.7%.

Your $1,000 Grew to $18,637

Initial Investment: $1,000

Current Value: $1,523.80

Total Return: 52.38%

S&P 500 (same period): $1,160.30 (16.03%)

5-Year Return

Current Value: $5,504.80

Total Return: 450.48%

10-Year Return

Initial Investment: $1,000

Current Value: $18,637.40

Total Return: 1,763.74%

Annualized Return: 33.98%

S&P 500 (same period): $3,634 (263.4%)

These figures reflect share price growth only. Lilly lifted its quarterly dividend from $0.51 in 2016 to $1.73 in 2026, so dividends received over the decade would add to the total.

The 10-year result is roughly 5.1 times what the S&P 500 delivered, and Lilly beat the index at every horizon. Holding still took nerve. Shares fell about 22% between February 4 and April 30, 2026, then recovered to $1,251.61. Luck mattered too. A 2016 buyer had no way of knowing how large the obesity drug market would become.

Volume Growth Battles Price Cuts as Retatrutide Nears Filing

The bull case rests on retatrutide and Foundayo extending the franchise. Retatrutide has a complete Phase 3 package, and Lilly plans a U.S. submission in Q1 2027. Management also says obesity treatment remains at “mid-single digit” utilization. In Q2 2026, revenue rose 47.7% to $22.97 billion, and full-year guidance moved up to $85.0 billion to $87.0 billion.

The bear case centers on pricing erosion outrunning volume. Realized prices fell 13% in Q2 2026, and Mounjaro plus Zepbound still account for most of Lilly’s revenue. Acquired IPR&D charges of $3.03 per share also cut into Q2 earnings.

So far, volume has the edge. A 60% jump in volume is more than offsetting the price cuts, and an 85.8% gross margin leaves plenty of cushion. Investors researching the stock should weigh how they would handle another 20%-plus pullback.

title: UPM inaugurates Leuna biorefinery, world's largest of its kind - Chemical Engineering
description:
UPM Global (Helsinki, Finland) inaugurated its biorefinery in Leuna, Germany, marking the start of a new industrial platform for renewable chemicals made from wood.
“The Leuna Biorefinery is a transformative investment for UPM and an important milestone in our growth journey.
Together with our renewable fuels, the Leuna Biorefinery forms a platform for profitable growth and shows the ambition and energy with which UPM innovates,” said Massimo Reynaudo, president and CEO of UPM.
UPM’s Leuna Biorefinery is also a milestone for Europe’s bioeconomy.
With Leuna, UPM turns Europe’s strengths in science and engineering into a new growth business,” said Reynaudo.
text:
UPM Global (Helsinki, Finland) inaugurated its biorefinery in Leuna, Germany, marking the start of a new industrial platform for renewable chemicals made from wood. The biorefinery converts lignocellulosic biomass, primarily wood from sustainably managed forests and sawmill residues, into biochemicals. With an annual capacity of 220,000 metric tons, it is the largest facility of its kind in the world. The ramp-up has progressed further. Enzymatic hydrolysis and the production of lignin-derived specialty chemicals have reached stable operation, and UPM is ramping up sales of these products.

“The Leuna Biorefinery is a transformative investment for UPM and an important milestone in our growth journey. Our high-performance renewable chemicals open new markets for UPM and new opportunities for our customers. Together with our renewable fuels, the Leuna Biorefinery forms a platform for profitable growth and shows the ambition and energy with which UPM innovates,” said Massimo Reynaudo, president and CEO of UPM.

The biochemicals will be used in everyday products, from clothing and packaging to cosmetics, construction materials and tires. Many of these are still made from fossil-based raw materials. Manufacturers and brands look for new ways to innovate and differentiate, and the Leuna plant gives them renewable alternatives with the required performance. At the same time, global warming underlines the need for continued de-fossilization, and a considerable share of consumers look for products made from renewable materials.

UPM’s Leuna Biorefinery is also a milestone for Europe’s bioeconomy. It shows that renewable carbon-based solutions can move beyond pilot projects into commercial-scale manufacturing, reducing dependence on imported fossil value chains and strengthening supply security.

“Europe’s competitiveness depends on creating new industries and scaling innovation. With Leuna, UPM turns Europe’s strengths in science and engineering into a new growth business,” said Reynaudo.

Automakers including Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Ford have been targeting more advanced automated-driving systems, from hands-free highway driving to self-driving in limited conditions.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told reporters in Stockholm that partnering with Volvo provided the chipmaker with a “tremendous opportunity” because of the automaker’s rigorous safety standards.
Besides Volvo, Nvidia has partnerships with a wide range of automakers, including Mercedes, Jaguar Land Rover and Hyundai.
The technology, which Volvo ultimately expects to support hands-free driving both in urban environments and on highways, should appear in Volvo vehicles before 2030 and will be launched in multiple regions simultaneously, excluding China, Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo Cars’ head of software ⁠engineering, said.

Volvo Cars is expanding its partnership with Nvidia to develop a new generation of driver-assistance and automated-driving technology, the companies said on Thursday, as carmakers race to bring increasingly advanced hands-free driving features to market.

The companies said Volvo would combine its safety systems and engineering expertise with Nvidia’s artificial intelligence and computing technologies, including the Hyperion sensor, computer architecture and autonomous-driving software stack.

Automakers including Mercedes-Benz, BMW and Ford have been targeting more advanced automated-driving systems, from hands-free highway driving to self-driving in limited conditions.

Tesla is pushing for broader approval of its assisted-driving technology in Europe, including urban areas with an EU-wide vote possible in December.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told reporters in Stockholm that partnering with Volvo provided the chipmaker with a “tremendous opportunity” because of the automaker’s rigorous safety standards. Huang said features would be rolled out gradually.

“As the car earns its trust and as Volvo becomes comfortable with the capabilities of the cars, they’ll continue to expand the services that are available. There’s no hurry, safety first,” Huang said.

Besides Volvo, Nvidia has partnerships with a wide range of automakers, including Mercedes, Jaguar Land Rover and Hyundai.

Volvo CEO Hakan Samuelsson said the company would take a cautious approach to deployment.

“We will never let it out under conditions which we know are not safe,” Samuelsson told reporters.

The technology, which Volvo ultimately expects to support hands-free driving both in urban environments and on highways, should appear in Volvo vehicles before 2030 and will be launched in multiple regions simultaneously, excluding China, Alwin Bakkenes, Volvo Cars’ head of software ⁠engineering, said.

Volvo, majority-owned by China’s Geely Holding, has not chosen a pricing model yet, Bakkenes said, but features would not be limited to higher-priced models.

text:
Supply is the tightest constraint on Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction). On its August 26, 2026 earnings call, CEO Jensen Huang said, “our entire supply chain is challenged,” and Taiwan now wants to move part of that chain to Texas.

In remarks reported October 16, 2026, Taiwan’s economics minister, Kung Ming-hsin, spoke. He said the government supports a plan for U.S. industrial parks, starting in Texas, with the first complex costing up to $4 billion. The parks target smaller suppliers that serve Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM) and AI server assemblers such as Foxconn, placing them near Nvidia and other data center hardware makers.

The two names dropped on October 15, 2026, during a wider tech selloff over AI funding worries. Nvidia closed at $217.23, down 1.84%, and TSMC’s U.S. shares closed at $422.25, down 1.80%.

If you own either stock, the question is whether a supplier park matters to companies this large. It matters more to TSMC’s U.S. ecosystem than to Nvidia’s earnings.

What Taiwan Has Committed

The plan is a statement of intent, backed by government support. The Taiwan Electrical and Electronic Manufacturers’ Association, an industry group, is expected to raise the money, and the government will offer loan guarantees, visas, and land access.

Kung Ming-hsin put each site’s estimated cost at $2 billion to $4 billion, and the government wants more than one U.S. location but has not set a number. Nvidia, TSMC and Foxconn have made no commitment to the parks, and no participating suppliers, schedule or customer contracts were named.

What Nvidia Gains From Local Suppliers

AI servers rely on smaller makers of power supplies, cooling systems, circuit boards, connectors and chassis. Placing them near U.S. assembly cuts shipping time and tariff exposure, which also helps Nvidia’s standing in Washington (we profiled seven of these non-chip AI infrastructure suppliers, from power to cooling, in a free report you can grab here).

One site is small, with $96.22 billion in quarterly revenue and $279 billion in supply commitments. U.S. production usually costs more, although forecast gross margin of about 74% suggests Nvidia has room to pass those costs to customers.

Taiwan also addressed AI hardware policy. Shipping restricted AI hardware to mainland China will become “a criminal offense under the Foreign Trade Act.” That lowers the risk of leakage, and Nvidia’s guidance already excludes Data Center compute revenue from China.

Why TSMC Sits Closer to the Buildout

TSMC’s planned U.S. investment reached $265 billion after it added $100 billion for Arizona in July. A Texas supplier park is small beside that, but it puts parts makers between the Arizona fabs and the server assemblers.

TSMC is also studying Texas. Describing capacity options outside Arizona on its October 15, 2026 call, management said, “And Texas is one,” and added that teams are evaluating options, with no investment announced.

Permitting, U.S. labor costs, and whether enough suppliers sign up are all unresolved. Larger Taiwanese firms are already moving on their own. Quanta Computer won approval to spend $973 million on server assembly in Tennessee, and Wistron won approval for $146 million to upgrade a Texas plant.

Taiwan’s semiconductor exports hit a record $87.22 billion in September, up 60.9% from a year earlier, so the demand exists now. The parks assume it holds up long enough to cover higher U.S. costs.

How Texas Supplier Parks Could Shape the Outlook for Nvidia and TSMC

Supply remains the main limit on Nvidia’s growth. Huang said the company has supply for about 70% of demand, so added U.S. capacity helps marginally.

TSMC has more direct exposure to the reshoring theme, because it runs the fabs a Texas cluster would serve. Its $1.95 trillion market value, against Nvidia’s $5.25 trillion, also gives local suppliers more weight in its story.

The signal to check is an announcement naming the first suppliers in a Texas park, along with a confirmed site and schedule. Until then, Kung Ming-hsin’s $4 billion figure is only an upper estimate for one site.

title: Nvidia is no longer a PC gaming company. Get used to it - PCWorld
description:
It can feel heartbreaking if you’re dedicated to the hardcore DIY PC gaming lifestyle, but you can take solace in the fact that the GeForce RTX 5080, RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5070 are still widely available and plenty good enough for high-res, high-speed PC gaming.
But I have to say, the sooner you make peace with the fact that Nvidia is no longer in the business of supporting PC gaming, the better.

text:
Welcome to The Full Nerd newsletter—your weekly dose of hardware talk from the enthusiasts at PCWorld. Missed the surprising topics on our YouTube show or the latest news from across the web? You’re in the right place.

Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website!

And honestly, it doesn’t seem that surprising when you consider that the RTX 5090 launched with an MSRP of $1,999 yet regularly sold for upwards of $5,000, due in no small part to massive demand from AI-pilled coders and companies looking to take advantage of that sweet, sweet 32GB of DDR7 memory. A casual search of the major retailers this week turned up precisely zero 5090 cards available for purchase, even at that exorbitant price, and I suspect that will remain true for the foreseeable future.

It can feel heartbreaking if you’re dedicated to the hardcore DIY PC gaming lifestyle, but you can take solace in the fact that the GeForce RTX 5080, RTX 5070 Ti and RTX 5070 are still widely available and plenty good enough for high-res, high-speed PC gaming. Heck, the same leak that suggests the RTX 5090 is done for also claims that Nvidia will launch a new model of RTX 5080 with 24GB of DDR7 memory, which should offer a noticeable improvement over the current 16GB RTX 5080 cards.

But I have to say, the sooner you make peace with the fact that Nvidia is no longer in the business of supporting PC gaming, the better. Don’t get me wrong, Nvidia will continue to make new desktop graphics cards and talk a big game about how it values PC game players first and foremost. But the numbers have shown otherwise for some time, and that’s likely to continue for years to come.

After all, the AI-driven explosion of demand for high-end GPUs and silicon helped Nvidia become the first trillion-dollar chip company, and recent financial reports and SEC filings show the company’s revenue from data center products is now 4-5x that of its consumer hardware revenue. That’s presumably part of the reason why the company recently stopped reporting GPU sales as a discrete category entirely, instead lumping all GPU hardware sales (for both commercial and retail customers) into one category on its balance sheet alongside robotics, automotive and telecom products.

So please, for your own mental health, I’m begging you: do not give in to Jensen’s sales pitches at the next Nvidia press conference. I believe the company will keep making new graphics cards for the foreseeable future, but only to hold on to its commanding hold of the GPU market and keep up appearances while it milks the AI boom for all its worth. If AI demand collapses the way crypto seemed to crash a few years ago, maybe we’ll see Nvidia take up the mantle of being a PC gaming company once again.

But I don’t expect that will happen any time soon, and making peace with that has done wonders for the stress I feel right now as a frustrated fan of PC gaming. It’s helped me realize that I don’t need the latest and greatest hardware to have a blast gaming on my PC, and the same can be true for you. Take this time to play some games in your Steam(ing) pile of shame, get deeper into Linux gaming and explore all the other cool things you can do without an RTX 5090. Because I don’t know that high-end GPUs will be affordable for regular folks like you and me in the next few years, if ever—and I don’t think I’ll be buying an Nvidia GPU any time in the near future.

In this week’s episode of The Full Nerd

This week your regular host Adam Patrick Murray was joined by PCWorld’s Brad Chacos and Michael Crider on episode 419 of The Full Nerd to chat about the rumored end of the GeForce RTX 5090, open-source Adobe Creative Cloud alternatives and the pending launch of RTX Spark laptops.

And of course, the trio also make time to answer your questions from the PCWorld Discord and the live chat about everything from the future of PC game streaming to the durability of flash drives. Make sure to check it out, and tune in to next week’s episode to get your questions answered on the air!

Nerd news of the week

From some fun new ideas about where to place your GPU to an elucidating new interview that reveals the PC gaming habits of one of Hollywood’s movers and shakers, here’s some fun nerd news I found around the web for you this week!

Modder discovers unusual GPU placement that lowers hotspot temps by 19 degrees: Who knew putting the GPU up front could make such a difference in terms of cooling?

Nvidia GPU prices spike in Japan; prices up to 41% higher than Amazon US: Photos of Nvidia GPU prices in Japan are a bit foreboding (and hopefully not a sign of things to come here in the States), with the price of mid-range 50-series GPUs spiking 25-40 percent.

Legendary FPS level designer Richard “Levelord” Gray dies at 68: Pour one out for a real one and a legend in the early PC gaming space, a veteran game maker who worked on everything from Blood and Duke Nukem 3D to Half-Life: Opposing Force and Counter-Strike: Condition Zero. RIP Levelord!

text:
MiniMed completed its separation from Medtronic, the companies said Thursday.

The diabetes technology firm, which went public in March, is now independent from its former parent.

Medtronic began an exchange offer last month to split off a portion of its MiniMed shares. The agreement included a provision where Medtronic could choose to sell all of its remaining shares in MiniMed if the offer is oversubscribed.

Because the offer was 5.4x subscribed, Medtronic chose to exchange all of its remaining interest in MiniMed for shares of Medtronic, the company said Thursday. It no longer holds a stake in MiniMed.

“As an independent company, we have the freedom to make the decisions we believe are right for our business and the people we serve, and the responsibility to see those decisions through,” MiniMed CEO Que Dallara said in a statement. “Our focus now is to put that independence to work and continue advancing what is possible in diabetes care.”

Shares of MiniMed closed at $17.50 on Thursday.

text:
The European Medicines Agency’s committee on Friday recommended approval of Eli Lilly’s weight-loss pill Foundayo, the second oral obesity drug to win the agency’s backing after Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill.

The European Commission will now review the recommendation and give a final nod for the company to launch the drug in the region. Novo’s Wegovy pill won EU approval in July.

The race to broaden access to their oral drugs has become the latest battleground in Novo and Lilly’s weight-loss drug rivalry, as both aim to secure a larger share of a market expected to surpass $100 billion by 2030.

Foundayo was launched in the U.S. in April and in the UK in August, and generated $98 million in sales in the second quarter. Novo’s Wegovy pill is available in the U.S., the UK and the UAE.

The EMA recommended a marketing authorization for Foundayo for weight management and treatment of type 2 diabetes in adults.

The recommendation for Foundayo in weight management is based on two studies involving more than 4,740 adults who were obese or overweight, the agency said. Patients treated with Foundayo lost up to 11% of their body weight.

Early U.S. prescription data for oral weight-loss drugs has supported expectations that pills could expand the obesity market by attracting patients who have been reluctant to use injections.

The pill, which Lilly has sought approval for in more than 40 countries, contains orforglipron, a small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist that can help reduce appetite and food intake.

Unlike Novo’s Wegovy pill, Foundayo can be taken at any time of day without food or water restrictions, a feature Lilly has touted as a key advantage of the drug.

text:
FORT COLLINS, Colo., Oct. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Woodward (NASDAQ: WWD), a global leader in aerospace and industrial energy control solutions, today announced the appointment of Paxton McVoy as Executive Vice President and Chief Information Officer (CIO), effective Oct. 19, 2026. He will join the company's Executive Leadership Team, reporting directly to Chief Executive Officer Chip Blankenship.

In this newly created role, McVoy will lead Woodward's global information technology organization and set the direction for the company’s digital strategy, including enterprise resource planning (ERP), data and analytics, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and technology-enabled business transformation.

McVoy joins Woodward from Veralto, where he was Senior Vice President and Chief Information Officer. Following Veralto's separation from Danaher, he led the new public company's global technology strategy and operations and helped build Veralto's technology organization after the company became independent. His responsibilities included enterprise technology, cybersecurity, data and AI, infrastructure, procurement, and oversight of the ERP portfolio across 13 operating companies. Earlier in his career, he held senior IT leadership roles at Medtronic, including Vice President and CIO for the company's Surgical Innovations business. He also previously led Medtronic's transition from Oracle to SAP.

"Paxton has a proven history of using technology to improve business performance and leading digital transformation across complex global organizations like ours. In this role he will help us to set the direction for how information technology will support our long-term growth strategy," said Chip Blankenship, Chairman and Chief Executive Officer of Woodward. "His experience shaping enterprise technology strategy, advancing AI capabilities, and building strong teams will help us strengthen Woodward's digital foundation in line with our efforts to serve customers and create shareholder value."

"I am looking forward to joining Woodward at an important point in the company's growth," said McVoy. "Woodward's focus on innovation, operational excellence, and creating value for customers and shareholders creates a real opportunity to use technology as a strategic advantage. I look forward to working with the leadership team and Woodward members around the world to help ensure the success of the company's digital transformation."

McVoy holds a Bachelor of Arts in Business from Otterbein University and an MBA from The Ohio State University.

Our innovative fluid, combustion, electrical, propulsion, and motion control systems perform in some of the world’s harshest environments. text:
As Albertsons struggles with its second straight quarter of same-store sales declines, company leaders are turning to better in-store CX and streamlining operations to improve the business.

The grocer has launched a number of initiatives with good reason and intentions, but it has created too many layers of complexity over time, CEO Susan Morris said on a Q2 2026 earnings call Tuesday. Now, Albertsons is turning its focus to a few areas that will create greater value for shoppers.

“We must deliver more consistently for our customers,” Morris said on the earnings call. “Price matters, promotions matter, freshness matters, convenience, selection and customer service matter. Our job going forward is to deliver all of those things better than we do today.”

Albertsons wants to sharpen its value perception, according to Morris. The amount customers are willing to pay is important, but aspects such as product variety, services and ease of shopping are vital as well.

“Our goal is not to be the cheapest guy in town, but rather to have the right balanced value proposition that resonates with the customers that we serve uniquely by market,” Morris said.

Albertsons has its work cut out for it. The grocer’s comparable store sales declined just shy of 1% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to an earnings report. Digital sales rose 11% year over year, but net sales and other revenue dipped 0.1% year over year to $18.9 billion.

The grocer’s plans include strategic price cuts, but it is avoiding broad-based price reductions. Instead, it’s making strategic price investments on a more individualized level via tools like the Albertsons for U loyalty program.

“It’s about our ability to leverage our very, very strong loyalty program and create personalized offers that may mean something very different to me as a consumer than it might to you as a consumer,” Morris said.

Getting the in-store experience right

As Albertsons pursues streamlining its operations, it must “double down on the basics,” Morris said. That includes getting the right products inside store formats customers enjoy.

Albertsons stores may be functional, but they fail to offer customers inspiration or excitement, according to Neil Saunders, managing director at GlobalData Retail.

“There’s also not nearly enough newness in the offer to showcase new brands and new products,” Saunders said in an email. “The whole experience is extremely average, below par even, but when the prices are expensive, that’s simply not good enough.”

One issue is that Albertsons’ stores feel like they “were made for a different era,” Saunders said. They tend to be too large for what modern customers expect from a grocer, but Albertsons has let them be rather than invest in reconfiguring the layouts.

Streamlining operations to improve the in-store experience

The grocer’s efforts to streamline its store operations and experience plans may include layoffs and closing stores in underperforming markets, according to Morris.

Albertsons has already reduced complexity by cutting the number of regional divisions from 11 to four in July. The change has CX implications, as the regional executive vice presidents who oversee the new divisions were charged with elevating store conditions and keeping store teams focused on taking care of customers, according to Morris.

“With that kind of focus on elevating store standards and execution, it eliminates the distractions from all the noise happening around us,” Morris said. “Our team knows that we have essentially two roles in our company: We either serve customers directly or we serve those that serve customers.”

Store execution is one of the key areas where Albertsons sees early opportunities for improvement, according to Morris. The company will reduce shrink, raise standards and commit to offering the best training for associates.

“These steps and more, taken together, will improve the customer experience and ultimately our business results,” Morris said.

name: Ralph Lauren
title: Ralph Lauren Replaces Sustainability Targets With AI Metrics in Executive Pay Plan
authors: Ericka Severino, Jazzmine Gayle S. Miguel, Trisha Andrada, Jepryll Santos Torremoro, Law Arboleda, Colleen Anne J Cristales, Jastine Beatrice Yap, Jewel P, KD Rossly
description:
Ralph Lauren has replaced citizenship and sustainability targets with artificial intelligence (AI) metrics in its fiscal 2026 executive bonus plan, making AI literacy and workplace enablement part of how the American fashion company assesses eligible senior leaders' performance.
A Ralph Lauren spokesperson told Reuters that the new target reinforced opportunities to use AI to enhance the company's work.
How AI Will Affect Ralph Lauren's Executive Bonuses Ralph Lauren introduced an AI scorecard in its fiscal 2026 executive compensation plan, using employee AI literacy, training and workplace enablement to assess performance.
Why Ralph Lauren Changed Its Executive Pay Criteria Ralph Lauren replaced its citizenship and sustainability modifier with AI-related objectives in its executive bonus plan, placing greater emphasis on technological understanding and adoption among senior leaders and employees.
AI Metrics Gain Ground Across Corporate America Ralph Lauren's decision comes as more companies incorporate AI-related objectives into executive compensation.
text:
Ralph Lauren has replaced citizenship and sustainability targets with artificial intelligence (AI) metrics in its fiscal 2026 executive bonus plan, making AI literacy and workplace enablement part of how the American fashion company assesses eligible senior leaders' performance. The change was disclosed in the company's 2026 proxy statement, filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on 18 June. The previous measure had been in place for four years.

Under the revised arrangement, AI performance serves as a strategic modifier alongside financial measures, including revenue and adjusted operating profit margin. The move comes as companies across industries explore ways to incorporate AI into their business strategies and assess its impact on productivity and operational efficiency.

A Ralph Lauren spokesperson told Reuters that the new target reinforced opportunities to use AI to enhance the company's work. The spokesperson added that the previous sustainability measures had contributed to meaningful progress and were now integrated throughout the business.

How AI Will Affect Ralph Lauren's Executive Bonuses

Ralph Lauren introduced an AI scorecard in its fiscal 2026 executive compensation plan, using employee AI literacy, training and workplace enablement to assess performance. The scorecard allowed the company to adjust short-term incentive payouts based on progress against specific targets.

The measures included completion rates for an internal AI learning programme and information security awareness training, as well as employee survey results on AI readiness and workplace support. The company reported that all four indicators exceeded their targets, prompting its Talent Committee to approve a 10 per cent increase to short-term incentive payouts under the strategic goal modifier.

Financial performance remained central to the compensation plan, with revenue and adjusted operating profit margin each accounting for 40 per cent of short-term incentives. Strategic growth accelerator revenue and adjusted selling, general and administrative expenses each accounted for a further 10 per cent. Ralph Lauren said strong financial results, performance against other business targets and the AI scorecard contributed to maximum payouts for applicable named executive officers.

Why Ralph Lauren Changed Its Executive Pay Criteria

Ralph Lauren replaced its citizenship and sustainability modifier with AI-related objectives in its executive bonus plan, placing greater emphasis on technological understanding and adoption among senior leaders and employees.

The change affects the criteria used to adjust short-term executive incentives and does not mean the company has abandoned its wider sustainability commitments. A spokesperson said the previous measures had delivered meaningful progress and were now integrated throughout the business.

AI Metrics Gain Ground Across Corporate America

Ralph Lauren's decision comes as more companies incorporate AI-related objectives into executive compensation. Data from the Conference Board and ESGUAGE cited by Reuters showed that 12 per cent of S&P 500 companies disclosed AI-related goals in their executive incentive plans in 2026, compared with five per cent in 2024.

The technology is being adopted across the retail sector for tasks such as inventory management, pricing decisions and customer-facing shopping assistants. Companies are also exploring how AI can improve internal operations and help employees work more efficiently.

Other businesses have introduced similar incentives. Reuters reported that Salesforce and Textron had also replaced environmental, social and governance (ESG) measures with AI-related metrics, while PepsiCo had cited progress on an AI agenda when determining annual payouts for certain executives.

Despite the increase, tying executive bonuses directly to AI performance remains relatively uncommon. A review of 2,500 public company proxy statements filed in 2026 by compensation advisory firm Pearl Meyer found that only two per cent of companies across sectors had incorporated AI into executive incentive structures. The figures suggest that AI is gaining a place in corporate performance assessments, although the approach has not yet become standard practice.

Measuring AI Performance Remains a Challenge

Cory Morrow, a partner at Korn Ferry who leads its consumer and retail practice for executive pay, told Reuters that companies were still developing measurable baselines for AI performance. He said annual incentive plans signal business priorities, while financial indicators such as sales growth and profitability are expected to remain central to executive compensation.

Ralph Lauren's fiscal 2026 incentive plan measures AI adoption through employee training completion rates and survey results. The indicators assess participation in AI learning programmes and whether employees feel adequately trained and supported in using the technology.

The company reported that all four AI scorecard indicators exceeded their targets for fiscal 2026. Its results come as other companies also introduce AI-related measures into executive compensation plans, although the practice remains relatively uncommon across industries.

text:
Microsoft (MSFT -0.58%) is planning a big change to its Azure cloud computing data centers starting next year. It will rely much more on its custom-designed silicon than on leading graphics processing units (GPUs) like those from Nvidia (NVDA +0.49%). It's already made significant progress in expanding workloads for its Maia 200 chips, and it expects its next-generation Maia 300 chips to deliver significant improvements when it starts deploying them next year.

"Starting next calendar year, we will scale our Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments, making it the primary inference system for our own product and services," CEO Satya Nadella said. That's great news for its custom chip partner, Marvell Technology (MRVL -1.92%), and bad news for Nvidia.

Nvidia is losing data center market share

Nvidia's extreme dominance of the data center GPU space during the first few years of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom left its market share with nowhere to go but down. Its biggest customers, including the hyperscalers and leading AI frontier labs, have developed custom solutions that can handle AI workloads, and that can deliver better price performance on specific tasks than Nvidia's GPUs.

That said, GPUs offer far greater flexibility in terms of the types of tasks they can perform, making them particularly valuable for companies deploying servers to sell compute capacity to third parties with dynamic demands. Notice that Microsoft is starting its Maia expansion by focusing on its own products and services, not on leasing Maia compute capacity to third parties looking to cut costs on their OpenAI GPT-based applications.

Apple used TPUs to train Apple Intelligence, and Anthropic is using gigawatts worth of TPUs to develop its large language models.

While Nvidia can continue to grow sales extremely quickly, other chipmakers' growth rates are likely to outpace it. That's reflected in its P/E valuation, which now sits below those of its biggest rivals.

Microsoft could be Marvell's fastest-growing customer

text:
Preparations for the 2027 budget are also taking centre stage in Bangkok. And personal income tax remains one of the key issues under discussion, even after the figures from the DPB were released. Returning to the subject is the Minister for the Economy Giancarlo Giorgetti, who was questioned on the sidelines of the meetings IMF meetings: ‘As regards personal income tax (IRPEF), given that all the pieces of the puzzle are currently coming together to make way for measures, the key decision we face is whether to implement selective or across-the-board measures.’

Collegial decision

The decision will be a collective one. As Giorgetti explained, ‘it is not right for the minister to decide alone; we will assess the situation together with the parties, the leadership and President Meloni. Two weeks ago I had an overview of income and expenditure; I’m not exactly optimistic, but we are heading in the right direction’.

Loading...

On the budget bill to wind up the parliamentary session next week

The timetable is tight. “Work on the Budget Bill will probably be finalised next week” and “we will present it to Parliament; as you know, a very constructive dialogue is continuing – I met Dombrovskis here too – regarding the NEC clauses on defence and energy”.

Banks’ contribution, but ‘sustainable’

Another key issue is how the banks are to contribute to the budget in terms of new revenue for the Treasury. The message from the head of Via XX Settembre is clear: “I can confirm that a contribution will be sought from the financial sector because we believe it can afford it, and we also believe that it will be a sustainable arrangement”. Giorgetti added that “keeping the spread under control is in everyone’s interest”, referring to the fact that the banks hold billions of euros’ worth of BTPs on their balance sheets.

On the prospect of possible legal challenges from the banks, the minister commented, ‘Every Italian could take the State to court for raising taxes. We will try to strike the right balance; I don’t think anyone will die as a result.’

name: Walmart
title: Amazon and Walmart Are Turning Retail Efficiency Into Someone Else's Expense
description:
Both developments illustrate a fundamental change in retail economics.
On Thursday (Oct. 15), Amazon introduced two new devices from Bee, the personal AI company it acquired last year.
Through the $11.99 monthly Bee Pro subscription, consumers can opt to connect the devices to Amazon.com and Alexa+.
The Next Retail Advantage Is Who Controls the Handoff Walmart’s robotics and Amazon’s conversational AI appear to address opposite ends of the retail value chain.
The other seeks to improve the identification and conversion of consumer demand.
text:
As Walmart pushes robotics deeper into its distribution network, and Amazon brings artificial intelligence into consumers’ everyday conversations with new product launches across its Bee wearable line, the two retail giants are pursuing different versions of the same economic ambition: reducing the distance between consumer demand and a completed sale.

But the more consequential story isn’t what their technology eliminates. It’s what happens to the costs, risks and commercial opportunities left behind.

Warehouse automation can reduce labor-intensive handling while requiring suppliers to redesign packaging and shipping operations. AI assistants can eliminate the need to search for products while giving technology platforms greater influence over which brands consumers discover and ultimately buy.

Both developments illustrate a fundamental change in retail economics. Innovation is no longer simply reducing the cost of commerce. It is changing which businesses bear that cost, which ones capture the savings and who controls the transaction.

See also: Amazon and Walmart Want Merchants’ Software Budgets

Walmart’s Robots Are Changing the Economics Outside the Warehouse

Walmart’s warehouse modernization program has become one of retail’s most ambitious experiments in industrial automation. The company has been deploying robotics and automated systems across its distribution network, seeking improvements in inventory handling, fulfillment productivity and operating efficiency.

Recent reporting has also highlighted the engineering challenges involved in automating the movement of everyday consumer merchandise. A warehouse full of machines, after all, still has to process products designed for a world of human workers.

And when a retailer changes the physical requirements of its distribution infrastructure, suppliers may have to change how merchandise arrives. Packaging dimensions, labeling, case configurations and shipping specifications can become prerequisites for participating efficiently in the network. The result is a potentially uncomfortable contradiction: A retailer’s investment in operational efficiency can generate new expenses elsewhere in its supply chain.

If Walmart captures productivity gains while suppliers shoulder substantial implementation costs, the financial returns will look very different depending on whose balance sheet is being examined.

Read more: Amazon Builds Its Own Answer to Walmart’s 5,000 Stores

Amazon Wants to Capture Demand Before It Becomes a Search

If Walmart is changing the economics of getting products to consumers, Amazon is experimenting with changing the economics of discovering what consumers want in the first place.

On Thursday (Oct. 15), Amazon introduced two new devices from Bee, the personal AI company it acquired last year. The $74.99 Bee Frontier wearable and forthcoming $99.99 Bee Eclipse phone attachment are designed to turn conversations into summaries, reminders and actionable recommendations. Through the $11.99 monthly Bee Pro subscription, consumers can opt to connect the devices to Amazon.com and Alexa+. Something mentioned in conversation, such as needing household supplies, can subsequently appear as a personalized product recommendation. Amazon says audio is processed and deleted, with users controlling their information.

The PYMNTS Intelligence report “Will the 2026 Shopping Season Go Agentic?“ found that roughly 132 million people have made a retail purchase with AI assistance, while 22% now begin online retail research in an artificial intelligence tool.

For brands, the opportunity is potentially lower-friction conversion. The risk is that another platform increasingly determines which products enter the consumer’s consideration set.

The Next Retail Advantage Is Who Controls the Handoff

Walmart’s robotics and Amazon’s conversational AI appear to address opposite ends of the retail value chain. One seeks to improve the physical movement of merchandise. The other seeks to improve the identification and conversion of consumer demand.

But both can strengthen the position of the platform that controls the infrastructure.

Walmart’s modernization illustrates how operational standards can affect the economics of supplier participation. Amazon’s AI expansion illustrates how ownership of the consumer interface can influence access to demand.

Walmart is working to control the transition from supplier inventory to automated fulfillment. Amazon is expanding its ability to connect consumer conversations with product discovery and shopping.

These are different operations, but they share a commercial characteristic: Whoever establishes the rules at the handoff can influence the economics of everyone participating.

That influence does not guarantee profits. Walmart’s automation difficulties demonstrate that owning infrastructure can bring significant capital, maintenance and execution costs. Amazon’s Bee expansion faces unresolved questions about consumer adoption, privacy expectations and whether personalized recommendations meaningfully change purchasing behavior.

Project Status

October 2026: Northwestern IT is modernizing the University's telephone services by transitioning from Cisco to Microsoft Teams Voice. This change will better reflect how individuals and teams use phones across campus and provide a more integrated communications experience by bringing calls, voicemail, meetings, and messaging together in Microsoft Teams. Northwestern IT is partnering with technology teams across the University to plan a collaborative rollout of these changes between January 2027 and June 2028.

Background

As part of this transition, Northwestern IT is replacing the University-wide Cisco telephony platform and devices with Microsoft Teams Voice. Microsoft Teams Voice provides equivalent calling services and introduces a modern communications platform designed to support how people work today. The new service will offer calling options on computers, mobile devices, and Teams-certified phones. While core calling capabilities will remain available, some features and workflows will function differently than they do today.

Benefits to the Northwestern Community

Microsoft Teams Voice will modernize Northwestern's telephone service by integrating University calling into Microsoft Teams. This transition will maintain essential calling capabilities while delivering a more unified communications experience for calls, voicemail, meetings, and messaging. It will also simplify the telephony environment by reducing dependence on aging Cisco infrastructure and underutilized desk phones.

Connected experience: Manage calls, voicemail, meetings, and messaging in Microsoft Teams.

Flexible calling: Use a University number from a computer, mobile device, or approved Teams phone.

Modern service: Retire aging infrastructure and reduce the number of underused physical devices.

Goals and Objectives

The Teams Voice transition is designed to preserve essential telephone services while enabling schools, departments, and administrative units to adopt a modern, flexible communications platform that supports how people work today.

Preserve assigned University phone numbers and core calling capabilities.

Enable eligible users to make and receive calls through Teams desktop and mobile applications.

Migrate shared lines, call groups, and other existing services accurately.

Prepare affected users with guidance and support before and after migration.

Deliver a consistent calling experience across computers, mobile devices, and approved Teams-certified phones.

Provide Teams-certified phones where approved business requirements exist.

Minimize disruption to University operations throughout the transition.

Reduce complexity and ongoing costs by retiring aging telephony infrastructure and removing unused or underutilized desk phones.

Approach

The project will be implemented over 18 months in coordinated phases by school, unit, or department.

title: As Albertsons embarks on a turnaround, what role will CX play? - Yahoo Finance
description:

text:
This story was originally published on CX Dive. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily CX Dive newsletter.

As Albertsons struggles with its second straight quarter of same-store sales declines, company leaders are turning to better in-store CX and streamlining operations to improve the business.

The grocer has launched a number of initiatives with good reason and intentions, but it has created too many layers of complexity over time, CEO Susan Morris said on a Q2 2026 earnings call Tuesday. Now, Albertsons is turning its focus to a few areas that will create greater value for shoppers.

"We must deliver more consistently for our customers," Morris said on the earnings call. "Price matters, promotions matter, freshness matters, convenience, selection and customer service matter. Our job going forward is to deliver all of those things better than we do today."

Albertsons wants to sharpen its value perception, according to Morris. The amount customers are willing to pay is important, but aspects such as product variety, services and ease of shopping are vital as well.

"Our goal is not to be the cheapest guy in town, but rather to have the right balanced value proposition that resonates with the customers that we serve uniquely by market," Morris said.

Albertsons has its work cut out for it. The grocer's comparable store sales declined just shy of 1% year over year in the second quarter of 2026, according to an earnings report. Digital sales rose 11% year over year, but net sales and other revenue dipped 0.1% year over year to $18.9 billion.

The grocer's plans include strategic price cuts, but it is avoiding broad-based price reductions. Instead, it's making strategic price investments on a more individualized level via tools like the Albertsons for U loyalty program.

"It's about our ability to leverage our very, very strong loyalty program and create personalized offers that may mean something very different to me as a consumer than it might to you as a consumer," Morris said.

Getting the in-store experience right

As Albertsons pursues streamlining its operations, it must "double down on the basics," Morris said. That includes getting the right products inside store formats customers enjoy.

Albertsons stores may be functional, but they fail to offer customers inspiration or excitement, according to Neil Saunders, managing director at GlobalData Retail.

"There's also not nearly enough newness in the offer to showcase new brands and new products," Saunders said in an email. "The whole experience is extremely average, below par even, but when the prices are expensive, that's simply not good enough."

One issue is that Albertsons' stores feel like they "were made for a different era," Saunders said. They tend to be too large for what modern customers expect from a grocer, but Albertsons has let them be rather than invest in reconfiguring the layouts.

Streamlining operations to improve the in-store experience

The grocer's efforts to streamline its store operations and experience plans may include layoffs and closing stores in underperforming markets, according to Morris.

Albertsons has already reduced complexity by cutting the number of regional divisions from 11 to four in July. The change has CX implications, as the regional executive vice presidents who oversee the new divisions were charged with elevating store conditions and keeping store teams focused on taking care of customers, according to Morris.

"With that kind of focus on elevating store standards and execution, it eliminates the distractions from all the noise happening around us," Morris said. "Our team knows that we have essentially two roles in our company: We either serve customers directly or we serve those that serve customers."

Store execution is one of the key areas where Albertsons sees early opportunities for improvement, according to Morris. The company will reduce shrink, raise standards and commit to offering the best training for associates.

"These steps and more, taken together, will improve the customer experience and ultimately our business results," Morris said.

Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), which has been building its own custom AI chips for longer than any of its competitors, has seen strong adoption of its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) by its Google Cloud customers for training and inference. Apple used TPUs to train Apple Intelligence, and Anthropic is using gigawatts worth of TPUs to develop its large language models.

While Nvidia can continue to grow sales extremely quickly, other chipmakers' growth rates are likely to outpace it. That's reflected in its P/E valuation, which now sits below those of its biggest rivals.

Microsoft could be Marvell's fastest-growing customer

During its 2026 investor day this month, Marvell said it expects that it will grow its share of the custom AI accelerator market over the next five years. Its work on the Maia 300 is likely a big reason why. Microsoft's plan to make that processor the primary inference system for its products and services is in line with earlier reports that it will make a big step up in custom silicon orders starting next year.

The revenue opportunity for Marvell is huge. Microsoft will spend approximately $175 billion in capital expenditures on data centers over the next year. Roughly two-thirds of that will go toward servers and networking equipment. If Marvell takes just a sliver of that spending, it would amount to a huge boost to its revenue, which totaled just $9.5 billion over the last four quarters.

Marvell believes the combination of its custom AI chips and its networking chips will help it grow revenue tenfold over the next five years. That is to say, Microsoft's ramp-up in Maia chips is just the start. Marvell also signed a deal with Google earlier this year to design and sell inference-optimized versions of its TPU chips. The deal also gives Alphabet the option to take a stake in Marvell.

Considering Marvell's growth potential, the stock's forward P/E of 63 looks inexpensive. If you look out to its fiscal 2029 (which mostly takes place in calendar 2028), the stock trades at just 21 times earnings estimates. Given its potential to capture a significant slice of the market for data center AI processors, that seems like a good price to pay.

text:
Carbon removal buyer coalition Frontier announced new offtake agreements with carbon sequestration technology company 44.01, on behalf of purchasers including Stripe, Google and Shopify, alongside Autodesk, H&M Group and Workday, based on 44.01’s process to turn CO2 into rock.

The agreement, worth $11.7 million will see nearly 21,000 tonnes of CO2 permanently removed between 2028 and 2031.

Founded in Oman in 2020, 44.01 provides solutions to eliminate CO2 captured from the air or from hard-to-abate industrial processes by turning it into rock, through its technology to accelerate the natural process of CO2 mineralization. The company’s solution takes captured CO2 and dissolves it in water, creating an acidic solution that mobilizes cations within rock that reacts with the CO2 and mineralizes it, and injects the fluid deep underground, where high pressure, temperature and high CO2 concentration causes a rapid mineralization process.

The company recently launched a project with building materials company Holcim in the UAE aimed at capturing, permanently storing, and mineralizing CO2 from cement production.

According to 44.01, the new Frontier-backed project will be the first of its kind at commercial scale to combine biogenic CO₂ with permanent storage through mineralization, and will provide operating data to inform the development of larger projects as the company works to establish in-situ mineralization as an economically viable, scalable global CO2 storage solution for permanent carbon removal and industrial decarbonization.

Talal Hasan, CEO of 44.01, said:

“This agreement marks an important step for 44.01: moving our technology from demonstration to commercial deployment. Frontier and its buyers are backing a fundamentally different approach to permanent carbon removal — turning captured CO₂ into rock. Our focus is now on delivering at commercial scale, continuously improving performance and driving down costs, so that more customers can benefit from this technology.”

Frontier recently announced that it raised $915 million from corporate buyers including Stripe, Google, Shopify, Salesforce, H&M Group, and Anthropic, doubling the initiative’s funding, and said that it will prioritize concentrating its purchases on a narrower portfolio of companies where it sees high conviction of gigaton-scale potential on the supply side, and requiring a clear line of sight to robust, long-term demand in every deal on the demand side. The new agreement marks Frontier’s first purchase of carbon removal using in-situ mineralization, and in the Middle East.

Hannah Bebbington Valori, Head of Frontier said:

“Where we can store CO₂ shouldn’t limit where we can remove it. In-situ mineralization could expand the storage map, making permanent storage practical in places conventional storage can’t economically reach. That’s why we’repurchasing from 44.01: to prove out the technology and ready it for commercial scale.”
