Interest in the future of data center infrastructure is so high that the organizer of this week's OCP Global Summit in Silicon Valley said it has reached “maximum capacity” and would refuse entry for anyone not registered, even those who already booked travel.

With a record 15,000 people reportedly attending the event organized by the Meta-founded Open Compute Project, major semiconductor companies Intel, AMD and Nvidia showed off how they will power future AI data centers with new disclosures, many of which are based around the standardized server specifications championed by OCP.

[Related: How Intel’s AI Chip Strategy Is Coming Into Shape After Years Of Struggles]

These disclosures included new details for Intel’s upcoming air-cooled data center GPU, new server racks packing more than 46,000 cores’ worth of Intel Xeon CPUs, a new flexible server rack reference design from AMD, the first AMD EPYC CPU to include an LPDDR memory interface as well as open-source and Vera Rubin news from Nvidia.

Some of these announcements were aimed at partners and customers building data centers for agentic AI workloads, especially when it came to the CPU-related news because of how important the processor type has become for enabling such applications. Others, on the other hand, are meant to help with the broader AI data center buildout.

While Nvidia is far ahead of Intel and AMD in the AI infrastructure market in terms of revenue, all three companies are needed to help channel partners fulfill the ongoing buildout of AI data centers, according to Bob Venero, CEO of Fort Lauderdale, Fla.-based solution provider Future Tech Enterprise, which ranked No. 90 on CRN’s 2026 Solution Provider 500.

“The channel needs AMD, Intel and Nvidia to continue to push the limits,” he said.

Though hyperscalers and neoclouds are building much of the data center capacity to support agentic AI right now, Venero sees a huge opportunity for the channel to help enterprises secure their own infrastructure due to security and cost concerns.

“Customers are definitely figuring this out because they spent a ton of money and blew through their token budgets because they let [AI] agents run unregulated within their organizations,” he said. “So you’re seeing customers now more looking at, ‘Hey, how do we control costs? How do we drive these agents internally that will use our internal models and do things that are not necessarily cloud-based but on-prem?’”

What follows are the most important details from these six big OCP 2026 announcements.

Intel Details 480-GB D-Series GPU For Air-Cooled Servers

Intel revealed that its upcoming 480-GB “Crescent Island” data center GPU for AI inference will be known as the Intel GPU D-series and feature up to 1.3 petaflops of 8-bit floating-point compute within a 350-watt power envelope.

The chipmaker said that the D-series GPU, which is sampling with customers now, will come in a standard, air-cooled PCIe form factor that will make it easy to slot into existing data centers, with up to eight PCIe cards per server.

Intel said it’s working with a “broad ecosystem” of OEMs, ODMs, neoclouds, ISVs, appliance providers and AI-native companies to bring the GPU D-series into production. These vendors include Asus, Cisco, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo, Supermicro, NetApp, Nutanix, IBM-owned Red Hat and Broadcom-owned VMware.

The GPU D-series represents Intel’s latest attempt to gain a foothold in the AI accelerator chip market after previous efforts, including its Gaudi line of chips, failed to catch traction. The new product makes use of the company’s new Xe3P architecture, which stems from the Xe architecture it began developing for client and server GPUs several years ago.

The semiconductor giant said the GPU D-series is designed for large language models, long-context workloads and concurrent services, with a single card supporting models with up to 300 billion parameters and an 8-GPU system supporting up to 1 trillion parameters.

The new product line is set to go head-to-head with Nvidia’s RTX Pro 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, which features 2 petaflops of 8-bit floating-point compute (FP8), 4 petaflops of 4-bit floating-point compute (FP4) and 96 GB of GDDR7 memory in a PCIe form factor that can be configured to consume up to 600 watts.

While Nvidia does not divulge the difference in performance between the air- and liquid-cooled versions of the RTX Pro 6000 on its website, a head-to-head comparison of public specifications to the Intel GPU D-series puts the former card ahead in terms of FP8 performance and offering FP4 support, which can help applications run faster.

The GPU D-series, however, packs far more memory, 480 GB, with roughly the same memory bandwidth at 1.5 TBps despite using LPDDR5X. And it seems to offer greater power efficiency by fitting 1.3 petaflops of FP8 compute into only 350 watts.

Intel said the GPU D-series falls in line with its strategy to offer open systems and software architecture that allows developers to easily deploy workloads on the right hardware.

New Intel Xeon Server Racks Pack 46,000 CPU Cores For Agentic AI

Intel showed off new server rack designs that can pack more 46,000 cores’ worth of the company’s Xeon 6+ CPUs for agentic AI workloads.

These rack designs come from server vendors such as Asus, Gigabyte and Supermicro. Many of them are based on the Open Compute Project’s Open Rack v3 standard to, in Intel’s words, “simplify deployment and integration within open data center infrastructure.”

The semiconductor giant made the display as it experiences a surge in demand for CPUs due to the meteoric rise of agentic AI workloads in data centers.

The server racks at the OCP Global Summit were designed with high densities of CPUs to “orchestrate workloads, process data, manage I/O and execute tasks that keep” accelerator chips such as GPUs running at full speed,” the chipmaker said.

In some configurations, these server racks can fit more than 46,000 cores from Intel’s Xeon 6+ processors in a rack power envelope of 133.45 kilowatts, according to the company.

Launched over the summer, the Xeon 6+ processors, code-named “Clearwater Forest,” feature up to 288 efficiency cores in a 450-watt power envelope.

AMD Reveals Flexible ‘Helion’ Server Rack Design For Agentic AI

AMD revealed a flexible server rack reference design called “Helion” that enables partners to customize compute needs for customers running agentic AI workloads.

Calling Helion an “open blueprint,” the chip designer said it’s based on an Open Compute Project spec-design that can use EPYC CPUs and Instinct GPUs—or just the CPUs.

AMD said server vendors plan to release Helion rack configurations starting this November. Supporting vendors include Cisco, Dell Technologies, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro.

It’s yet another move by AMD to challenge Nvidia’s dominance of the AI infrastructure market and keep the pressure on other rivals such as Intel, particularly as agentic AI workloads creates unprecedented demand for CPUs.

The idea with Helion is to let customers “match CPU performance, core density and power with GPU acceleration for the work their AI agents perform,” AMD said.

This means customers can create “virtually any configuration” to meet their workload requirements, and this includes options for liquid- and air-cooled versions of Helion.

For instance, AMD said a CPU-only rack with 6th-Gen EPYC processors can pack up to 32,768 cores for hyperscalers that need “dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure.”

Helion can also enable an all-in-one rack that brings together “AMD EPYC CPU nodes, AMD Instinct MI350P GPU nodes and general-purpose compute on one platform” for enterprise customers running agentic AI workloads, according to the company.

Nvidia Open-Sources Run:ai, Other AI Data Center Software

Nvidia said it has made software components for various aspects of running AI data centers, including Run:ai, available under open-source licenses.

The vendor said it’s open-sourcing these software components as part of its DSX AI Factory platform, which brings together software libraries, workflow guides and reference designs to help partners and customers maximize tokens per watt in AI data centers.

The push is part of Nvidia’s strategy to provide a “vertically integrated” platform that is “horizontally open,” which has become a common line by the company this year.

The most notable move is with Run:ai, the Kubernetes-based workload management and orchestration software that Nvidia acquired for a reported $700 million in late 2024.

When Nvidia announced the acquisition earlier that year, the company said it planned to use Run:ai to boost its DGX Cloud, which launched in 2023 as a full-stack commercial service that was meant to simplify AI training in public cloud environments.

However, the company switched gears in late 2025 when it reportedly restructured the DGX Cloud business and shifted its focus to an “internal cloud environment for building and operating AI,” as Nvidia’s web page for DGX Cloud now says.

With the open-source move, Nvidia said, “it is now possible for every NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner and AI cloud to increase workload throughput, improve GPU utilization, and operate shared AI infrastructure more efficiently and effectively.”

This involves making available the full Run:ai platform as well as individual components: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management and Workload Map. Partners and customers can determine whether to adopt the full platform, use it to build their own products or integrate individual components, according to Nvidia.

Outside of Run:ai, the company said it open-sourced software components for “configuring networks, validating clusters, managing racks and provisioning bare metal.”

These components, originally designed for DGX Cloud, consist of Nvidia Config Manager, Nvidia Cluster Readiness Engine, Nvidia Rack Management Service and Cluster API Provider for Nvidia Infrastructure Controller.

With the software components, Nvidia said, cloud providers and software partners can “integrate AI factory capabilities directly into their multi-tenant platforms.”

Nvidia Contributes Vera Rubin MGX Rack Design To OCP

Nvidia said it has contributed the third generation of its MGX AI data center reference design to help manufacturers build interoperable platforms around the AI infrastructure giant’s Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPU server racks.

“Combined with open liquid-cooling technologies such as MQD and MQDB, the effort helps turn proven AI factory designs into industry standards that others can adopt, manufacture and scale,” the company said.

The MGX 1.2 specification, as it is called, features “rack-scale blind-mate liquid cooling, interoperable rack-scale interconnect infrastructure and liquid-cooled 5,000-amp busbar designed for higher-power AI systems,” according to Nvidia.

The vendor said the spec also expands the modularity of MGX with “configurable I/O bays, fanless liquid-cooled compute trays, standardized power and cooling interfaces.

“It improves assembly, test and service times to streamline manufacturing and field service to enable faster and more efficient infrastructure buildout,” the AI infrastructure giant wrote. “The architecture supports rack deployments up to 250kW while simplifying serviceability, deployment and infrastructure reuse.”

text:
US lawmakers have unveiled a new bill to hold Wall Street’s “Epstein-connected” bosses to account for helping finance the late sex offender’s crimes.

It came as top Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren condemned the UK bank Barclays for “dodging responsibility” over its failure to vet former boss Jes Staley and his ties to the once well-connected billionaire.

A bipartisan group of politicians, led by Warren and House representative Robert Garcia, are introducing a bill on Thursday known as the Epstein Wall Street Records Act. The bill follows a months-long investigation into the financier, who died in prison in 2019 while awaiting trial on child sex-trafficking charges.

If passed, the bill would force regulators including the Federal Reserve and the Securities and Exchange Commission to investigate “Epstein connected” financial firms and executives for potential breaches of banking, investment or illicit funding laws; and fine or even ban wrongdoers from the US financial sector.

The bill – which is also being backed by House Republican Thomas Massie – will also force regulators to publicly disclose any records relating to Epstein and his associates; and refer any potential criminal violations to the US justice department.

Warren said: “Since the big banks won’t hold themselves accountable – and the Trump administration won’t either – Congress must act to force real transparency and accountability for them and their executives who enabled Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes.”

News of the bill came as Warren condemned the bosses at Barclays, one of the UK’s biggest banks, over their failure to adequately answer questions about its former chief executives Jes Staley and his links to Epstein.

Staley’s ties with the well-connected billionaire spelled the end of his career. The American banker resigned from Barclays in November 2021, after UK regulators started investigating the true nature of his relationship with Epstein, whom he met in 2000 during his three-decade stint at JP Morgan.

The Financial Conduct Authority’s original investigation, triggered by a cache of more than 1,200 emails between Staley and Epstein, concluded that the pair were “indeed close” and had a relationship that “went beyond one that was professional in nature”.

Staley was eventually banned from the UK’s financial sector in 2023 for playing down those ties, and failed to overturn that decision in a court battle that revealed intimate details of the pair’s friendship last year.

That included Staley admitting to having sex with a member of Epstein’s staff in New York – an encounter he said was “consensual”. The case also revived a 2010 exchange referring to Disney princesses, in which Staley said: “That was fun. Say hi to Snow White.” Staley denied knowledge of the exchange during a UK court hearing.

After the loss of his legal challenge against the FCA, Staley said he was disappointed by the outcome but was “never dishonest”.

In July, Warren and a team of House Democrats wrote to the Barclays chair, Nigel Higgins, asking how it had vetted its former chief executive, and whether the bank had investigated potential “deficiencies” in its executive hiring process, given it had “allowed the board to hire a CEO who held extensive professional and personal ties to a convicted sex offender”.

Barclays has since responded with a letter from its head of US government relations, Lance Williams, that Warren said was not sufficient.

The letter focused on the findings of the UK regulators’ investigation. Williams stressed that Staley had “concealed information about his actions and the nature of his relationship with Mr Epstein” and only after Staley’s resignation had “previously unknown information come to light through various public disclosures”.

“This information paints a fundamentally different picture of Mr Staley than what he presented to Barclays,” Williams said, noting that Barclays had relied on external executive search firms to recruit Staley in 2015, when he was “known for his accomplishments in the banking industry”.

Warren said Barclays’ lacklustre response illustrated why it was time for regulators to launch formal investigations into Wall Street’s ties to Epstein: “Barclays continues to dodge responsibility over its apparent failure to vet its former CEO Jes Staley’s close professional and personal ties to Epstein.”

Barclays declined to comment. Staley’s legal representatives were contacted for comment.

text:
© Jo Panuwat D - stock.adobe.com

In 2027, Medicare will enter an important transition in its continued evolution toward accountable care. The Long-term Enhanced Accountable Care Organization Design (LEAD) Model will begin a 10-year test intended to make accountable care more stable, inclusive and responsive to patients with complex needs.

Additionally, next year the Comprehensive Kidney Care Contracting (CKCC) Model, Medicare’s principal accountable care model for people with advanced kidney disease, is scheduled to sunset. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) has not announced whether accountable kidney care will continue through an extension, a successor model or a defined specialty track within LEAD.

The parallel timing of LEAD and CKCC allows CMS to preserve and strengthen accountable kidney care, just as LEAD builds on lessons from nearly 15 years of primary care-based accountable care models. As CMS designs the next generation of accountable care, it must preserve a dedicated model for kidney care. The clinical improvements achieved through CKCC, combined with CMS’s recent financial reforms, make a strong case for building on the model. Allowing it to end without a successor risks losing the clinical infrastructure and provider investments built over the life of the model.

Keith Bellovich, D.O., MBA

Mary Dittrich, M.D., FASN

Jeffrey Giullian, M.D., MBA

Carney Taylor, M.D., MBA

Heather Trafton, MBA

Patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (CKD) and end-stage renal disease (ESRD) are among Medicare’s most clinically complex beneficiaries. They frequently live with multiple chronic conditions, experience 1.5 hospitalizations per person-year, and require intensive care coordination across providers and care settings.

As a result, this population generates outsized cost for the health care system. According to the United States Renal Data System (USRDS), the cost of care for the 3.8 million Medicare fee-for-service (FFS) beneficiaries living with CKD increased to $141.1 billion in 2023, accounting for 36% of total 2023 costs. The yearly per-person cost for Medicare FFS beneficiaries who live with CKD was more than $31,000 in 2023, according to USRDS, about 2.5 times the cost for Medicare FFS beneficiaries without CKD, diabetes or heart failure. For Medicare FFS beneficiaries receiving in-center hemodialysis, annual spending averaged more than $103,000 per person in 2023, according to USRDS.

Despite the need for higher levels of care and more coordination, traditional FFS payment models do not reliably support the interdisciplinary teams, patient education, clinical analytics, medication management, transition planning and continuous outreach necessary to coordinate this complex care. Today, nearly half of patients with Stage 4-5 CKD do not see a nephrologist, and up to 70% begin dialysis unexpectedly in an acute setting, according to USRDS, leading to poorer outcomes and significantly higher Medicare spending.

CKCC was designed to address this fragmentation in care. Kidney Contracting Entities bring nephrologists together with transplant providers and, in many cases, kidney care organizations and other partners. They invest in care coordination and accept accountability for the quality and total cost of their patients’ care. Unlike a model built primarily around a patient’s relationship with a primary care practice, CKCC recognizes that as kidney disease advances, the nephrologist is frequently the principal clinician managing the patient’s care, with the expertise to drive improved outcomes.

The model is working. CKCC encourages organizations to develop interventions tailored to the kidney disease continuum, such as slowing progression where possible, preparing patients for dialysis before a crisis occurs, increasing the uptake of home dialysis, improving access to kidney transplantation and educating patients to make informed decisions about their care.

The second independent evaluation of the model, released earlier this year, found significant improvements across several measures closely linked to patients’ experiences and outcomes. Optimal starts to treatment for ESRD increased by 31%. Home dialysis increased by 10%, home dialysis training increased by 22%, and preemptive transplant waitlisting increased by 37%. Patients in the model also reported receiving more information about their treatment options, while patient activation scores improved over time.

Kidney care needs a dedicated place in accountable care

The CMS Innovation Center now faces a consequential choice about the future of specialty-led accountable care. LEAD creates new opportunities to integrate specialists into accountable care, but it remains organized around primary care.

One of those tools is CMS-Administered Risk Arrangements (CARA), a voluntary LEAD initiative that allows accountable care organizations (ACOs) to establish episode-based risk arrangements with specialty providers. Through CARA, ACOs and specialists can negotiate target prices for defined episodes of care and share accountability for their cost and performance.

CARA could strengthen specialist participation in accountable care, but it is not a substitute for a kidney-specific model built around longitudinal, nephrologist-led accountability. Patients with advanced kidney disease require sustained management across CKD, dialysis, transplantation and supportive care — not accountability limited to individual episodes of care.

A specialist arrangement within a broader ACO may complement that work, but it does not necessarily replicate the focused accountability, clinical expertise and care coordination that CKCC was designed to provide. As kidney disease progresses, nephrologists often become the clinicians most responsible for treatment decisions, care coordination and patient outcomes.

As CMS shapes the next generation of accountable care, it should determine how to preserve a model for accountable kidney care, whether through a dedicated successor model, a clearly defined track within LEAD where patients align through nephrologists, or an extension of CKCC while a longer-term approach is developed.

CKCC’s early results do not tell the whole story

By law, the Innovation Center must design models that either generate savings for Medicare, improve quality or — ideally — both. But formal evaluations, like those for all but a handful of models CMS has tested, have found that the models have resulted in a net increase in Medicare spending after accounting for incentive payments. The most recent evaluation found CKCC increased net Medicare spending by an estimated $275 million in 2023.

CMS responded to the model’s early spending results by making substantial changes beginning in 2026. The agency increased benchmark discounts, reduced the CKD Quarterly Capitation Payment, eliminated the kidney transplant bonus and extended CKCC through 2027. CMS stated these changes were intended to improve the model’s financial performance while preserving its quality gains.

An independent actuarial analysis by Wakely Consulting Group illustrates how consequential those changes may be. Wakely applied the 2026 payment policies retrospectively to historical financial data. It estimated that the revised policies would have reduced total model payments by approximately 45% in 2023 and 40% in 2024. Under that counterfactual analysis, the model would have generated an estimated $26 million in net savings to CMS in 2023 and $90 million in 2024. Those potential net savings jump to $112 million and $118 million in 2023 and 2024, respectively, if current model participants were in full-risk tracks. Those findings tell us that policy makers should not rely solely on financial results from a model design that CMS has already substantially revised.

The Wakely analysis also reinforces a key lesson from Medicare payment reform. Accountable care models rarely reach their full potential immediately. Building clinical infrastructure, integrating data, changing practice patterns and engaging patients takes time. The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), for example, did not generate cumulative net savings for CMS until its fifth year, yet has since produced substantial and sustained savings. In 2024 alone, MSSP generated more than $6.6 billion in savings and returned $2.5 billion back to CMS. CKCC deserves the same opportunity to mature under its revised financial structure before a final judgment is made about its long-term value.

A road map for the future

A successor could take several forms: an additional extension of CKCC, a refined kidney-specific model or a dedicated specialty track within LEAD. Whatever form the next model takes, its design should preserve the progress already made while addressing the operational and financial barriers that could undermine long-term participation.

First, CMS should expand access for patients and nephrologists. Model participation should be managed at the tax identification number level, consistent with LEAD, while allowing providers in hospital systems, multispecialty groups and academic institutions to seek exceptions when overlap rules would otherwise prevent participation.

Beneficiary alignment should similarly reflect how kidney care is delivered. A 12-month look-back based on qualifying nephrology services would create a clearer and more current connection between patients and participating providers. CMS should also establish an appropriate pathway for patients with Stage 3B CKD, when education, medication management and earlier intervention are critical to delay progression.

Second, the financial methodology must accurately reflect the complexity and changing health status of the population. Patients with Stage 4 or 5 CKD and ESRD should be treated as high-needs beneficiaries, with a consistent concurrent risk-adjustment methodology that captures disease progression and changes in treatment status during the year.

Benchmarks and trends should also be based on the populations served. Spending trends for patients with late-stage CKD should reflect their experiences, not those of the broader Medicare population. CMS should avoid policies that punish organizations for savings they have already produced, preserve prior savings and maintain advance shared savings payments that support up-front investment. Benchmark discounts should be limited to 3%, with the discount for ESRD applied only to nondialysis spending, as dialysis costs are largely nondiscretionary and difficult for participants to influence.

Third, quality accountability should be meaningful, predictable and proportionate. CMS should reduce the quality withhold to 3%, consistent with LEAD. Kidney care measures frequently involve small denominators and year-to-year variation that may not reflect genuine differences in care. A smaller, better-targeted withholding would preserve a strong incentive for improvement without making financial performance excessively dependent on statistical volatility.

The model should focus on three or four measures that participants can understand and influence. Optimal Starts and the Patient Activation Measure should remain central and be supported by more timely data and clearer calculation methods. A hospitalization or readmission measure could also be appropriate if benchmarked against comparable kidney populations and incorporating kidney-specific acuity.

Finally, CMS should evaluate the model that exists today, not only the version that operated in its earliest years. Formal evaluations should continue to report observed results in accordance with the policies in place during each performance year. But CMS should also publicly reassess earlier years using the major design changes now governing CKCC, including reduced capitation payments, stronger savings guarantees, elimination of transplant bonuses, changes to skin substitute payment and the removal of providers that have exited the model. This would help policy makers distinguish between the effects of specialty-led care delivery and the consequences of an early payment design that CMS has already changed.

Together, these refinements would create a model or track that is easier to enter, more stable to operate, more accurate in measuring financial performance and more focused on outcomes that matter to patients.

Build on what Medicare has begun

CKCC has demonstrated that specialty-focused accountability can change how kidney care is delivered. Patients are more likely to begin dialysis under optimal conditions, use home dialysis, receive earlier consideration for a transplant and obtain information that helps them make consequential decisions about their care.

CMS has already revised the features most responsible for the model’s early net spending. The rational next step is to assess those changes, preserve the clinical infrastructure that has been built and establish a stable long-term program for accountable kidney care.

Medicare is designing the next generation of accountable care. Patients with advanced kidney disease — and the specialists who care for them — must have a clear place in it.

text:
AstraZeneca adds an AI discovery partner for liver and heart disease, with $40 million upfront and no efficacy or safety data yet reported. Credit: Stock.Adobe.com/Askar

AstraZeneca has signed a drug discovery collaboration and licensing agreement with insitro to apply artificial intelligence (AI) to target identification and therapeutic design in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH) and cardiomyopathies, the companies announced Oct. 15.1,2 Insitro will receive $40 million upfront and is eligible for up to approximately $1.46 billion in milestones.1,2

Sharon Barr, executive vice president and head of BioPharmaceuticals research and development at AstraZeneca, tied the agreement to target selection: “We know that disease biology is incredibly complex, and one of the most critical decisions in R&D is selecting the right target. This strategic collaboration underscores our commitment to maximizing the potential of cutting-edge AI to tackle the root cause of disease. Partnering with insitro, we will use advanced AI to identify the biological drivers of disease to support the rapid discovery of high-quality novel targets, advancing our ambition to deliver the next generation of medicines to patients faster.”1

“MASH and cardiomyopathies are prevalent, underdiagnosed diseases where high-content data holds immense potential for uncovering disease drivers. By applying AI to these complex datasets, we can unlock greater discovery power and reveal novel genetic insights.”

What are AstraZeneca and insitro agreeing to do?

Insitro will use its Virtual Human platform to identify causal disease biology in both indications and advance AstraZeneca-nominated targets from discovery to development candidate.1,2 The platform combines large-scale human and cellular data with AI-enabled target identification and medicine design.1

AstraZeneca will take the clinical development and regulatory work and holds exclusive worldwide rights to the selected programs; insitro’s release adds that AstraZeneca will also lead commercialization.1,2

Beyond the upfront payment, insitro is eligible for single-digit royalties on global sales.1,2 The two releases describe the milestones slightly differently: AstraZeneca cites development and commercial milestones, while insitro includes discovery milestones.1,2

The upfront payment represents less than 3% of the combined headline value, and neither company disclosed the number of targets, program timelines or payment schedule.

Why are MASH and cardiomyopathies difficult to treat?

Insitro’s release says each disease is defined by heterogeneity, with a single diagnostic label covering patients whose underlying biology differs, which has complicated treatment.2

Daphne Koller, Ph.D., founder and CEO of insitro, said: “MASH and cardiomyopathies are prevalent, underdiagnosed diseases where high-content data holds immense potential for uncovering disease drivers. By applying AI to these complex datasets, we can unlock greater discovery power and reveal novel genetic insights. Our platform simultaneously deconvolutes disease biology and identifies causal drivers of disease pathologies. Partnering with AstraZeneca allows us to pair our deep biological precision with their pharmaceutical expertise and scale with potential for accelerated advancement of novel programs through development and to patients.”2

In MASH, the treatment landscape has changed recently. The FDA approved resmetirom (Rezdiffra) in March 2024 under its accelerated approval pathway for adults with noncirrhotic disease and moderate to advanced liver scarring, to be used with diet and exercise. The agency, which at the time referred to the condition as nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, said patients had previously lacked a medication that directly addressed their liver damage, and cited an estimate of 6 million to 8 million U.S. patients at that disease stage.3

The cardiomyopathy picture is less defined in the releases, which do not specify which forms are in scope. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the most common inherited cardiovascular disorder, is estimated to affect 1 in 500 people, and a published review notes that existing studies may have underestimated its prevalence.4

That offers one illustration of the underdiagnosis Koller describes, though it should not be read as the collaboration’s target population.

How does the collaboration fit each company’s portfolio?

AstraZeneca describes cardiovascular, renal and metabolism as one of its main disease areas and a key growth driver, with an emphasis on the links among the heart, kidneys, liver and pancreas.1 A program spanning a liver disease and heart muscle diseases fits within that framing.

Insitro says it has built a multimodal corpus of human and cellular data since 2018 and is advancing nine programs, including genetic regulators of liver fat and fibrosis expected to enter the clinic in early 2027.2 The company reports more than $750 million in capital and existing collaborations with Bristol Myers Squibb, Lilly and Gilead.2

The release does not say how its internal liver programs relate to targets AstraZeneca will nominate.

What remains unknown about the collaboration?

No candidate, efficacy data or safety data accompany the announcement, and the collaboration sits at the discovery stage. Targets identified through AI-driven analysis of human data will still need validation through preclinical work and clinical trials, where heterogeneity of disease could also affect trial design.

Milestone and royalty figures are potential payments contingent on progress that neither company has timed publicly. Neither release addresses market reaction, and independent verification of the platform’s performance in these indications was not available at the time of publication.

text:
Nadella recalled a meeting in around 2008-2009 called by then-chairman Bill Gates to review a potential acquisition involving a team working on parallel data warehousing. Nadella, who was leading Microsoft’s search engine team at the time, thought the deal made little sense.

“I looked at it, [and thought], it is completely architecturally stupid in that time to go buy that,” Nadella said on an episode of the Confession with Ali Partovi podcast released this week. But rather than challenge the proposal, he sat through the review without voicing his concerns.

“It haunts me to think that I may be in a review where there’s somebody in that meeting who sees the future a lot more clearly than I do and the other person presenting—but does not really advocate for it,” Nadella said. “And so that’s what I did.”

He left the meeting thinking it had been a “waste of time.” In hindsight, however, the experience became a reminder of how easy it can be to stay quiet rather than challenge a decision—even when you believe speaking up could lead to a better outcome.

How Steve Ballmer taught Satya Nadella to voice concerns

Nadella admitted that voicing dissent can be difficult at any company, especially one as large as Microsoft. But a conversation with then-Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer helped shape his view of leadership: Employees should think beyond their individual responsibilities and take an “owner mindset,” considering what’s best for the company as a whole.

“Life’s not lived by just being so transactional about everything,” Nadella said. “Because at the end of the day, we all perish, and nobody’s going to look at any balance sheet or income statement. It’s going to be like, hey, ‘How do you live your life?’”

In other words, career success isn’t just about checking off boxes or avoiding conflict. It’s about having the courage to stand up for what you believe is right and helping the company make better decisions—even when that means challenging your colleagues. The key, Nadella said, is learning how to push for the right outcome without putting others on the defensive.

And now that he’s leading the $4 trillion giant, Nadella’s building a culture where employees can consistently speak up and push for the best possible outcome remains a challenge.

“To create an environment in which somebody feels like, ‘Wow, I always want to go for the global maxima’—and to have that be a cultural norm is a tough thing to orchestrate.”

Reed Hastings and Ray Dalio say disagreeing at work isn’t disloyal—it’s essential for success

The ability to respectfully challenge a colleague or boss is a trait many business leaders value—but fostering that kind of candor takes deliberate effort.

Netflix cofounder Reed Hastings has acknowledged that disagreeing with a boss or coworker doesn’t come naturally to most people. At Netflix, however, managers are encouraged to “farm for dissent” among employees.

“To disagree silently is disloyal,” Hastings said in 2024.

Bridgewater Associates founder Ray Dalio has a similar philosophy, boiling the principle down to a simple rule: “Speak up, own it, or get out.”

“Just like everything else, principles need to be questioned and debated,” Dalio wrote. “What you’re not allowed to do is complain and criticize privately– either to others or in your own head. If you can’t fulfill this obligation, then you must go.

Former PepsiCo CEO Indra Nooyi has offered a practical way for leaders to make sure dissenting voices are heard: actively invite them into the conversation.

“At the end of the meeting, the person who is the head of the table should always go around and ask everybody else, ‘Do you have anything else to add,” so that any quiet voices are allowed to speak up,” Nooyi said in a MasterClass course.

“It’s very, very important because sometimes people just feel like they’re not going to be heard, or people talk over them.”

description:

text:
With today's launch of NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, we're collaborating with NVIDIA to help enterprises customize Nemotron open models for the work that matters most to them. We've had early access to the model and have been post-training it ahead of the launch with enterprises like Skydance and EY.

Starting today, this service is available to any enterprise through Scale Post-Training, a new offering within Scale GenAI Portfolio that helps enterprises customize leading open-weight models, including Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and the full Nemotron open model family. Post-training teaches an existing model a particular job using examples of that job done well, turning a general-purpose model into a specialist. For Nemotron, we combine our evaluation methodology, data and training expertise with NVIDIA post-training tools, so enterprises can balance cost, performance and control in building agentic systems and workflows that run natively in their environments.

This collaboration advances our mission to develop reliable AI systems for the world's most important decisions. For more than a decade, our data and evaluations have helped train the world's leading AI models. Now, we're bringing that same work to enterprises customizing open-weight models.

Turning Open Models Into Enterprise Specialists

The question for enterprises is no longer which model is best in general. It's which model is best for a specific job, at a sustainable cost and speed for the business. At production volume, inference costs add up quickly. Deployments will increasingly combine multiple models of different sizes, modalities, providers, strengths and costs, and open-weight models are a growing part of that mix – especially when paired with expert post-training in service of a specific use case or workflow. They can run inside a company's own infrastructure and be tuned to specific tasks, which gives enterprises more control over quality, cost and where their data is processed.

“Open models give enterprises a head start on building with their own data and intelligence,” said Joey Conway, senior director of Nemotron Models and Software at NVIDIA. “With NVIDIA Nemotron open weights, datasets and post-training tools, Scale AI is creating specialized models that boost accuracy with custom business intelligence, powering efficient systems of models for advanced agentic systems and workflows.”

"NVIDIA is giving enterprises open models they can actually make their own, and Nemotron is a big step forward,” said Francis deSouza, CEO of Scale AI. “The future of enterprise AI is multi-model, and the advantage will go to organizations that can prove which model is best for each job. With NVIDIA, Skydance and EY, we’re showing that with Scale Post-Training, an open-weight model can match or outperform the models enterprises run today at a fraction of the cost."

Every general-purpose model – open-weight or closed – starts as a generalist that doesn't know a company's policies, terminology or workflows. Closing these gaps takes more than access to the weights. Someone has to define what "correct" means for each workflow through a representative evaluation dataset, build the data that teaches the model and prove the system is ready for production. This is the work Scale does. We measure the model a customer runs today on tasks from their own workflow, build training and evaluation data for that workflow, find the right post-training recipe, post-train Nemotron with NVIDIA's open tools and test each version inside the same agent workflow it will run in production. Along the way, our engineers contribute improvements back to those tools for the open-source community. Read more about our NVIDIA partnership here.

Enterprises Building With Nemotron

With Skydance, we’re using Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to automate a core finance workflow. The agent reviews vendor credit memos, statements and invoices, many of them scanned, and matches them against the company’s financial records to find credits it’s owed. Tested on real tickets from the production workflow, Nemotron post-trained by Scale matched the accuracy of the frontier model Skydance runs in production today, at about 40x lower inference cost and 5x faster response times.

With EY, we’re building a due diligence agent that answers deal questions by finding and reconciling information across the hundreds of files in an M&A virtual data room. In evaluations across hundreds of questions from held-out data rooms, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL post-trained by Scale matched the accuracy of the frontier model EY uses today, at about one-eighteenth of the inference cost and with answers returned more than twice as fast.

We're also working with a global insurance company on a copilot that helps customer service representatives during live French-language roadside assistance calls, where getting the answer right the first time builds customer trust and keeps costs in check. The copilot pulls out the key facts of each case, recommends the benefits the customer's policy covers and flags when a representative might promise something that policy doesn't include. In controlled evaluations, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with Scale Post-Training was up to 31 percentage points more accurate than the model the company uses in production today, at about a quarter of the inference cost. Learn more about this in our technical blog.

text:
Deloitte has launched Risk Clarity, an AI-native solution designed to support organisations across the enterprise risk life cycle through agentic capabilities.

The offering is delivered through Ascend, Deloitte’s AI-enabled service delivery platform.

Risk Clarity aims to improve consistency, clarity and visibility across enterprise processes, risks and controls, while reducing manual work.

It includes six modules and more than 25 agents covering automated testing, control optimisation, issue management, key risk indicators, process mapping, reporting and risk assessment.

Deloitte said the platform gives clients a single point of access to its industry experience, proprietary data, agentic workflows and alliance technologies.

It can be used throughout the delivery life cycle, from strategy and design to programme management, code generation, data validation and testing.

The company said organisations can use Risk Clarity to replace fragmented and manual risk activities with a more connected, agile and data-driven operating model.

Deloitte Global and US Regulatory, Risk and Forensic leader Gina Primeaux said: “Organisations are under growing pressure to understand risk clearly, act faster, and do so across increasingly complex environments.

“Risk Clarity brings together Deloitte’s deep risk experience, AI-powered intelligence and a modular set of capabilities to help clients modernise how they manage, execute and oversee risk across the enterprise.”

The company added that the modules allow organisations to start with selected use cases and scale deployment over time.

The capabilities include translating regulations into actionable requirements; linking process documentation directly with risks, regulations and controls; and automating risk identification alongside effectiveness scoring.

They also cover reviewing and rationalising controls, automating control testing, and supporting issue creation, early data-quality detection and thematic root-cause analysis.

Human-in-the-loop validation remains part of the process, allowing risk teams to focus on higher-value work and more informed decision-making.

text:
Agilent Technologies, announced on October 13, 2026 that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Proscia, a Philadelphia-based provider of digital pathology software for clinical and life sciences customers. The all-cash transaction is valued at $240 million at closing, with up to an additional $30 million based on achieving future performance milestones.

“Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market,” said Agilent President and CEO Padraig McDonnell. “The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia’s leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data.”

A Central Operating Layer for Digital Pathology

Proscia’s software platform serves as a central operating layer for digital pathology, connecting slide scanners, laboratory information systems, image-analysis applications, AI tools, people, and data so customers can manage images, data, and workflows in one environment. The company serves more than 4,000 laboratories, hospitals, and clinics, as well as 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies, with trailing 12-month revenue exceeding $18 million. Its platform holds FDA 510(k) clearance for primary diagnosis.

“This agreement with Agilent marks an exciting milestone for Proscia and reflects the strength of the platform our team has built,” said David West, Co-Founder and CEO of Proscia. “Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows. I am grateful to the entire Proscia team, whose dedication made this milestone possible, and look forward to building on our work as part of Agilent.”

From Partners to One Company

The acquisition builds on a multi-year distribution agreement Agilent and Proscia signed in September 2022 to offer a comprehensive digital diagnostic pathology system. It also follows Agilent’s recently completed transaction with Biocare Medical. Agilent says the deal will:

Strengthen its pathology portfolio: Agilent’s pathology instruments and reagents will be paired with Proscia’s vendor-agnostic digital pathology platform and established customer base.

Enhance companion diagnostics and drug discovery offerings: Proscia’s growing repository of real-world data offers AI-enabled synergies with Agilent’s companion diagnostics business, adding value for biopharma partners and clinical and translational research customers.

Support long-term growth: Proscia’s recurring-revenue software model adds a high-growth, high-margin business to Agilent’s pathology portfolio.

The transaction is subject to customary closing conditions and is expected to close early in Agilent’s fiscal year 2027. Proscia will then become part of Agilent’s Life Sciences and Diagnostics Markets Group.

About Proscia

Proscia is a Philadelphia-based pathology AI company rewiring pathology for precision medicine across drug discovery, development, and diagnosis. Its Concentriq platform brings intelligence to the scientists, pathologists, and laboratory leaders behind the most critical decisions in medicine, helping more breakthroughs reach the patients they were made for. Proscia is trusted by 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies and was named Global 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology in Europe.

title: CPG, Food & Retail Sector Trends and Upcoming Deals (October 7, 2026)
description:
Which five CPG, food and retail sub-sectors are pulling ahead?
Each sub-sector is indexed against the rest of the CPG, Food & Retail cohort, so 1.00 = the cohort rate.
Custom Furniture Manufacturing contributes 14, Bakery & Confectionery Production 12, Outdoor Apparel Manufacturing 10, Fashion and Apparel Retail 9, and General Retail Stores 6.
A sector reading of 1.20x means CPG, food and retail companies are showing 20% more deal-preparation behaviour than the market.
Each is indexed against the rest of the CPG, food and retail cohort, where 1.00 equals parity.
text:
The CPG, food and retail consolidation story is being told about the wrong companies. The headlines belong to food: McCormick taking Unilever's food business for $44.8 billion, Keurig Dr Pepper absorbing JDE Peet's, Kraft Heinz splitting itself in two, Intersnack paying a 91% premium for Utz. But in the middle market, where Fintent tracks 36,200 CPG, food and retail companies with 26 to 1,000 employees, the sub-sectors actually preparing to sell are apparel manufacturers, apparel retailers, custom furniture makers, bakeries and general-merchandise stores. Food processing, beverage production and personal care manufacturing sit at the bottom of the table.

That gap is the point of this post. The sector as a whole is running an M&A Propensity of 1.20x the all-company baseline, heating up 1.8 points versus last quarter, with the index touching 1.23 — 23% above market. Underneath, the spread runs from 1.63x in outdoor apparel manufacturing to 0.70x in agricultural food processing. A dealmaker covering this sector on the strength of the food headlines is spending time where the mid-market pipeline is thinnest.

Where is CPG, food and retail deal activity actually heading in 2026?

Deal value in consumer markets is being carried by a handful of portfolio-reshaping mega-deals while the number of transactions keeps falling, and the mid-market preparation signal says the next wave comes from discretionary categories, not food. KPMG counted 554 consumer, retail and hospitality deals in Q1 2026, down 23.7% year over year, while value jumped 130.8% to $101.4 billion on McCormick-Unilever Foods and a few peers (kpmg.com). PwC puts CPG deal value up 119% in Q1 versus a year earlier on three transactions worth close to $120 billion combined, and notes that volume has now fallen for four straight years (pwc.com). RSM's October update has consumer products deal volume down roughly 15% in the first half (rsmus.com). Fewer, bigger deals is the shape of the tape.

Fintent's index reads the other end of the market, and it says the cohort is heating up rather than cooling. The 36,200-company CPG, food and retail cohort carries an M&A Propensity of 1.20x the all-company baseline, up 1.8 points on the quarter, with the peak reading still the 1.23 set against 2024-Q4. The 30-day change is a modest -1.0 point, so this is a plateau at an elevated level rather than a spike. Because the index measures pre-announcement behaviour — engagement with investment banks, valuation work, exit and earn-out research — it leads the deal count the trade press reports.

The macro backdrop explains why the preparation is showing up in apparel, furniture and specialty retail first. The Fed raised its target range 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00% on September 16, 2026, in a unanimous vote, citing inflation that "remains elevated" (federalreserve.gov); RSM notes officials signalled one more increase this year and that PE sponsors are extending hold periods and turning to continuation funds as planned exits slip (rsmus.com). Apparel faced a near-record 24.6% average effective tariff rate in 2025 (aafaglobal.org), and 46% of fashion executives expect conditions to worsen in 2026, with tariffs the number-one hurdle (mckinsey.com). PwC's observation that leveraged transactions in the $100 million to $1 billion range "remain difficult to finance" is the mechanism: owners of tariff-exposed, discretionary mid-market businesses are preparing to sell into a market where strategic buyers, not sponsors, set the pace (pwc.com).

So what: the dealmaker's job in this sector right now is coverage reallocation. The food headlines are real but they are large-cap, strategic, and already announced. The mid-market opportunity is in founder- and family-owned apparel, furniture, bakery and specialty-retail businesses whose owners have started the work of a sale and have not yet hired a banker — or have, and have not yet gone to market.

Which five CPG, food and retail sub-sectors are pulling ahead?

Outdoor Apparel Manufacturing leads the eligible table at 1.63x, and the external record says these are tariff-era sellers rather than growth stories. Apparel makers absorbed a near-record 24.6% effective tariff rate in 2025 (aafaglobal.org), and the deals getting done look like Lever Style's $13 million asset purchase of Active Apparel Group's activewear and outerwear operations — a buyer citing "tariff-related pressure on US sales" and summarising the moment as "bad times are the best times to buy" (finance.yahoo.com). The momentum reading is a mild +0.03, so this is sustained preparation, not a new surge. So what: lead with M&A, not financing. Owners here are weighing exits while margins are compressed; the buyers are strategics and vertically integrated producers consolidating capacity, and the window is before the January 2027 tariff resets listed by the AAFA land.

Fashion and Apparel Retail sits at 1.42x on nearly 2,000 tracked companies, and the sell-side preparation is happening against the worst store-closure backdrop of any retail category. Apparel accounted for 1,090 of the 3,321 US store closures Coresight tracked by midyear 2026 — 32.8% of the total (retailtouchpoints.com) — and Cato alone is closing roughly 120 stores this fiscal year from a 1,057-store base as quarterly sales fell 6% (chainstoreage.com). The brand-level deals are already printing: G-III signed for Marc Jacobs on May 14, 2026, with WHP Global taking the IP into a 50/50 venture and G-III running wholesale, retail, and e-commerce (whp-global.com). The -0.03 momentum says the hottest point has passed. So what: this is a sell-side and restructuring-advisory pocket. Cover the 1,989 names for carve-outs, brand sales and owner exits, and expect PwC's "take-privates are accelerating" dynamic to reach regional chains, since it describes retail as "broadly mispriced, not broadly impaired" (pwc.com).

Custom Furniture Manufacturing at 1.19x is the quiet one — building momentum (+0.08) on a structural tariff shelter rather than demand. A 25% Section 232 tariff has applied to imported upholstered wooden furniture, kitchen cabinets and vanities since September 29, 2025, and the scheduled increase to 50% was pushed back one year, to January 1, 2027 (thompsonhinesmartrade.com). Demand itself is flat: January new orders were flat year over year, shipments down 7%, inventories up 9%, with new home sales down 11.3% (interiordaily.com). RSM separately notes that valuations for home and durable goods were up in the first half (rsmus.com). The combination — protected domestic capacity, soft volumes, firm multiples — is exactly what pushes a family-owned shop to take a strategic buyer's call. So what: work the 1,901 names for strategic roll-ups of domestic capacity before the 2027 tariff step-up re-prices the category; the evidence here is regulatory and valuation-based rather than deal-count-based, and we say so.

Bakery & Confectionery Production is heating up fastest among the top five (+0.13 momentum) at 1.14x, and this is the one top-five read the announced-deal record already confirms. Industry coverage calls M&A "the defining feature of the sector in H1 2026" as buyers build platforms spanning premium, health and value (millingmea.com). The two deals that matter for the middle market are both European family-owned bakers buying US family-owned bakers: Europastry agreed in June to acquire Highland Baking, a premium foodservice bread maker with plants in Illinois and South Carolina (theshelbyreport.com), and Griesson-de Beukelaer bought the Pirouline maker DeBeukelaer Corporation in July, a Mississippi business with more than $40 million in 2025 revenue (foodbev.com). So what: inbound cross-border strategics are the buyer class to map here, and succession is the seller motive. The 1,520 tracked names skew toward founder-run businesses; the ones researching valuation and seller financing are the ones to call.

General Retail Stores round out the top five at 1.10x on the largest cohort in the report (4,020 companies), and the read is selective rather than hot. Momentum is flat (+0.01). The relevant transaction is small and telling: PlanetArt's $45 million purchase of Things Remembered and PersonalizationMall.com from 1-800-Flowers, a seller "sharpening its portfolio focus" after a fiscal-2026 net loss (asicentral.com). Coresight's full-year estimate of roughly 6,428 closures is well below 2025's pace (retailtouchpoints.com), which argues the forced-seller wave has crested and what remains is orderly portfolio pruning. So what: cover for non-core divestitures and specialty-chain carve-outs rather than distress; Bain's finding that divestitures are approaching half of consumer products M&A applies with full force to multi-banner retail groups (bain.com).

CapRaise Propensity is shown for completeness.

Which five sub-sectors are cooling, and why?

Agricultural Food Processing is the coldest eligible sub-sector at 0.70x, and the mechanism is a margin squeeze that leaves mid-market processors unable to sell on their own terms. Fed cattle hit a record $2.65 live weight on May 15, 2026, off the smallest January herd since 1951; packer spreads compressed from roughly $0.40 per pound of carcass weight to about $0.16 by June, and JBS, Tyson and Cargill have each closed or idled plants this year (provisioneronline.com). The deals that are printing are large strategics buying scale: Hormel's $1.055 billion agreement for family-owned Brakebush, a value-added chicken processor with about $1.2 billion in sales (fooddive.com). So what: deprioritise orderly sell-side coverage here. The mid-market opportunity, if any, is distressed-asset and plant-level, and it belongs to restructuring and special-situations teams rather than growth-oriented M&A.

Food Processing & Packaging reads 0.76x on nearly 4,000 companies, and it is the clearest case in the report of headlines running ahead of the mid-market pipeline. Intersnack's $2.9 billion take-private of Utz at a 91% premium (frozenfoodeurope.com) and Butterfly Equity's purchase of founder-led Sabert, a 3,000-employee food-packaging maker (packagingdive.com), are both scale assets well above the 1,000-employee cohort this index measures. Below that line, the data points the other way: US food and beverage transactions held at 81 in Q1 2026 while global volume fell about 14% (pmcf.com), and North American mid-market F&B deal value fell 27% and volume 24% in 2025 (consultancy.uk). RSM attributes the constraint to volume weakness, consumer trade-down, and input-cost uncertainty (rsmus.com). So what: this is where coverage time is most over-allocated relative to signal. Keep a watchlist for the handful of mid-market processors that do start preparing — momentum is faintly positive at +0.03 — but do not staff it like a hot sector.

Home Furnishing Retail sits at 0.84x because its deal flow is distress-led, which is a different behaviour from orderly sale preparation. Sleep Number filed Chapter 11 in June 2026 with Sleep Country Canada as the $415 million stalking-horse bidder, its CEO stating that "our capital structure remains unsustainable" (wsbtv.com). Store-level demand is flat to down, with new home sales off 11.3% year over year in January (interiordaily.com). An owner facing that picture rarely runs a banker-led process; the signal shows up as restructuring research instead. So what: cover selectively for Section 363 sales and lender-driven transactions, and expect the buyers to be category consolidators with balance sheets, not sponsors.

Beverage Production at 0.87x is cooling (-0.05 momentum) because closures are outrunning sales. The Brewers Association estimates craft volume fell 4% in the first half of 2026 and counts 9,344 breweries operating in June, down 1.8% year over year (brewersassociation.org). The consolidation that is happening sits at the very top — Keurig Dr Pepper's JDE Peet's acquisition and planned separation (bain.com) — not in the mid-market. So what: treat beverage as a selective, brand-by-brand market. Functional and better-for-you brands with distribution still clear; the long tail of regional producers is more likely to close than to sell.

Personal Care Product Manufacturing is the read we hold with the least confidence, because the tape disagrees with it. The index says 0.89x and cooling (-0.04). The market says the opposite: BeautyMatter tracked 83 beauty and wellness transactions in Q1 2026, up 40.7% year over year (beautymatter.com), RSM calls beauty and personal care "a clear bright spot" (rsmus.com), and Regent agreed in August to buy Avon North America from LG H&H (globalcosmeticsnews.com). Our reconciliation is that the deal flow is brand-led and often asset-light, while this sub-sector is the manufacturing base — contract and private-label producers whose owners are not the ones running processes. That is a hypothesis, not a finding. So what: keep covering the brands through whatever channel you already use, and watch this 1,055-company manufacturing cohort for a turn; if the brand deals need capacity, the manufacturers are the next call.

Two notable sub-sectors are too thin to call. Audio Equipment Manufacturing prints the highest raw reading in the report at 1.81x but on only 517 tracked companies, and Food and Beverage Retail reads 1.35x with the strongest momentum in the report (+0.19) on 626 companies. Both fall under the 1,000-company signal floor and are excluded from the rankings. Kroger's $1.65 billion agreement for family-owned Giant Eagle — 197 supermarkets and about $9 billion in sales (supermarketnews.com) — sits in that second pocket, and we flagged it 23 months early; it is evidence for the direction, not the magnitude.

How big is the middle-market CPG, food and retail universe Fintent tracks?

Across the five focus sub-sectors, Fintent tracks 11,138 middle-market companies with 25 to 1,000 employees: 3,137 in Fashion and Apparel Retail, 2,406 in Custom Furniture Manufacturing, 2,196 in Outdoor Apparel Manufacturing, 1,925 in General Retail Stores and 1,474 in Bakery & Confectionery Production. These counts come from Fintent's firmographic database, mapped to each sub-sector by business-type classification, and they are the universe the scores below are drawn from. Across the broader CPG, food and retail universe — every tracked consumer-goods, food, beverage, apparel, furniture, personal-care and retail business in the same size band — the count is roughly 69,000.

What are we tracking right now in CPG, food and retail?

In the last month, 51 companies across the five focus sub-sectors scored 50 or higher on Fintent's M&A score — the sector's upcoming deals, visible before any announcement. Custom Furniture Manufacturing contributes 14, Bakery & Confectionery Production 12, Outdoor Apparel Manufacturing 10, Fashion and Apparel Retail 9, and General Retail Stores 6. A score of 50 means a company's observed financial-intent behaviour — investment-bank engagement, valuation research, exit and succession topics — is running at a level that, in our back-tests, precedes an announced transaction far more often than the base rate. The announced deals in this sector's prediction record carried that signal a median of 23 months before the press release. These 51 are the names a sector banker, sponsor or corporate development team should be meeting now.

What does 'M&A Propensity' actually measure?

M&A Propensity is the rate at which companies in a cohort exhibit pre-transaction behaviour, indexed to a fixed baseline where 1.00 equals the rate for all US companies with 26 to 1,000 employees. A sector reading of 1.20x means CPG, food and retail companies are showing 20% more deal-preparation behaviour than the market. Inside the report, each sub-sector is indexed against the rest of the sector's sub-sectors, so 1.63x for outdoor apparel manufacturing means 63% more preparation than the typical CPG sub-sector, not 63% more than the whole market. The index blends Fintent's Deal-Maker (M&A) score, which captures engagement with advisors, and its M&A score, which captures the research topics that precede a sale. CapRaise Propensity is the financing analogue — the sector currently reads 1.16x — and it is shown in the tables for completeness only; this post ranks and argues on M&A.

How are these trends built from financial-intent data?

Fintent reads company-level financial-intent signals, scores and dates them, aggregates them to the sub-sector, and benchmarks against the peer baseline. The signals are observed behaviours — which advisors a company is engaging, whether it is researching valuation, seller financing, earn-outs, leveraged buyouts or succession — captured weekly across the 36,200-company cohort. Quarterly aggregation produces the propensity index; the momentum figure is the four-quarter slope of that index relative to the rest of the sector, so +0.13 for bakery means it has been gaining on its peers for a year. Because the inputs are early behaviours rather than announcements, the trend leads reported deal flow — in this sector's own prediction record, by a median of 23 months. Sub-sectors with fewer than 1,000 tracked companies are excluded from the rankings because a high multiple on a few hundred companies is noise; the app flags them the same way.

Frequently asked questions

Which CPG, food and retail sub-sectors have the highest M&A propensity in 2026?

As of the October 2026 report, the five highest eligible sub-sectors are Outdoor Apparel Manufacturing (1.63x), Fashion and Apparel Retail (1.42x), Custom Furniture Manufacturing (1.19x), Bakery & Confectionery Production (1.14x) and General Retail Stores (1.10x). Each is indexed against the rest of the CPG, food and retail cohort, where 1.00 equals parity.

Which CPG, food and retail sub-sectors are cooling for M&A?

The five lowest eligible readings are Agricultural Food Processing (0.70x), Food Processing & Packaging (0.76x), Home Furnishing Retail (0.84x), Beverage Production (0.87x) and Personal Care Product Manufacturing (0.89x). These are the categories where mid-market companies show less deal-preparation behaviour than the sector average, even though several carry the sector's biggest announced deals.

Why does the index disagree with the food M&A headlines?

The headline deals — Utz, Brakebush, Giant Eagle, McCormick-Unilever — involve companies above the 1,000-employee cohort the index measures. Among middle-market food processors, external data shows North American mid-market food and beverage deal volume fell 24% in 2025 and remains constrained by volume weakness and consumer trade-down, consistent with the low propensity reading.

What is financial-intent data?

Financial-intent data captures observable, company-level behaviour that precedes a transaction: engagement with investment banks and corporate law firms, research into valuation, seller financing, earn-outs, leveraged buyouts and succession. Fintent scores and dates these signals weekly for each company, then aggregates them into sector and sub-sector propensity indices benchmarked against a peer baseline.

How early does Fintent detect M&A intent in CPG, food and retail?

In the 24 CPG, food and retail acquisitions Fintent flagged over the May–October 2026 prediction files, the first M&A signal appeared a median of 23 months before the announcement, with every deal showing signals at least 18 months early. Half were already flagged at the start of the 24-month lookback window, so true lead times may be longer.

Why are some sub-sectors excluded from the rankings?

Sub-sectors with fewer than 1,000 tracked companies are excluded as low-signal. A high multiple on a few hundred companies can be noise, so Audio Equipment Manufacturing (1.81x on 517 companies) and Food and Beverage Retail (1.35x on 626) are noted but not ranked. The platform applies the same floor.

text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the chipmaker “absolutely must” work with Chinese AI companies on monitoring risks around the “potentially dangerous” technology.

“We absolutely should work with each other so that we advance the technology safely,” he told CNBC during a media briefing on Wednesday evening in London.

Discussions around AI safety have intensified in recent months, after researchers from AI labs including OpenAI and Anthropic called for a slowdown on developing the tech and warned of existential risks to humanity.

While OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei have called for greater regulation, Huang has emerged as a prominent voice in opposition to that view.

Huang said that “dialogue” was the way to work with Chinese AI companies, adding that he has “dialogues with many of the researchers in China.”

“We ought to enhance the dialogue,” he added. “The United States should do it... I advocated that the U.K. do the same thing.”

AI safety has become a key topic between the U.S. and Chinese governments, with both countries weighing how to address the risks posed by the rapidly advancing tech.

Prior to U.S. President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed the prospect of a “U.S.-China AI dialogue” with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, in September, including a channel for incidents “up to a national security level.”

A Chinese readout of the meeting said President Xi pointed out that China and the U.S. “may have competition, but they may cooperate even more” in AI. “The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI,” Xi said, per the readout.

Huang said that the U.K. is in a position “in the world to be able to be a convener of many of these dialogues” related to AI, because of the country’s “intellectual capital.”

text:
David Vaillant has been a lawyer, a central banker, a dealmaker and a professor. Now he has a new job: finding roughly $1.5bn of investor money every week.

That is the pace at which the World Bank Group’s three main lending arms, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Development Association (IDA), and the International Finance Corporation (IFC) raised funds in the 2026 financial year, totalling nearly $82bn from international capital markets. As the group’s new Managing Director and Chief Financial Officer, announced on 8 October, Vaillant will run that global funding machine. Alongside its own borrowing, President Ajay Banga wants Vaillant to pull far more private money into emerging market infrastructure and energy transition projects.

Finance executives managing cross-border capital structures, debt issuances and corporate acquisitions, Vaillant’s appointment offers a useful look at how big institutions are trying to share risk with private money.

Lawyer, Central Banker, Dealmaker, Professor

Vaillant’s career trajectory covers an unusually broad set of disciplines. He began in corporate legal practice advising companies on cross-border transactions before joining the Banque de France, where he gained firsthand exposure to central banking regulation and systemic risk oversight. At BNP Paribas, his responsibilities expanded into sovereign advisory, counselling governments and central banks across both developed and developing economies. He also taught finance, sustainable finance and international macroeconomics at HEC Paris and Sciences Po.

His most prominent corporate milestone came as Global Head of Finance, Strategy and Participations at BNP Paribas Asset Management. There, Vaillant led the €5.1bn ($5.6bn) acquisition of AXA Investment Managers, a transaction that created one of Europe’s largest asset managers with approximately €1.6tr in client assets.

Banga highlighted this breadth of experience upon the appointment, noting that Vaillant has spent his career managing finance at scale while working closely with investors, governments and central banks. The modern World Bank CFO role requires a leader who can navigate complex cross-border legal frameworks, structure multi-party transactions and manage diverse public and private stakeholders simultaneously.

Balancing an $82bn Funding Program with Private Capital

The $82bn annual borrowing programed cements the World Bank’s status as one of the world’s largest supranational debt issuers. Yet public multilateral lending alone cannot close the global infrastructure financing gap, which is estimated to require trillions of dollars in annual capital allocation.

Banga’s vision does not replace traditional bond issuances; rather, it aims to use the bank’s balance sheet to attract commercial capital that currently stays on the sidelines. To achieve this, Vaillant inherits an operation tasked with making emerging market assets viable for risk-averse institutional investors like pension funds and insurance firms.

First, this requires de-risking foreign exchange and sovereign credit exposure. Tools the group already uses include political risk guarantees, first-loss equity tranches and specialized currency hedging mechanisms. By absorbing early-stage project risks, multilateral lenders lower the overall cost of capital for private co-investors who would otherwise find emerging market yields insufficient relative to the perceived risk.

Second, one priority is likely to be the standardization of blended finance assets. Private institutional investors often avoid emerging market infrastructure because individual deals are too small, fragmented and bespoke to manage efficiently. By pooling infrastructure loans into standardized, rated financial instruments, the World Bank can create tradable asset classes that global institutional investors can syndicate or purchase at scale.

Lessons for Corporate Finance Leaders

While few corporate treasurers manage an annual funding engine of $82bn, Vaillant’s background and the mandate he inherits offer practical parallels for enterprise finance strategy.

The decision to buy scale through the AXA Investment Managers acquisition rather than relying on organic growth illustrates a key lesson for corporate strategy: when market fragmentation threatens margins, aggressive consolidation can lower operating costs over time and yield capital efficiencies. Corporate CFOs evaluating strategic growth can look to large asset management consolidations as a template for building operational scale.

Furthermore, as corporate borrowing costs remain elevated compared to the prior decade, finance leaders managing heavy capital expenditure programes (particularly in energy, supply chain infrastructure and technology) can adopt multilateral co-investment techniques. Structuring joint ventures, private credit facilities or syndicated debt vehicles with institutional partners allows corporate treasurers to fund large-scale investments while sharing risk and preserving balance sheet capacity.

Lawyer, central banker, dealmaker, professor. For a CFO job in 2026, that CV no longer looks unusual.
