text:
Always more. Six years after the launch of its ALL program, based on a platform combining booking and loyalty, Accor is evolving its message by giving ALL a new signature: «Stay for more». With more than 120 million customers as members, the ALL program is embarking on a new chapter by moving away from the transactional relationship to meet the primary expectations of travelers accustomed to visiting the group’s hotels throughout the year.

This evolution is based, in particular, on a study conducted by Opinion Way among 7,000 travelers, also divided between France and the United Kingdom, the United States and Brazil, China, India and the Middle East. The results show that, although expectations naturally revolve around the leisure dimension, they also reflect the hectic daily lives of professionals and their desire to let go and relax for a weekend or a well-deserved vacation.

The need for a break, the first trigger for travel

More than discovering new horizons or new destinations, the need for a break after a busy work period is the primary trigger for the desire to travel for 43 % of the respondents.« All the markers in our questions point in that direction: I was going through a stressful period, I needed to take a step back, I felt trapped in my routine. There is really a need to get out of the pressure of everyday life. »This is a very important result," notes Clara de Pirey, director of the Luxury division at the NellyRodi firm, who drew the lessons from this survey.

To alleviate the mental burden, 21 % of the travelers surveyed place total disconnection among the most anticipated benefits of loyalty, and 33 % believe that a wellness experience can truly rejuvenate holidays. All of this adds up to the cherished moments spent with loved ones and the memories that beautiful trips can create.

" Making life more meaningful for our members »Stéphanie Gabriel, marketing and sponsorship director at All Accor, explains the underlying philosophy behind the «Stay for more» signature change:« Points are obviously very important; they are the foundation of the program. But we are now observing the transition from a transactional value to an emotional value., "She remarks," she notes. And within this framework, it is obviously important to have members who adhere to our program. But even more important: to be proud of being part of it. ".

Thousands of hotels offered to families by the group and its 45 brands, more than 2,300 establishments offering sports activities and 1,500 that are «pet-friendly», as well as 10,000 restaurants and bars present in the French group’s hotels: focused on all this diversity, a communication campaign, developed by the creative agency Saatchi & Saatchi, will promote this new «stay for more» promise, both online and through displays in many global airports.

The announcement of this evolution of the ALL Accor program follows the launch a few weeks ago of All Concierge, an AI assistant capable of natural language searches that are more emotional than functional. It also comes after the officialization, last April, of a partnership with Uber to allow members to earn points for meal delivery and mobility services.

A B2B section for SMEs and business travelers

But other steps are yet to be taken next spring. While the program is based on unique experiences accessible to members – a football tournament on the Parc des Princes pitch with PSG legends, concerts in Paris, London, Sao Paulo or Sydney among others – Accor plans to launch a new platform of experiences, directly integrated into our ALL app and website.« We have been working on this for more than two years with our partner Fever, of which Accor has become a shareholder., ," explains Mehdi Hemici, General Manager of Loyalty and E-commerce at Accor. Our observation is that today, no hotel group has managed to create a digital platform for experiences that is user-friendly and intuitive. ".

In addition to wanting to remedy this shortcoming in order to better highlight these Limitless Experiences, the ALL program will see, in a third phase, the launch next year of a B2B segment aimed at small and medium-sized businesses and business travelers. So, patience is required until next year.

text:
David Ellison won the battle for Warner Bros., but the war is just beginning.

Ellison and his co-CEO Ynon Kreiz must get through the wolves of Wall Street to make the finances of smashing together two studios in an eye-popping $110 billion acquisition work.

And they’re off to a rough start.

In order to fund the deal, Ellison and co. had to raise money through various sources, including around $24 billion from Middle Eastern sovereign funds, a few more billion from RedBird Capital and the Ellison family chipping in. The company is also raising $42.4 billion from the bond market.

But Skydance has certain financial targets it promised its debt holders — the first one being in 2028. It’s not a specific amount, but rather a ratio of its debt compared to its earnings.

Naveen Sarma, sector lead for U.S. media and telecom at S&P Global, doesn’t believe Skydance can hit its target in 2028. “There’s a gap they’re going to have to bridge,” Sarma says, believing they’ll have to cover anywhere between $10 billion and $15 billion to bridge that gap. “How much of that comes from an additional equity infusion from [David’s dad] Larry Ellison?”

Much of the attention has been paid to the elder Ellison and his $180 billion-ish net worth. (Though much of that is tied to Oracle’s stock, and his ability to backstop the company going forward.)

Adding to the financial load, the antitrust lawsuit from California Attorney General Rob Bonta and the WGA delayed the merger’s closing months. During that time, the cost of borrowing money (i.e. interest rates) went up as did Treasury yields. All told, Paramount will have to pay up to an additional $500 million per year due to the spike in borrowing costs, per Bloomberg estimates.

“It just means a deeper hole for them to dig out of,” Sarma tells Page Six Hollywood. “There’s going to be a challenge to de-lever anyway, it just makes it more of a challenge.”

In plain English, “de-leveraging” means paying down debt. And with so much of it on the books, Skydance isn’t expected to generate positive cash flow — meaning it brings in more cash than it spends — until 2028 at the earliest.

The company also has around $6 billion in synergies — the amount of operating costs it has promised to cut, which typically involves layoffs — but Ellison has promised other ways of reducing costs that don’t involve laying off thousands of employees. (Though to be clear, hefty layoffs are still expected.)

Since CEO David Ellison promised Bonta 30 movies a year and increased spending on content, there are fewer ways to reduce debt than is typical in prior big mergers.

Meanwhile, investors in the bonds were sitting on more than $100 million in paper losses on just the first day of trading.

Much of the angst surrounding the deal has focused on the ramifications for Hollywood’s creative community. But Wall Street has been fretting about the math.

After all, investors don’t care about winning Oscars. They just don’t want to lose money.

text:
Agilent has agreed to acquire digital pathology provider Proscia in a deal worth up to $270m to bolster its existing pathology portfolio with more instruments, reagents, and software.

Under the all-cash transaction, Agilent will pay $240m up front, with the deal swelling by up to $30m pending future performance milestones being met.

Agilent highlighted that the acquisition builds on a multi-year global distribution agreement it established with Proscia in March 2023 to offer a digital diagnostic pathology system combining its pathology staining toolkit with Proscia’s Concentriq Dx. The digital pathology software platform, which went on to obtain US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) clearance in 2024, allows pathologists to view, interpret, and manage whole slide images within a digital environment.

Following its recently completed $950m acquisition of Biocare Medical in June, Agilent asserted that acquiring Proscia will result in various strategic and financial benefits. Most notably, Agilent said the takeover will strengthen its existing position in pathology instrumentation and reagents by combining its diagnostic capabilities with Proscia’s Concentriq Dx and the platform’s established customer base.

Proscia serves more than 4,000 laboratories, hospitals, and clinics as well as 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies, according to Agilent.

According to Agilent, Proscia’s product offerings will also help to realise “additional AI-enabled synergies” with the California-based company’s companion diagnostics (CDx) business. This factor is expected to provide value-add to the company’s biopharma partners and clinical and translational research customers.

“Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market,” said Agilent’s president and CEO, Padraig McDonnell.

“The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia’s leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data,” McDonnell continued.

The transaction is expected to close in Agilent’s fiscal year 2027, with Proscia set to become part of Agilent’s Life Sciences and Diagnostics Markets business.

Commenting on the buyout, Proscia’s co-founder and CEO, David West, said: “Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows.”

Recent research from Randstad found that the traditional, linear approach to career advancement—modeled after a pyramid—is antiquated. In fact, nearly three-quarters of leaders surveyed said vertical advancement up the standard career ladder is an outdated concept, while only about 40% of employees said they would want to follow such a traditional path.

That has involved a greater emphasis on rotation opportunities and mobility efforts; not easy for an organization that has viewed advancement through the traditional pyramid lens for over a century.

"When you've operated for decades the same way and all of a sudden you say, 'We've got to shift to a place where we can allow people to move around the organization more nimbly,' that creates tension within the organization," Carlier says. "But that is what we were starting to see as the demand coming from our workforce."

Faced with a shortage of skilled tradesworkers like drivers and technicians, the organization doubled-down on

creating new pathways for workers to move across the company.

Walmart Chief People Officer Donna Morris, HR Executive's 2025 HR Executive of the Year, previously detailed how the organization is investing $1 billion in career-focused training by the end of this year. Efforts include its global Walmart Academy and Live Better U, which provides debt-free educational opportunities.

"We've taken the supply of our own internal talent and have focused on, where do we see the future going in terms of skills and capabilities? How do we equip our own associates with those skills and capabilities?" Morris told HR Executive.

At the Forbes summit, Stomski recalled one associate who went from working behind the deli counter to becoming one of Walmart's fleet drivers, now making six figures.

"We built our own training and started creating pathways and programs," Stomski said. "The worker went from being behind a deli counter to being a driver and she loves it. There are creative strategies you have to think through, beyond the stereotype that promotion is up. It can go many different ways."

Elise James-DeCruise, chief culture and learning officer at The Ad Council, characterized the moment we're in with a sports analogy: Not everyone is going to lead the team, but everyone has a role to play on the team, if equipped with the right skills. Create experiential opportunities, job shadowing, mentorships and sponsorships, she advises, while reimagining manager and leadership training.

text:
The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research.

The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released.

Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”.

Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents had attacked Hugging Face, a tech startup.

Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London.

The computing power will be delivered via UK-based datacentres using Nvidia chips.

“The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.”

Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”.

On Monday Narayan confirmed that AISI was conducting tests on US-developed AI models before they are released, after reports that the White House had restricted access.

The AI minister also warned that the UK faces agentic attacks similar to the one carried out by OpenAI agents on Australia’s healthcare system this year.

“It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached,” said Narayan.

Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, warned of a new AI safety threat on Monday after it published a blogpost stating its models could soon become self-replicating. They find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart ovens and lawnmowers, the company said.

Under such a scenario the models could power themselves without datacentres, and instead could use a “botnet” of interconnected devices, Anthropic said, adding that the world should prepare for a future where such botnets were here to stay.

“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” Anthropic’s researchers wrote.

text:
Albertsons Companies has withdrawn its fiscal 2026 outlook as it conducts an operational review following lower second-quarter profit and falling identical sales.

The US food and drug retailer will withhold updated forecasts until the review concludes in its fourth quarter, when it plans to present refreshed financial frameworks alongside a turnaround plan.

In its first quarter, it had forecast identical sales between -1.5% and -0.5%, adjusted EBITDA of $3.55bn to $3.62bn and adjusted net income per Class A common share of $1.75 to $1.85.

The ongoing examination covers customer strategy, cost structures, operating models, banner portfolios, market assets, and capital allocation priorities.

It follows the ACI Edge programme launched in July 2026, which consolidated 11 divisions into four regions and centralised centre-store merchandising under a single team.

For the second quarter ended 12 September 2026, net income fell 69.4% to $51.5m, and diluted earnings per share dropped to $0.11 from $0.30.

Adjusted net income declined 27.9% to $179m, with adjusted earnings per share decreasing to $0.36 from $0.44.

Operating income fell to $174.5m from $295.3m, whilst adjusted EBITDA declined to $784m from $848.4m.

Net sales and other revenue dropped to $18.89bn from $18.91bn, driven by a 0.8% decrease in identical sales.

Digital sales grew 11%, whilst higher fuel takings and pharmacy revenue – despite headwinds from the Inflation Reduction Act – partially offset the top-line reduction.

Gross margin narrowed to 26.8% from 27% due to digital delivery and handling costs alongside higher shrink, partly offset by improved pharmacy margins.

Cost management offset operating inflation and merger litigation costs, while store impairments and equipment disposals lifted property disposition losses to $42.4m from $4.4m.

First-half net sales reached $43.83bn, compared with $43.79bn a year earlier, but operating income fell to $438.1m from $744.6m, and net income dropped to $136.2m from $404.9m.

Capital expenditure reached $899.6m, funding 38 remodels, seven store openings, and digital investments.

As of 12 September 2026, the company operated 2,240 stores, including 1,709 pharmacies and 408 fuel centres.

Albertsons CEO Susan Morris said: "We are launching a comprehensive business review to speed up improvements in Albertsons' performance and tackle even harder a cost structure we can no longer afford. Our work will find opportunities to simplify the organisation, improve decision-making, reinvest savings in customer value, and boost long-term shareholder returns."

text:
The agreement marks an important step in the industrial roll-out of Perpetual Next’s Biomethanol Blueprint, a standardised concept designed to enable the serial development and replication of large scale biomethanol facilities based on proven industrial technologies.

Under the Agreement, Air Liquide Engineering and Technologies will provide its RectisolTM and LurgiTM Methanol technology. The technology is designed to process syngas from a broad range of sources, including syngas from biomass and has been deployed in numerous industrial plants worldwide.

Perpetual Next’s Blueprint integrates torrefaction, gasification, syngas cleaning and upgrade, with methanol synthesis to convert low-grade organic waste, including waste wood, into biomethanol. The standardised approach is intended to reduce development complexity, support repeatable project execution and create economies of scale across a portfolio of facilities.

Perpetual Next is developing its biomethanol portfolio to address growing demand for renewable carbon-based methanol in the chemical industry and maritime sector. Its Delfzijl facility in the Netherlands is planned with a planned biomethanol production capacity of 220 000 tpy, while the company’s broader global development pipeline is intended to create significant production capacity through replication of the Blueprint.

Rolf Bosma, Managing Director, Perpetual Next: “This suite of agreements marks an important milestone in the industrialisation of our Biomethanol Blueprint. Delfzijl will be the first application of the concept, providing the foundation for subsequent projects in Moerdijk, Poland, Estonia and other sites worldwide. By establishing a framework with Air Liquide for multiple biomethanol sites, we are creating a scalable technology platform that supports the roll-out of our biomethanol portfolio.”

The agreement combines Perpetual Next’s standardised project concept and feedstock strategy with Air Liquide’s established technology and engineering capabilities, providing a platform for the development of multiple industrial-scale biomethanol facilities.

For Roche to catch up to Eli Lilly and Novo in metabolic medicines, it needs its drugs to offer differentiation from those rivals. Roche might have just found a way, agreeing to pay $100 million to license a contender that brings a different modality to a new obesity target.

The drug comes from Shanghai-based Rona Therapeutics. According to deal terms announced Tuesday, Roche gains global rights to the molecule, whose name was not disclosed. It’s the latest in a series of Roche business deals to build up the company’s metabolic drug pipeline.

Formed in 2021, Rona develops RNA interference (RNAi) drugs, an approach that uses small interfering RNA (siRNA) to degrade messenger RNA, interfering with the translation of a disease-driving protein. This approach is sometimes called “gene silencing.” RNAi drugs first reached patients as treatments for liver disorders, but the field has been working to expand the modality beyond the liver. Roche’s new drug comes from a Rona platform technology that enables extrahepatic drug delivery. Rona also claims its therapies offer the potential to be best in class with longer duration, deep knockdown of target proteins, and improved tolerability.

The Rona pipeline lists two obesity drug, both in preclinical development for undisclosed targets. The target of Roche’s newly licensed drug is activin receptor-like kinase 7 (ALK7), a protein that is primarily expressed in fat cells. ALK7 plays a role in a signaling pathway that regulates fat storage, the breakdown of stored fats, and the balance of the intake and expenditure of energy.

Rona points to genetic studies showing that reducing ALK7 activity is associated with favorable results in fat distribution and metabolic measures. Unlike the currently available peptide drugs designed to mimic gut hormones to affect appetite and energy intake, Ronas say ALK7 inhibition acts directly on the biology of fat tissue. This different approach offers the potential for use as a standalone treatment or in combination with established obesity drugs.

“Obesity represents a significant health challenge that requires differentiated treatment options for patients,” Boris Zaïtra, Roche head of corporate business development, said in a prepared statement. “We are excited to partner with Rona Therapeutics, complementing our robust [cardiovascular, renal & metabolic disease] pipeline and reinforcing our commitment to delivering next-generation metabolic therapies.”

Roche jumped into obesity drug R&D with the $2.7 billion acquisition of Carmot Therapeutics in 2024. The Carmot drugs address GLP-1 and GIP receptors, the same targets as Lilly and Novo’s obesity drugs. Last year, Roche began a partnership on petrelintide, a Zealand Pharma peptide designed to activate the receptor for amylin, a hormone key to regulating blood sugar and appetite. One goal for petrelintide is reducing fat in a way that does not also lead to muscle loss, a known problem for obesity drugs. Roche added yet another approach to obesity in August, licensing a Hanmi Pharmaceutical peptide designed to activate CRF2 receptors to reduce fat and increase muscle mass.

With the Rona drug, Roche joins a growing group of companies testing siRNA therapies in obesity. Wave Life Sciences’ siRNA drug WVE-007 goes after a different but related target. It’s designed to silence INHBE, the gene that provides the instructions for activin E, a liver-secreted protein that activates ALK7. Wave has said WVE-007 is intended to stimulate the breakdown of fat while preserving muscle. Late last year, Wave announced preliminary Phase 1 results that it said support once- or twice-yearly dosing. Last month, the company began a Phase 2a study testing WVE-007 in combination with the Lilly obesity drug Zepbound.

GSK joined the ALK7 chase in May, licensing rights to Suzhou Siran Biotechnology’s SA030, a long-acting siRNA in development for metabolic and vascular diseases. The deal calls for SiranBio to complete the ongoing Phase 1 study. After that, GSK will be responsible for further development of the drug outside of Greater China.

Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals has two siRNA therapies in development for obesity: the ALK7-targeting drug ARO-ALK7 and the INHBE gene-silencing therapy ARO-INHBE. Both are in Phase 1/2a testing. Meanwhile, RNAi therapies pioneer Alnylam Pharmaceuticals has an INHBE-targeting siRNA drug in preclinical development for obesity.

Biotech company iBio takes yet another approach with IBIO-610, an antibody designed to block activin E. In July, iBio reported results in monkey tests showing a single dose achieved near complete inhibition of the target protein through eight weeks. These results also showed fat loss and muscle preservation.

The $100 million that Roche agreed to pay Rona consists of an upfront and near-term milestone payments. Rona could receive up to $1.06 billion more if the drug achieves milestones, plus royalties from sales if it reaches the market.

text:
Stronger local capabilities and steadier China-US ties could support innovation worldwide by connecting China's research and manufacturing strengths with global expertise, a senior executive of a United States-based technology company said.

Jonah Kirkwood, senior vice-president and chief commercial officer at Agilent Technologies, a California-headquartered company in analytical and clinical laboratory technology, said China's skilled workforce, extensive supply chains and readiness to adopt new technologies further underpin its commitment to the market.

"Today, China is both an important market for us and an integral part of our global supply chain, manufacturing and innovation network," Kirkwood said.

According to the company, the Chinese market delivered 9 percent year-on-year revenue growth on a core basis in the quarter ended July 31, driven by double-digit growth in pharmaceutical and food markets.

"A more stable bilateral relationship would give us greater confidence to advance long-term collaboration," Kirkwood added, calling for sustained dialogue to create a more transparent and predictable business environment.

Greater policy certainty and smoother movement of people and commerce would help companies plan long-term investments and allow researchers and businesses in both countries to work together on shared challenges, he said.

For Agilent, that cooperation runs in both directions — global technologies help meet Chinese customers' needs, while insights from China inform products and solutions for international markets.

Within the company, Chinese customers are increasingly helping define research problems and develop solutions, Kirkwood said, with their needs feeding into global product plans.

"This means that China is an important market for applying advanced technologies and also a source of customer insight, engineering experience and innovative ideas that can inspire our global solution development," he said.

The senior executive sees that contribution in laboratories seeking to integrate artificial intelligence into experimental design, data analysis and daily operations, moving beyond purchases of individual instruments.

"Chinese customers' emphasis on real-world application, together with their ability to test, iterate and scale new technologies quickly, makes China an important window into the future of laboratory development," he said.

Agilent's partnership with Chinese technology company Purspec offers another example. The partners combined Purspec's lipidomics hardware, software and databases with Agilent's chromatography and mass spectrometry platforms to develop a solution for studying lipid structures.

During the project, Chinese researchers contributed original technologies and knowledge of emerging scientific needs, while Agilent brought instrumentation and an international market network.

"These collaborations reinforce my confidence that China can contribute a wealth of original scientific achievements, engineering capabilities and application insights," Kirkwood said.

Looking forward, Kirkwood sees particular promise in China-US cooperation in areas such as life sciences and biopharmaceuticals, food and environmental safety, green energy and laboratory digitalization, where progress depends on scientists, companies and customers working across borders.

"Enduring collaboration often begins with a specific challenge," he said, adding that translating positive momentum from high-level dialogue into lasting outcomes requires companies to pursue open innovation, invest in local capabilities and build long-term trust with customers, suppliers, research institutions and industry partners.

Agilent plans to put that approach into practice by deepening local manufacturing and research collaboration in China over the next two to three years, Kirkwood noted.

text:
Collaboration will bring together NVIDIA AI technologies and Danaher's scientific instruments, laboratory workflows and data

WASHINGTON, Oct. 14, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Danaher Corporation (NYSE: DHR) today announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of scientific discovery. As part of Danaher's broader effort to shape the future of AI-enabled science, the companies are working to combine Danaher's scientific instrumentation, automation technologies, laboratory workflow software and domain expertise with NVIDIA accelerated computing and AI technologies. The goal is to help researchers move faster from prediction to experimental evidence, creating a continuous learning cycle where experiments inform models and models help design better experiments.

"AI is reshaping how science is conducted, and Danaher is at the forefront of that transformation," said Julie Sawyer Montgomery, President and Chief Executive Officer of Danaher. "We are collaborating around a shared vision for more connected, adaptive and accessible innovation, helping researchers solve consequential challenges and translate discovery into human impact."

"The next era of scientific discovery will be driven by a continuous loop between AI and experimentation," said Kimberly Powell, Vice President of Healthcare at NVIDIA. "Together with Danaher, we are bringing accelerated computing and physical AI into the lab - connecting models with instruments and real experimental data, where experiments improve models and models design better experiments, helping researchers compress years of discovery into months."

Danaher and NVIDIA are working to integrate AI into scientific instruments through edge computing like NVIDIA DGX Spark, accelerated analytics and data processing with RAPIDS, real-time inference, scientific reasoning and foundation model technologies, including BioNeMo Open Models. Initial efforts focus on a select group of priority instruments, with the potential to expand across a broader portfolio over time. The companies are exploring how scientific and physical AI, such as NVIDIA Cosmos world models and Omniverse Digital Twins, can support more intelligent instruments and laboratory workflows, while keeping experimental evidence at the center of scientific decision-making.

The collaboration seeks to advance Danaher's commitment to connected science by bringing AI, accelerated computing, instruments, workflows and experimental data together to produce experimental evidence. Danaher aims to help researchers reduce the time and complexity of moving from an AI-generated prediction to the experimental evidence needed to act on it, while preserving customer choice in models, standards and technology providers.

text:
Whilst the global spotlight remains fixed on the power struggle between the United States and China for dominance in artificial intelligence, France is building its own digital sovereignty. This is no longer merely a matter of political ambitions proclaimed in European forums, but of large-scale industrial implementation that is bringing agentic computing – artificial intelligence systems capable of acting autonomously, without constant human supervision – directly into the vital nerve centres of the real economy. The picture that emerges is that of an ecosystem spanning the entire value chain, from hardware to applications, yet one in which there remains a single key supplier. This marks a significant shift, recently documented on NVIDIA’s official blog, demonstrating how the seeds sown during the AI Action Summit in February 2025 and the ‘Choose France’ summits are generating a tangible return on investment.

Strategic independence depends on the ability to process data in-house and control the physical infrastructure. It is in this context that Bull’s expansion of AI server production in Europe should be viewed; from 2028, the company will manufacture systems based on the powerful NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 architecture directly at its newly opened plant in Angers. The concept of the ‘sovereign vault’ also extends to intangible data. The CANUT framework agreement, for example, has made Twake.ai (based on the NVIDIA Nemotron model) the only certified digital workspace for over 2,500 French public bodies, managed by LINAGORA and Docaposte. Meanwhile, in the financial sector, the operator SBS is creating secure platforms that will enable banks to develop generative AI services whilst keeping data strictly within their own corporate boundaries – a non-negotiable requirement for credit institutions.

If hardware is the security perimeter, software is the competitive driving force behind this French revolution in technological infrastructure. Here, France is playing the open-source card, with Mistral AI (which has just released its Large 4 model) leading the way. But it is the application in the real economy that is truly surprising. The most fascinating example comes from the space economy. The Altair-1 satellite, successfully launched this month (the result of integration with Loft Orbital), literally takes AI into orbit. Thanks to the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin modules and Mistral models, the satellite is capable of performing real-time Earth observation processing and autonomous operations directly in space, bypassing the traditional – and slow – transfer of data to the ground.Even the traditional manufacturing and cosmetics industries are reaping a competitive advantage. L’Oréal has integrated the NVIDIA ALCHEMI architecture for in silico research: by combining computational simulations with laboratory experimentation, the cosmetics giant has accelerated the process of discovering new active ingredients by up to a hundred times, demonstrating that AI does not replace traditional research but exponentially multiplies its efficiency. In Côte-d’Or, ThinkDeep and Akila are managing around 5,800 kilometres of roads and buildings using a digital twin-based agent, achieving a 10 per cent reduction in operating costs, with a target of 30 per cent once fully operational. Bouygues Telecom and Prisme.ai have launched AI Studio V2, which enables employees to build agents in a controlled environment. In the field of quantum computing, Alice & Bob and Quandela are integrating the NVQLink platform to connect GPUs and quantum processors.

The ‘French model’ provides clear evidence that the technological drive towards sovereignty does not end with the purchase of advanced semiconductors. It requires an integrated ecosystem where the state’s vision (with its catalysts) is seamlessly integrated with private infrastructure, academic excellence and national software leaders. This is a crucial lesson for Italia – which is currently seeking to chart its own path to digital sovereignty – and for Europe as a whole. The next signs will come from Jensen Huang’s keynote speech at GTC Berlin on Wednesday 21 October. This is no longer merely a matter of political ambitions proclaimed in European forums, but of large-scale industrial implementation that is bringing agent-based computing – artificial intelligence systems capable of acting autonomously, without constant human supervision – directly into the vital nerve centres of the real economy. title: Agilent to Acquire Proscia for Up to $270M to Build Scientific Intelligence Layer in Digital Pathology
description:
What You Should Know Analytical and clinical laboratory technology giant Agilent Technologies Inc. announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire digital pathology software and AI company Proscia®.
Closes the loop on a four-year commercial partnership: Agilent and Proscia originally entered into a multi-year global distribution agreement in September 2022 to co-market an open digital diagnostic pathology ecosystem.
Assembling the Full Pathology Stack By acquiring Proscia, Agilent secures the missing software operating system.
Agilent and Proscia originally entered into a multi-year global distribution agreement in September 2022 to co-develop and sell integrated diagnostic pathology workflows.
Top-Tier Biopharma Validation: Proscia software currently supports translational research and trial operations for 16 of the top 20 global pharmaceutical companies.
text:
What You Should Know

Analytical and clinical laboratory technology giant Agilent Technologies Inc. announced that it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire digital pathology software and AI company Proscia®.

Transaction financial terms: an all-cash acquisition valued at $240M in cash at closing, plus up to an additional $30M contingent on achieving future operational and financial performance milestones (total potential deal value of $270M).

Closes the loop on a four-year commercial partnership: Agilent and Proscia originally entered into a multi-year global distribution agreement in September 2022 to co-market an open digital diagnostic pathology ecosystem.

Unifies an end-to-end precision medicine triad: merges Agilent’s established portfolio of automated slide stainers, pathology instrumentation, diagnostic reagents, and companion diagnostics (CDx) with Proscia’s vendor-agnostic enterprise software platform, Concentriq®, which serves as an operational orchestration layer across scanners, LIS networks, and AI algorithms.

Assembling the Full Pathology Stack

By acquiring Proscia, Agilent secures the missing software operating system. Instead of selling discrete instruments and reagents, Agilent can now deliver an end-to-end ecosystem: tissue preparation reagents, automated staining instrumentation, vendor-neutral whole-slide ingestion, and regulatory-cleared diagnostic software.

Agilent and Proscia originally entered into a multi-year global distribution agreement in September 2022 to co-develop and sell integrated diagnostic pathology workflows. Acquiring Proscia transitions an external commercial alliance into an owned intellectual property core.

Agilent is a primary diagnostic partner for global pharma, co-developing FDA-approved companion diagnostic tests that determine patient eligibility for targeted cancer immunotherapies. Integrating Concentriq gives Agilent a direct digital data conduit into 16 of the top 20 biopharmas, creating an R&D feedback loop that unites prospective biomarker discovery with downstream clinical commercialization.

Transaction Economics & Target Operating Benchmarks

The acquisition brings a high-margin, recurring-revenue software foundation into Agilent’s diagnostic portfolio:

Valuation Multiple & Purchase Price: Agilent is deploying $240M in cash at closing plus up to $30M in earnouts against Proscia’s trailing twelve months (TTM) revenue exceeding $18M —representing an upfront enterprise value-to-revenue multiple of approximately 13.3x (expanding to 15.0x including full earnouts), reflecting high market demand for enterprise software operating layers in diagnostics.

Commercial Scale and Penetration: Proscia’s platform—anchored by its flagship Concentriq® software—is deployed across more than 4,000 laboratories, hospital systems, and clinics across North America and Europe.

Top-Tier Biopharma Validation: Proscia software currently supports translational research and trial operations for 16 of the top 20 global pharmaceutical companies.

Clinical Performance Benchmarks: Proscia earned 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology (securing the highest vendor performance score across both U.S. and European markets) and holds U.S. FDA 510(k) clearance for primary clinical diagnosis.

“Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market,” said Padraig McDonnell, President and CEO of Agilent. “The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia’s leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data.”

Taylor Farms has indefinitely suspended sourcing iceberg lettuce from central Mexico during certain months of the year following a summer cyclosporiasis outbreak that sickened thousands across multiple states.
The CDC designates the period as May 1 through Aug. 31, which Taylor said mirrors central Mexico’s rainy season.

text:
By Sanskriti Shekhar

Oct 13 (Reuters) – Albertsons withdrew its fiscal 2026 forecasts on Tuesday and launched a review of its business aimed at cutting costs, lowering prices and reversing sluggish sales.

The US grocer has battled cautious consumer spending, particularly ​by lower-income shoppers, as food and fuel costs climb, alongside market share ‌loss to mass retailers such as Walmart, discount chains and private-label brands.

The review builds on a restructuring, announced in July, and is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter ending February 2027.

By then, Albertsons also aims to provide fresh short- and long-term financial targets alongside a “comprehensive turnaround plan”.

“We must turn ‌things ​around,” Meg Whitman, the former eBay and Hewlett-Packard CEO ⁠who was named executive chair last ⁠month in a newly created role to help the grocer “sharpen its strategy and strengthen execution”, said on a post-earnings call.

The company needs to move faster to cut costs and reinvest much of those savings to lower prices and improve store ​experience, she said.

CEO Susan Morris said Albertsons had accumulated too many initiatives, processes and layers of complexity over time, slowing the organization and increasing costs.

“We’re not satisfied with ⁠the results and the current trajectory of our ⁠business,” she said.

The expanded turnaround effort comes nearly two years after ​Albertsons’ proposed $24.6 billion merger with Kroger collapsed after a federal court blocked the deal on ​antitrust grounds. Albertsons subsequently terminated the agreement.

The company’s shares rose 2% on ‌Tuesday, reversing premarket losses. They had fallen 27% so far this year.

“They have hard time remaining competitive on price as some mass merchants such as Walmart have used grocery as a traffic driver and have other high margin categories such as fashion to offset ⁠food’s low margins,” said Bruce Winder, an independent retail consultant.

In July, Albertsons outlined plans to expand private-label offerings and improve e-commerce, while restructuring its 11 divisions into four regions and ⁠centralizing merchandising.

Albertsons on Tuesday described ‌those changes as the first step in its broader turnaround.

“We’ll ⁠exit areas that are underperforming,” Morris said on Tuesday.

Albertsons in July ​forecast fiscal ‌2026 adjusted earnings per share in the range of $1.75 to $1.85 ​and projected ⁠annual identical sales to decline in the range of 0.5% to 1.5% after trimming its annual target.

The grocer on Tuesday reported that its same-store sales in the second quarter ended September 12 fell 0.8%.

But adjusted profit of 36 cents per share beat estimate of 33 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG.

(Reporting by Sanskriti Shekhar in Bengaluru; Editing by Sahal ​Muhammed and Sriraj Kalluvila)

Q: Chuck Cerankosky (Northcoast Research) asked about comps performance across Albertsons' various banners and the role of geography.A: CEO Susan Morris
text:
Q & A Highlights

Q: Mark Carden (UBS) asked why now is the right time to announce a comprehensive business review, coming right after ACI Edge, and how the updated approach impacts ACI Edge's ramp and scope.A: CEO Susan Morris explained this is an evolution of ACI Edge, aimed at moving faster and more aggressively. While Q2 met expectations, the pace of improvement hasn't been fast enough to translate into sales, share growth, traffic, and earnings. She acknowledged that too many initiatives over the last 18 months created complexity and competing priorities. Going forward, focus will be on three things: driving customer experience, improving financial performance, and aggressively removing cost and complexity. Initiatives not aligned with these will be paused or stopped, with a more comprehensive plan to come at the Q4 earnings call.

Q: Edward Kelly (Wells Fargo) asked how much more room there is on cost savings given the sizable cost cuts already underway, and how the company balances speed of change with associated risk, particularly regarding the philosophy of savings versus upfront investment.A: CEO Susan Morris stated there is still substantial "blue sky" in cost-out across three areas: cost of goods (via Buying Better Together), goods not for resale (aggregating demand of an $80 billion company), and SG&A (more headcount reduction expected in the next 12-18 months). She also cited store conditions, including shrink and waste management. On speed, she emphasized that focus on fewer initiatives will drive stronger results faster, balancing risk against conflicting priorities. Interim CFO Cody Perdue added there is a lot more room to run on the cost side at a more accelerated pace to fund investment.

Q: Leah Jordan (Goldman Sachs) asked about the level of inflation seen in the business during the quarter, transportation expense trends, supplier feedback, and how inflation should trend in the back half of the year.A: CEO Susan Morris reported CPI picked up to about 2.5% in Q2, while the company passed along less than that, roughly 2% to 2.1%. Interim CFO Cody Perdue added that suppliers are coming with some cost increases, and the company has a playbook to handle them. Inflation is being seen across the P&L, but this is not new, and they will continue to manage these headwinds.

Q: Simeon Gutman (Morgan Stanley) asked for perspective on pricing position nationally and locally, and any progress since Susan took over.A: CEO Susan Morris said the approach is surgical, looking at pricing market by market, category by category, and item by item, as opportunities vary across the country. Last year, the company engaged in three price campaigns with strong success. They are learning from those pilots to understand what drove faster unit and profitability inflection, and will make strategic investments as part of the larger plan to be discussed in Q4.

Q: Rupesh Parikh (Oppenheimer) asked for puts and takes on the top line for the back half of the year, including headwinds like IRA and Cyclospora, and whether the company can quantify them.A: Interim CFO Cody Perdue unpacked the headline ID sales of minus 0.8%, noting pharmacy was up low to mid-single digits, leaving the core down just over 1.5%. He said nothing has fundamentally changed from the Q2 exit rate. The 30-basis point Cyclospora impact and 30 basis points of egg deflation are considered cyclical, not structural headwinds.

Q: John Heinbockel (Guggenheim) asked about value perception versus reality and the speed with which the company can improve value perception, noting it requires significant investment and aggressive marketing in chosen markets.A: CEO Susan Morris said value perception is a blend of product quality, variety, services, ease of shopping, and price. The goal is not to be the cheapest but to have the right balanced value proposition by market. Price investments will be surgical and strategic by market and category, not broad-based reductions. The approach is methodical and data-driven, with more details to come in Q4.

Q: Tom Palmer (JPMorgan) asked for an update on the CFO search and whether Board changes and the comprehensive review affect the timeline or candidate profile.A: CEO Susan Morris said the CFO search is underway and making good progress. She believes the evolving Board shape is exciting and that having Meg Whitman onboard sends a strong signal of support. She is confident they will find the right fitsomeone aggressive, who wants to drive change and help shape strategy. She is very optimistic about the search.

Q: Robbie Ohmes (Bank of America) asked about owned brands and whether to expect an acceleration in efforts, and about the balance between promotions versus tightening price spreads and SKU rationalization.A: CEO Susan Morris confirmed the company is absolutely accelerating owned brands efforts, improving variety, quality, and cost. On pricing versus promotions, she said it's a balance with surgical frontline pricing changes by market and category, and a refined promotional strategy. On SKU rationalization, the company is optimistic about growing owned brand share and aggressively pursuing cost reductions while carrying the products customers want and being efficient from a labor perspective.

Q: Kelly Bania (BMO) asked for a specific update on the Buying Better Together program, including the percent of national buying on the program and how savings are coming in, and whether the business review might cause a rethink or pause.A: CEO Susan Morris said the company is centralizing center store and has clearly communicated this to vendor partners. Negotiations have begun with the largest suppliers to secure lower frontline cost of goods and refine promotional strategy. She does not believe potential portfolio exits would be large enough to dramatically impact vendor negotiations, so it does not weigh into that decision at this moment.

Q: Joseph Feldman (Telsey Advisory Group) asked how the company is thinking about CapEx given the current situation, and whether the $1.9 billion to $2 billion range from last quarter still holds.A: CEO Susan Morris said the company is investing behind highest-return opportunities, including fleet investments, with a focus on returns. Interim CFO Cody Perdue added that many projects contemplated in the 2026 spend are already underway and are good ROI projects expected to continue, so he would not fundamentally call it a reset in the back half.

Planned rollout across the 772-room precinct combines service robotics with research into future humanoid housekeeping and banquet applications

SINGAPORE, Oct. 13, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- YYForce Inc. (NASDAQ: YFOR), Novotel Singapore on Stevens and Mercure Singapore on Stevens today announced a partnership to introduce service robots across the hotels’ 772-room precinct and advance AI and humanoid robotics development. The collaboration will combine a confirmed operational rollout with research informed by hotel workflows, aiming to improve guest service and develop future hospitality capabilities.

YYForce and Novotel/Mercure representatives at the Memorandum of Understanding signing ceremony.

The collaboration creates a real-world operating environment spanning 772 guestrooms, restaurants and event spaces. The hotels will contribute hospitality operating expertise and an environment in which the technology can be evaluated, while YYForce will provide robotics capabilities and technical support as it develops an integrated human, AI and robotics workforce model. The operating objective is to improve service consistency while reducing repetitive delivery, transport and cleaning work so hotel Heartists can devote more time to guest-facing service.

An initial pre-deployment comparison projects approximately 10% lower monthly operating costs across selected housekeeping, concierge and food and beverage operations, including the robot costs reflected in the model. Actual costs, productivity and guest-service outcomes will be evaluated after rollout.

“In a hotel, every journey to deliver an item and every repetitive task takes time. We want to use robotics thoughtfully, so our teams can focus their attention where it matters most to the guest,” said Piotr Kupiec, General Manager of Novotel Singapore on Stevens and Mercure Singapore on Stevens.

“Across two hotels, the opportunity is to rethink how work moves through the operation. Our measure of success will be whether we deliver more consistent service and make everyday work more manageable for our Heartists.”

The confirmed first phase will introduce specialized service robots for guest deliveries, food and beverage logistics, scheduled cleaning and concierge support. Deployment preparations include lift integration, route mapping, network requirements and guest arrival notifications. The rollout is intended to establish an operating environment in which YYForce can evaluate robotics across hotel logistics, facilities and guest-facing services.

A separate second phase is intended to focus on YYForce’s humanoid system and future iterations. Selected housekeeping and banquet workflows will inform development of robotic hardware, software and AI systems through permitted observations and agreed operational data-use arrangements.

“Working in an operating hotel environment gives us the opportunity to move robotics development from controlled demonstrations toward real-world workflows,” said Mike Fu, Chief Executive Officer of YYForce. “This collaboration connects technologies that can be deployed today with the operational learning required to develop the next generation of workforce solutions.”

“Our objective is to build the technology, operational knowledge and permitted training data needed for a future in which people, AI, specialized service robots and humanoid robots work together across hospitality, facility management and other service-intensive industries. This is a practical step toward YYForce’s 2030 Vision and our commitment to Forging Forward Together.”

Together, the partners aim to build practical knowledge of how people, AI and robotics can improve hospitality operations. The collaboration connects the hotels’ focus on guest service and more manageable work for Heartists with YYForce’s 2030 Vision for an integrated workforce ecosystem. The accompanying factsheets set out the deployment scope, AI research programme and longer-term strategy.

About YYForce Inc

YYForce Inc. (NASDAQ: YFOR) is a technology-enabled provider of workforce solutions and integrated facility management services. The Company is developing a workforce ecosystem combining human talent, on-demand staffing, artificial intelligence, autonomous robotics, humanoid robotics and smart facility management technologies. Through its operating businesses and technology platforms, YYForce seeks to improve workforce productivity, operational efficiency and service delivery across hospitality, commercial facilities and other service-intensive industries.

Annex A Deployment and operating context

The service robotics rollout is confirmed for Novotel Singapore on Stevens and Mercure Singapore on Stevens. Deployment has not yet begun. The applications below describe the planned scope; individual robot assignments and operating arrangements will be finalised before launch.

ApplicationPlanned roleIn-room deliveryDelivering guest amenities and in-room dining orders. Food Exchange and Winestone feature in the operational planning.CleaningScheduled cleaning of selected public areas, lobbies and guest corridors, with restaurant cleaning also included in operational planning.Concierge supportSupporting guest directions and basic enquiries. Check-in assistance remains subject to separate assessment and approval.

Deployment preparation

Preparations will address robot route mapping, lift configuration, network requirements and guest notifications. Tasks and operating areas will be matched to the robots’ capabilities and the hotels’ service requirements. Technical readiness will determine the implementation sequence.

Technology and support

YYForce will provide hardware, software updates, maintenance and technical personnel under the MOU. The scope of support and commercial arrangements will follow the parties’ final agreements.

Why operational capacity matters

Singapore’s hotel sector recorded average occupancy of 81.9% in 2025, up from 81.4% in 2024, while international visitor arrivals reached 16.9 million, according to the Singapore Tourism Board. These sector-wide figures provide context for the partnership’s focus on service capacity and productivity.

Source: Singapore Tourism Board, 3 February 2026, “Record Singapore tourism receipts from January to September 2025”.

Operating objectives

The initial comparison projects approximately 10% lower monthly costs for selected operations with robotics support, including the robot costs listed in the model. This estimate applies to the operations covered by the comparison. A separate planning assumption estimates a potential 5% reduction in rooms-department overtime costs. The estimates use different bases and do not represent a combined saving. Both are subject to the model’s cost scope, operating coverage and service assumptions; actual results will be assessed after deployment. Proposed performance measures include delivery turnaround, tasks completed per labour hour, reliability, colleague workload and guest feedback.

Annex B AI and humanoid robotics development

Research into future hotel applications

The collaboration envisages a second phase focused on training and developing YYForce’s humanoid robotic system and future iterations. The intended research uses hospitality workflows to help the company understand the physical tasks and service requirements that future humanoid systems would need to handle.

How hospitality workflows inform AI development

The programme is intended to connect observation of selected hospitality tasks with the development of robotic hardware, software and AI systems. YYForce’s humanoid units are expected to train alongside hotel personnel in agreed settings, helping researchers understand how people move, handle tasks and adapt to different service environments.

Housekeeping research.

Selected room-attendant workflows would be observed to map movements, physical environments and spatial requirements. This work is intended to help YYForce understand complex housekeeping tasks and translate them into future automated room-cleaning capabilities.

Banquet and guest-service research.

Selected banquet workflows would help researchers understand movement requirements, service protocols and adaptability to event settings. These observations are intended to support future banquet and guest-service applications.

YYForce intends to use permitted observations and agreed operational data to refine robotic hardware, software and AI systems. The research concerns future capabilities; it does not establish that humanoid systems are ready to clean occupied guestrooms or operate banquets independently.

An operating environment for technology development

Hotels bring together housekeeping, logistics, food and beverage, facility management and guest services. The collaboration is designed to move YYForce’s robotics strategy beyond demonstrations and allow the company to evaluate how specialised service robots and future humanoid systems can work alongside people across these functions. YYForce expects the insights to contribute to applications that could be adapted to other service-intensive environments.

Research data and intellectual property

The parties’ agreed contractual arrangements will govern research activities, permitted data use and ownership of research outputs. YYForce’s objective is to develop proprietary robotics know-how and operational datasets from permitted research, while the hotels retain rights to their operational protocols, confidential business information and brand assets. Any use of guest or employee personal data would require separate review and appropriate safeguards.

Additional YYForce commentary

“We can deploy specialized robots for tasks that can already be automated while simultaneously training humanoid systems to understand more complex hospitality activities such as housekeeping and banquet operations.”

Mike Fu, Chief Executive Officer, YYForce Inc.

Annex C YYForce 2030 Vision and corporate statements

YYForce 2030 Vision

The collaboration aligns with YYForce’s 2030 Vision to develop an integrated future workforce ecosystem combining:

• Human workforce solutions and on-demand staffing

• Artificial intelligence

• Autonomous service robotics

• Humanoid robotics

• Smart facility management technologies

• Data-driven workforce and operational management systems

The Company’s long-term objective is for automation to handle selected repetitive, logistics-intensive and physically demanding activities, while people focus on service, decision-making and customer engagement. YYForce expects insights from hospitality operations to support applications that may be adapted to other service-intensive environments.

The Company believes hospitality offers an important environment in which this human-and-machine workforce model can be developed and evaluated. The initiative is intended to build operational knowledge and robotics capabilities that may support future commercial applications across service industries.

“This collaboration represents another step toward YYForce’s 2030 Vision and our commitment to Forging Forward Together.”

Mike Fu, Chief Executive Officer, YYForce Inc.

Officials discussed setting up a mechanism for the two countries to notify each other of AI incidents which could threaten national security.

By framing their efforts as a “slowdown” rather than an industry-wide push for better security standards, AI labs may have set themselves up for years of regulatory headaches.

description:

Azure Maia 300 is described as "a complete intelligent system" designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today.
Its next-gen chip is created with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads, according to a blog post by Microsoft's EVP for Cloud and AI, Scott Guthrie.

text:
Microsoft has lifted the lid on the next generation of its Azure Maia custom AI chips, saying it will usher in a new phase of its compute infrastructure where everything is closely integrated to meet the demands of agentic inference.

The Redmond giant says its Azure Maia 200, announced earlier this year, is now serving production workloads and that a successor is already planned for 2027.

Azure Maia 300 is described as "a complete intelligent system" designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today. Microsoft claims a full 96-accelerator configuration will deliver up to seven times Maia 200's rack-scale token throughput, while offering 40 percent more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems.

Its next-gen chip is created with an inference-first architecture optimized for long-context, memory-intensive and decode-heavy AI workloads, according to a blog post by Microsoft's EVP for Cloud and AI, Scott Guthrie.

The firm envisions it being deployed in rack-scale systems comprising up to 96 accelerators, while each Maia 300 will feature eight HBM4 memory stacks providing up to 18 TB/s of peak memory bandwidth, the better to support execution of large models and long-context workloads.

This sounds similar to the kind of rack-scale AI equipment that has already been developed by Nvidia for its GPU accelerators, and more recently by AMD with its Helion and Helios infrastructure, all designed to make the most of their own specific silicon and software stacks.

Microsoft says that Maia 300 is "built as a complete system, with software, silicon, physical rack infrastructure, networking, and datacenters co-designed to operate as a single platform to meet the demands of cloud-scale agentic inference."

It insists that this system-level approach is necessary for agentic workloads, which involve multi-step execution, long-context decoding and tool use, and "change the computational profile and arithmetic intensity of inference."

The growing emphasis on in-house integration contrasts with Microsoft's 2024 "AI Access Principles," which stressed partnerships across its technology stack.

The firm even complained to the European Commission's competition authorities that Google had a competitive advantage because of its approach.

"Only one company – Google," said Microsoft at the time, "is vertically integrated in a manner that provides it with strength and independence at every AI layer from chips to a thriving mobile app store. Everybody else must rely on partnerships to innovate and compete."

Microsoft now has its own AI chips, rack-scale designs, and internally developed MAI models, giving it more control over its stack. It plans to scale Azure Maia to "multi-gigawatt deployments" starting in 2027.

We asked Microsoft for comment.

Guthrie said that the firm will share more details on its strategy at next month's Microsoft Ignite 2026 event in San Francisco. ®

text:
OpenAI may be one of the world's most recognizable AI brands. To sell its business, its strongest marketing channel is decidedly offline.

"Field is the one I would definitely put out as our strongest channel right now," said Leila Woodington, OpenAI's head of B2B marketing, EMEA, during a panel at Semrush Spotlight in London today.

The reason is the gap between using ChatGPT and buying it. Most people know the product, Woodington said, but that awareness does not tell a company how to deploy it across thousands of employees, or persuade several executives who sign off on the purchase.

In-person events are one piece of a broader effort by the ChatGPT maker to explain the product to businesses. OpenAI also works with what Woodington called a "bench of really carefully curated creators and influencers who genuinely love our products," who are brought in when the company ships something new, alongside leveraging social media.

OpenAI doubled its sponsored Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT from 61 in June to 122 in July, according to Business Insider.

"This is a complex buying decision that we're influencing," said Woodington. "No single one of those things is going to persuade the CEO of Fortune 500 companies to buy our technology."

OpenAI Wants ChatGPT Ads to Become a Permanent Line Item in Agency Media Plans

But keeping a constant brand message is its own challenge as OpenAI's product lineup grows.

The company launched Dots, a persistent AI agent, at its developer conference in San Francisco last month alongside a plethora of tools. Instead of building a fresh campaign for each launch, Woodington's team runs a fixed calendar, including about two webinars a month, and slots new products into it.

"We have a set of activities that are predefined, and then we plug launches into them, rather than taking every single launch and then spinning our wheels trying to figure out a way to get it to market," she said.

The company is also building local teams in the markets it sells to, including people who understand local languages, cultures, and trade organizations.

Woodington, who previously spent more than a decade building Facebook's B2B marketing function before working at Snap and an AI-powered video startup, joined OpenAI more than a year ago to help build its marketing operation.

"[CMOs] seem to expect that I'm completely on top of every single AI technology, at least within our own tools," Woodington said. "[But] we are trying to keep up in the same way as others."

text:
The investigational RNAi candidate targets activin receptor-like kinase 7: © Dr_Microbe - stock.adobe.com

Rona Therapeutics (Rona) announced October 13, 2026, that it has granted Roche an exclusive worldwide license for Rona's investigational RNA interference (RNAi) candidate targeting activin receptor-like kinase 7 (ALK7) for treating obesity and metabolic diseases.¹ The candidate uses Rona's proprietary extrahepatic delivery platform.

Under the agreement, Rona will receive upfront and near-term milestone payments of up to $100 million. It is also eligible to receive up to $1.06 billion in additional development, regulatory, and commercial milestone payments, plus tiered royalties on global net sales.¹

"ALK7 is a compelling obesity and metabolic disease target with the potential to directly address adipose tissue biology," said Stella Shi, CEO and founder of Rona Therapeutics, in a company press release.¹ "This collaboration combines Rona's pioneering extrahepatic RNAi R&D platform with Roche's strong expertise and commitment in global development and commercialization of medicines for the treatment of obesity and metabolic diseases to bring this important therapeutic candidate to patients."

Key facts

Drug: Investigational ALK7 (ACVR1C)-targeting RNAi candidate; Rona Therapeutics, licensed to Roche

Class: RNA interference therapy delivered via Rona's extrahepatic delivery platform

Target rationale: ALK7 regulates adipocyte lipid storage and lipolysis; genetic variants link reduced ALK7 activity to lower diabetes risk

Indication studied: Obesity and metabolic diseases (preclinical/discovery-stage program)

Deal terms: Up to $100 million upfront and near-term milestones; up to $1.06 billion in additional milestones; tiered royalties

Differentiation: Acts directly on adipose tissue, unlike CNS-acting incretin therapies

Related pipeline: Rona's RN3161 (INHBE siRNA) completed phase 1 cohort 1 dosing in December 2025

Geography: Worldwide license

What is ALK7, and why is it a validated target for obesity?

ALK7, encoded by the ACVR1C gene, is a member of the transforming growth factor-beta receptor superfamily and is expressed predominantly in adipose tissue, where it regulates lipid storage, lipolysis, and energy homeostasis.¹ Human genetic evidence supports the target. For example, in an analysis of more than 300,000 UK Biobank participants, carriers of ACVR1C coding variants had a lower waist-to-hip ratio and up to 30% lower risk of type 2 diabetes, and carriers of predicted damaging variants in a separate exome-sequencing cohort had a 54% lower risk, consistent with reduced ALK7 activity protecting against adverse fat distribution and metabolic disease.²

How does this approach differ from existing obesity treatments?

Unlike incretin-based therapies, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, which act primarily in the central nervous system to reduce appetite and energy intake,³ ALK7 inhibition is designed to act directly on adipocytes, with the potential to selectively reduce visceral and other ectopic fat depots while preserving lean mass.¹ Rona and Roche describe this mechanism as potentially complementary to, rather than purely competitive with, incretin drugs, raising the possibility of combination use.¹

What else is in Rona's pipeline?

Founded in 2021, Rona has raised roughly $200 million from healthcare investors and strategic partners and has advanced 4 programs into clinical development using its extrahepatic delivery, multi-valency, and oligo chemistry platforms.⁴ Its most advanced obesity program, RN3161, a short interfering RNA targeting INHBE, completed dosing of its first cohort in a phase 1, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in December 2025, with Rona reporting a favorable initial safety and tolerability profile. Additional cohorts are expected in 2026.⁴

"We are excited to partner with Rona Therapeutics, complementing our robust CVRM [cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic] pipeline and reinforcing our commitment to delivering next-generation metabolic therapies," said Boris L. Zaïtra, head of corporate business development at Roche, in the release.¹

What are the limitations?

The licensed ALK7 candidate has not been named or disclosed to be in clinical testing, unlike Rona's INHBE program, so no human safety or efficacy data exist for it yet.¹ The human genetic associations between ACVR1C variants and metabolic outcomes do not necessarily guarantee that RNAi-mediated silencing of ALK7 will replicate those effects therapeutically or prove safe in patients.² The $1.06 billion milestone figure represents the maximum potential payment contingent on development, regulatory, and commercial success, not a guaranteed sum.¹ Roche, as exclusive worldwide licensee, now controls the candidate's further development and commercialization timeline.¹

Autologous cell therapies face unique challenges for patient access. Such highly personalized treatments must contend with geographic barriers. Cell and gene therapy (CGT) products cannot serve their purposes if patients struggle to access them. Geographic barriers and regulatory considerations must be managed hand in hand.

This eBook features insights from bioprocessing experts on the evolving landscape of access for autologous cell therapies. First, a roundtable discussion reveals how hybrid distributed models could provide a bridge from centralized manufacturing to point-of-care models. Regional and hub-and-spoke approaches offer a pragmatic balance between patient proximity and centralized quality oversight. Standardization is the key to decentralization, quality systems must be redesigned for distribution, and digital orchestration is a strategic requirement. As CGTs gain traction commercially, the distance between patients and specialized collection centers threatens to exacerbate current problems with accessibility.

text:
OpenAI may be one of the world’s most recognizable AI brands. To sell its business, its strongest marketing channel is decidedly offline.

“Field is the one I would definitely put out as our strongest channel right now,” said Leila Woodington, OpenAI’s head of B2B marketing, EMEA, during a panel at Semrush Spotlight in London today.

The reason is the gap between using ChatGPT and buying it. Most people know the product, Woodington said, but that awareness does not tell a company how to deploy it across thousands of employees, or persuade several executives who sign off on the purchase.

In-person events are one piece of a broader effort by the ChatGPT maker to explain the product to businesses. OpenAI also works with what Woodington called a “bench of really carefully curated creators and influencers who genuinely love our products,” who are brought in when the company ships something new, alongside leveraging social media.

OpenAI doubled its sponsored Instagram posts promoting ChatGPT from 61 in June to 122 in July, according to Business Insider.

“This is a complex buying decision that we’re influencing,” said Woodington. “No single one of those things is going to persuade the CEO of Fortune 500 companies to buy our technology.”

But keeping a constant brand message is its own challenge as OpenAI’s product lineup grows.

The company launched Dots, a persistent AI agent, at its developer conference in San Francisco last month alongside a plethora of tools. Instead of building a fresh campaign for each launch, Woodington’s team runs a fixed calendar, including about two webinars a month, and slots new products into it.

“We have a set of activities that are predefined, and then we plug launches into them, rather than taking every single launch and then spinning our wheels trying to figure out a way to get it to market,” she said.

The company is also building local teams in the markets it sells to, including people who understand local languages, cultures, and trade organizations.

Woodington, who previously spent more than a decade building Facebook’s B2B marketing function before working at Snap and an AI-powered video startup, joined OpenAI more than a year ago to help build its marketing operation.

“[CMOs] seem to expect that I’m completely on top of every single AI technology, at least within our own tools,” Woodington said. “[But] we are trying to keep up in the same way as others.”
