text:
Enterprise AI conversations have moved from experimentation to implementation. At Capgemini SPARK 2026, the focus shifted from implementation to value realization. The gathering explored the theme, “Make it real: from action to value,” and how organizations apply AI at scale for outcomes. SPARK revealed the same transition as FinOps X earlier this year, and leaders are consequently asking how their AI investments will translate into outcomes.

Value Measurement Is Becoming The New Executive Imperative

SPARK’s clearest thread was from action to value. The fireside chat, “The AI Value Imperative: Scaling Impact Across the Insurance Enterprise,” featured leaders from Grange Insurance and Capgemini. The implications extend beyond insurance: As AI enters operations, success must connect to outcomes rather than activity. Models deployed, users onboarded, agents created, or tokens consumed describe activity — not enterprise value. Instead, the next phase connects AI investment with growth, productivity, customer experience, risk reduction, innovation, and better decisions. Consequently, enterprise AI is entering its value management era.

The Industry Is Moving From Automation To Agency

Agentic AI, not surprisingly, was prominent. For example, AWS framed its session as “A Leader’s Guide to Agentic AI: From Automation to Agency,” while “The Agentic Economy Is Here” featured executives from Uber, Meta, and Universal Entertainment. Agentic systems can coordinate work toward outcomes, but the economic question is whether greater machine autonomy produces better business outcomes. The value puzzle still needs to be solved.

AI Strategy Is Not Just A Technology Strategy

AI transformation requires rethinking decisions, work, governance, and outcomes. The AI-first enterprise is becoming this generation’s digital-first enterprise, except AI increasingly participates as a resource in the form of agents, tools, and workflows rather than merely digitizing workflows.

Governance, Trust, Security, And Data Become The Foundation For Scale

As enterprises move from pilots to scale, governance, security, and trusted data become foundational. Moreover, controls are not solely compliance obligations; they enable confident deployment. The divide may emerge between organizations with sophisticated models and those able to operationalize them across trusted data, governance, security, and processes. Ultimately, AI advantage increasingly depends on the enterprise operating model surrounding the model.

AI’s Economic And Workforce Impact Is Moving To The Foreground

Gita Gopinath, Harvard professor and former IMF chief economist, broadened the conversation to AI, productivity, inequality, the macroeconomic outlook, and labor markets. Consequently, AI’s implications extend to work, talent, skills, and productivity gains. For CEOs, therefore, it is increasingly a workforce, operating model, and economic agenda.

Power And Prediction: When The System Becomes The Product

Perhaps the most riveting session was the closing keynote from Ajay Agrawal, professor of economics of machine intelligence, focused on “power and prediction” and transitional AI. As AI makes prediction cheaper and more capable, the economic value of individual tasks will decline while value shifts toward the systems that orchestrate decisions, judgment, and action. The implication is not simply that enterprises must redesign work but that leaders must rethink where value accrues as AI changes the economics of decisions. This raises the stakes for AI value management.

The Bottom Line: Stop Automating Yesterday’s Enterprise

text:
Albertsons Companies reported Oct. 13 that second quarter net income fell 69 percent to $51.5 million, or 11 cents per share, as identical sales declined 0.8 percent for the second straight quarter. The Boise, Idaho-based retailer also withdrew its fiscal 2026 outlook and said it is launching a comprehensive review of its cost structure, operating model, banner portfolio and capital allocation.

The results cover the 12 weeks ended Sept. 12. Albertsons said the quarter was in line with the reduced outlook it issued in July, when it announced the ACI Edge restructuring that consolidated 11 divisions into four regions and centralized center store merchandising. The company now says it will not provide updated guidance until the review is finished in the fourth quarter.

“Although our second quarter performance was in line with the expectations in our revised outlook, our results do not reflect the potential of the company,” said Susan Morris, CEO of Albertsons Cos. “We are launching a comprehensive business review to speed up improvements in Albertsons’ performance and tackle even harder a cost structure we can no longer afford.”

Morris said the review will look for ways to simplify the organization, improve decision-making and reinvest savings in customer value.

In her first earnings call since being named executive chair in September, Meg Whitman told investors the grocer’s performance “has fallen short” despite strong local banners, robust pharmacy and e-commerce businesses and substantial cash flow.

“We must also take a close look at our portfolio of banners, markets, assets, and businesses as well as at potential strategic actions we can take to enhance shareholder value,” Whitman said. “Susan and I agree that everything should be on the table as we figure out how Albertsons should be structured to better compete in the years ahead. Albertsons must become a simpler, more focused company that gets the basics right every day.”

Sales and margins

Net sales and other revenue slipped 0.1 percent to $18.89 billion from $18.92 billion a year earlier. The identical sales decline was partly offset by higher fuel sales. Digital sales grew 11 percent, down from 13 percent growth in the first quarter, and pharmacy sales continued to grow despite ongoing headwinds from the Inflation Reduction Act.

Gross margin rate fell to 26.8 percent from 27 percent. Excluding fuel and LIFO expense, the rate was down 17 basis points, which Albertsons attributed to higher delivery and handling costs tied to digital growth and higher shrink. Pharmacy margins improved, and the company said it continued to fund investments in price and value through productivity initiatives.

Selling and administrative expenses rose to 25.6 percent of revenue from 25.4 percent, driven by sales deleveraging. Dollar expenses were roughly flat, with cost controls offsetting inflation and higher litigation costs related to the terminated Kroger merger.

Charges weigh on the bottom line

Several items pushed net income lower. The company recorded $42.4 million in property disposition and impairment losses, up from $4.4 million a year ago, mostly from store impairments and equipment disposals. Interest expense rose to $125 million from $105.3 million on higher borrowings.

Adjusted net income was $179 million, or 36 cents per share, down from $248.4 million, or 44 cents, a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA fell 7.6 percent to $784 million, or 4.1 percent of revenue, compared with $848.4 million, or 4.5 percent, in the prior-year quarter. The company’s net debt ratio climbed to 2.42 from 2.02.

Capital spending and buybacks

Through the first 28 weeks of fiscal 2026, Albertsons spent $899.6 million on capital projects, completing 38 remodels and opening seven new stores. The company repurchased 26 million shares for $387.6 million during the period and declared a quarterly dividend of 17 cents per share, payable Nov. 6.

Albertsons said it expects to deliver a refreshed financial framework alongside its turnaround plan on its fourth quarter earnings call and plans to hold an investor day in spring 2027. Cody Perdue is serving as interim CFO following the retirement of Sharon McCollam.

As of Sept. 12, Albertsons operated 2,240 stores in 35 states and the District of Columbia, down from 2,257 a year earlier, under 22 banners including Albertsons, Safeway, Vons, Jewel-Osco, Shaw’s, ACME, Tom Thumb and Randalls.

text:
Jensen Huang says Nvidia will announce $2B of European investments within a week, on top of $8B over the past year, and named four French startups in Paris. Nvidia committed more than $40B to AI equity in the first four months of this year alone.

Jensen Huang says Nvidia will announce $2B of European investments within a week. He was speaking in Paris on the first day of a tour that also takes in London and Berlin.

That follows $8B put into the continent over the past year, Bloomberg reported. He also announced funding for four French startups, Doctolib, Genesis AI, Pigment and Entalpic.

The sums are modest by Nvidia’s standards. The company was worth about $5.7T this month, while ASML, Europe’s most valuable listed company, stood near $700B in July.

“Europe needs to get in the race,” Huang said at the event, where he pitched open-source models as cheaper, more adaptable and the way for the continent to close the gap.

One cheque explains the ranking. Nvidia was reported in September to be weighing up to $10B as an anchor investor in Anthropic’s flotation, more than Mistral’s entire round.

That round, €3B at a valuation above €21B, is the largest any European tech company has raised. Huang has pledged hundreds of billions worldwide.

Nvidia also owns much of its own demand. Its equity holdings reached $99B by July, in companies that buy its chips, up from about $7B a year earlier.

The pitch to Europe is sovereignty. Open models matter because they can be customised for languages and for your own sovereignty, Huang said, and they cost less to run.

He is not the first supplier to say it. Alibaba’s chairman told a Turin audience six days earlier that open source is the only way for Europe to be truly independent.

Neither man is European and both sell the inputs. Open weights lower the cost of the model and leave the hardware bill exactly where it was, which is with Nvidia.

Mistral is the test. It trained Large 4 on 4,000 Grace Blackwell GPUs in European data centres, and publishes the weights on 27 October.

One of the new investments has already repriced. A secondary sale in April valued Doctolib at €3.6B, a 38% discount to the €5.8B it carried after its 2022 raise.

The venue is probably Berlin. Nvidia’s GTC conference runs there from 20 to 22 October, inside the week Huang described, and he arrives as European calls to slow AI development grow.

To change course, Albertsons will concentrate on better serving shoppers by focusing on core areas like price, promotions, freshness, convenience and customer service, she said.

"We recognize the need to simplify how we work, sharpen accountability, and move with greater speed and discipline to deliver better results," said Morris. "Going forward, our focus will be much narrower. Our resources will be concentrated on the right projects that most accelerate our results, and our expectations and accountability for results will be significantly higher."

Morris indicated that Albertsons will examine its workforce as it looks to save money. "We did some work last year and saw a substantial reduction in headcount, but quite frankly, there's more to be had, and you'll see us taking aggressive action there in the next 12 to 18 months as well," she said.

Albertsons expects to provide details about its turnaround strategy during its fourth-quarter earnings call, Morris said.

Albertsons did not provide updated projections about how it sees the business performing during the coming quarters. "Although the business performed in line with our revised guidance expectations during the second quarter, we do not believe it is prudent today to provide an incremental update to our financial outlook," Cody Perdue, Albertsons' interim CFO, said during the earnings call.

text:
As technology heavyweights including OpenAI, Amazon, Anthropic, Tesla, Google and Microsoft pour massive resources into custom in-house processors, former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger has offered a reality check: designing specially made silicon with AI will not solve the artificial intelligence industry's most stubborn physical shortages. In discussions exploring how AI is changing semiconductor design, Gelsinger acknowledged that machine-learning tools are accelerating the creation of microprocessors. However, he warned that the true bottlenecks constraining the global AI infrastructure race extend far beyond the speed of chip design itself. “AI will make chip design faster. It won’t make chips easier. It’s not just compute,” Gelsinger wrote, highlighting a discussion he held with Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) partners Raghu Raghuram and Guido Appenzeller on what is actually limiting the broader rollout. He highlighted four key chokepoints:1) Silicon still takes quarters to manufacture, no matter how fast we design2) Memory bandwidth and advanced packaging are huge choke points3) Copper is giving way to optical4) Energy capacity is becoming economic capacityI also think today's explosion of specialized AI chips will consolidate around fewer architectures.

Where AI helps in chip design, and where it falls flat

Addressing whether current industry hardware, like Nvidia's Blackwell, represents the final generation of processors designed prior to automated AI engineering, Gelsinger noted that the shift is already well underway, pointing to OpenAI’s custom silicon effort, code-named “Jalapeno.” He characterized projects like Jalapeno as an example of designing from first principles, where machine learning automates vast portions of the workflow and discards legacy design conventions. Yet, Gelsinger stressed that significant parts of semiconductor engineering remain outside the reach of automated AI tools. “When you look at things like Jalapeno (OpenAI chip) today, you say that’s sort of a first principle’s use of AI in the chip design process where you throw out a lot of those things. Now, there are pieces of design that are still really hard right in that sense and a lot of the analog aspect is probably the best example that there are things that are still not ‘AI-able’. You just need lots of silicon data to get those. So you either get so conservative in your analog design that you're able to say ‘AI it” or you have to do those the hard way,” he said during the conversation. To cope with these limits, Gelsinger explained that engineers must either design their analog systems with extreme conservatism to allow AI tools to process them, or continue engineering those components “the hard way.”

title: Microsoft's CEO Just Called for a Kill Switch on AI. Here Is What It Means for the Stock.
description:
Satya Nadella spent a weekend post saying that AI systems need emergency off switches, by which he means authorized humans who can shut a model down in the middle of a task.
Microsoft holds about a 27% stake in OpenAI and spent $115.95 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2026.
The timing matters because over the past year the stock rose only 6.78%, while the S&P 500 gained 19.15%.
Customers stop renewing software whose output they cannot trust, and renewal rates are how this industry gets valued.
The governance positioning adds value because it ties AI usage to identity and compliance contracts that customers rarely replace.
text:
Satya Nadella spent a weekend post saying that AI systems need emergency off switches, by which he means authorized humans who can shut a model down in the middle of a task. The idea stands out. He runs Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT | MSFT Price Prediction), the company with the greatest commercial exposure to frontier AI, and he is publicly asking for a way to stop his own product mid-sentence.

Here is the key passage in full: “We can’t treat superintelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers and actions. We must build containment systems whose behavior we can observe, limits that we can test, and actions we can always contain.”

For investors, this is a product decision. Microsoft holds about a 27% stake in OpenAI and spent $115.95 billion on capital expenditures in fiscal 2026. Now it wants to sell customers the controls that can stop those systems.

The timing matters because over the past year the stock rose only 6.78%, while the S&P 500 gained 19.15%.

What an AI Emergency Brake Looks Like Inside Your Company

In engineering terms, an emergency off switch is four ordinary pieces of software, the first of which is a set of breakpoints inside long-running agent tasks, so a person can pause the job between steps.

The second is permission scopes that limit which files, systems, and accounts an agent can touch, and the third is logging that records what the agent did and why it did it.

The fourth is an identity layer that decides who is allowed to stop the agent. Companies already buy every one of these tools to manage their employees.

Microsoft already sells the version built for agents. Agent 365 had nearly 40 million agents registered two months after it launched.

Verification Tax Could Decide Copilot Renewals

The most useful idea in this debate is what you might call the verification tax. If employees spend hours checking what a model produced, the checking eats part of the promised productivity gain. Customers stop renewing software whose output they cannot trust, and renewal rates are how this industry gets valued.

Microsoft 365 Copilot passed 30 million paid seats. Purview, Microsoft’s compliance tool, tracked more than 15 billion Copilot interactions, up nearly 360% year over year.

That audit volume shows customers already want a record of what the AI did. When a system’s behavior can be observed, checking it costs less, and that protects the renewal.

Containment Favors the Company That Owns Identity

Governance, audit trails, and permissions are enterprise software problems. Microsoft already runs the identity and compliance layer where corporate customers manage their people, so selling control over agents extends a business it already has.

Nadella has said “every model is substitutable,” and Azure AI Foundry offers more than 11,000 models. If you can swap one model for another, the lasting value sits in the control layer around them.

A more cynical read has merit. The incumbent with the largest frontier position gains when safety rules raise the cost of entry for everyone behind it, because only well-funded companies can afford to make powerful models observable, testable, and interruptible. That incentive can exist even if Nadella’s concern about safety is genuine.

Capex Is Climbing Faster Than Proof of Return

The market wants to see a return on the spending before it shows up in reported numbers. Fourth-quarter capex was $35.80 billion, up 109.6%, and management expects fiscal 2027 spending to grow again. A containment framework will not answer that question soon, although it protects the renewal base that pays for the spending.

The picks-and-shovels side of AI is in demand. The power, cooling, and networking suppliers behind every hyperscaler’s capex line are why we pulled seven of them into a free report you can grab here.

Demand data supports the spending, as Azure grew 43%, and revenue already under contract but not yet recorded reached $678 billion.

Two signals would weaken the bull case. The first is AI features handed out free to defend seats when they should be sold as paid add-ons to existing enterprise agreements. The second is capex guidance that keeps rising without matching revenue growth.

What Investors Should Weigh in MSFT Stock Now

At about 30 times earnings and $541.15 a share, investors pay a modest premium for a company whose net income rose 31.3% in fiscal 2026.

The governance positioning adds value because it ties AI usage to identity and compliance contracts that customers rarely replace.

A year of trailing the market has brought down expectations, although a 0.66% dividend yield offers little buffer if capex keeps rising.

Microsoft holds a distinctive position in this market. Standalone model developers lack the enterprise control layer, and Microsoft also collects OpenAI’s $250 billion Azure commitment.

title: Preparing Pharmacists for Psychedelic Medicine | Pharmacy Times
authors: Jarret LeBeau, PharmD, BCACP, RPh, Andrew Krut, PharmD, RPh, Jarret LeBeau, Andrew Krut
description:

Many Required Competencies Are Already Familiar to Pharmacists Psychedelic medicine is novel, but many of its medication-management challenges are not.
Rather, psychedelic care offers another opportunity to use multidisciplinary teams in which each profession practices according to its competencies to optimize patient outcomes.
A Timely Opportunity for Pharmacy The federal government is increasingly preparing for the potential entry of psychedelic medicines into clinical care.

text:
Psychedelic medicines are moving closer to potential integration into clinical practice. Although much of the public discussion has previously focused on whether these therapies are effective, an equally important question is emerging: If psychedelic medicines receive FDA approval, how can they be implemented safely within the US health care system?

Image credit: 24K-Production | stock.adobe.com

Recent clinical development and efficacy data have strengthened the rationale for considering this question seriously. Two phase 3 trials of 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA)–assisted therapy demonstrated significant improvements in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms compared with therapy plus placebo.1,2 However, the FDA declined to approve the initial application and requested an additional phase 3 study.3

More recently, two phase 3 trials of COMP360 synthetic psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) met their primary efficacy endpoints, and a rolling new drug application submission and initial FDA review are underway.4 Other compounds continue to advance, such as BPL-003 (mebufotenin benzoate), an intranasal formulation of 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine (5-MeO-DMT) also in development for TRD, with encouraging early-phase clinical data.5

In July 2026, Eli Lilly and Company announced an agreement to acquire AtaiBeckley, the developer of BPL-003, illustrating growing pharmaceutical-industry investment in this therapeutic area.6 None of these developments guarantee FDA approval. They do, however, create questions surrounding clinical implementation increasingly relevant.

As psychedelic drugs transition from substances historically associated with illicit use toward potential regulated therapeutics, clinical evidence is developing within a complex and unique cultural context. Psychedelic drugs and the people who use them continue to carry substantial stigma shaped, in part, by decades of prohibition. Stigma is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of health that can influence interactions within the health care system.7 Emerging evidence suggests that concerns about stigmatization and clinician knowledge can directly affect patients’ experiences and willingness to discuss psychedelic use with health care professionals.8

As evidence evolves, pharmacists should educate themselves on potential therapeutic applications and evaluate them objectively, without allowing either historical perceptions or contemporary enthusiasm to substitute for evidence.

Preparing for Safe Clinical Integration

Psychedelic therapies present implementation challenges different from those associated with most conventional psychiatric medications. Administration may occur episodically under supervision, potentially requiring prolonged monitoring, careful patient screening for interactions and contraindications, coordination of psychiatric medications before and after treatment, and systems for managing both psychological and physiologic adverse events.

These challenges are receiving increased attention from federal legislators, regulators, and agencies. In 2024, the bipartisan Congressional Psychedelics Advancing Therapies (PATH) Caucus issued a request for information (RFI) seeking stakeholder recommendations regarding the infrastructure, standards, and policies that could support safe implementation of psychedelic therapies.9 The Psychedelic Pharmacists Association (PPA), a professional organization focused on education, research, policy, and the pharmacist’s role in psychedelic medicine, responded with recommendations emphasizing multidisciplinary care, medication management, practitioner training, patient screening, pharmacovigilance, ethical safeguards, and pharmacist participation throughout the psychedelic continuum of care.

Federal engagement gained further momentum in 2026. The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) requested stakeholder input on workforce training and care-delivery models for potential FDA-approved psychedelic therapies in ambulatory settings, including Federally Qualified Health Centers and Rural Health Clinics.10 PPA’s response emphasized roles pharmacists already perform across health care, including medication screening and consultation, mental health pharmacotherapy, Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) implementation, medication education, drug information, research, and controlled-substance management. The response also encouraged consideration of pharmacists with appropriate additional mental health and psychedelic-specific training for more direct roles in administration and monitoring.11

Most recently, FDA finalized guidance addressing clinical investigations of psychedelic drugs and convened a September 2026 public hearing and request for comments regarding the potential future therapeutic use of psychedelic drugs in supervised and supportive settings.12,13 PPA submitted written comments and participated in the public hearing, addressing FDA's four requested domains—provider training and credentialing, patient safety, access, and data collection and standardization—while continuing to emphasize appropriate pharmacist participation within multidisciplinary models of care.

Together, PPA’s engagement with the PATH Caucus, HRSA, and FDA reflects a broader point: pharmacists should participate in designing systems for psychedelic medicines before those systems are finalized, rather than attempting to define the pharmacist's role after implementation has already begun.

Many Required Competencies Are Already Familiar to Pharmacists

Psychedelic medicine is novel, but many of its medication-management challenges are not. Pharmacists routinely evaluate drug-drug and drug-disease interactions, conduct medication reconciliation, develop medication tapering strategies, educate patients, monitor adverse effects, manage controlled substances, and collaborate with other health care professionals. These competencies may be particularly important among patients with treatment-resistant psychiatric disorders, who frequently present with complex medication regimens.

Board-certified psychiatric pharmacists (BCPPs) represent an especially clear example. Their specialized training in psychiatric pharmacotherapy and experience practicing within interdisciplinary mental health teams make them well positioned to contribute to psychedelic care models; however, meaningful roles need not be limited exclusively to BCPPs. Pharmacists with appropriate mental health experience and additional role-specific training may contribute across screening, medication management, patient education, monitoring, drug information, research, pharmacovigilance, and policy.

This position is increasingly supported outside PPA. A 2026 Comment published in Nature Mental Health specifically examined current and future roles for psychiatric pharmacists in psychedelic therapy, concluding that integration of BCPPs could improve patient safety, address workforce shortages, and expand access while acknowledging unresolved questions involving training, regulation, and reimbursement.14

Importantly, possessing a PharmD alone should not be interpreted as sufficient preparation for every potential role. Direct participation in psychedelic administration or facilitation would require additional competency-based education, with requirements likely varying according to the drug, clinical setting, and responsibilities of the pharmacist. The appropriate scope of pharmacist involvement has not yet been established and will likely vary according to the therapy, treatment setting, regulatory requirements, and pharmacist competencies. Standards in this area remain under development.

REMS and Medication Safety May Provide a Familiar Framework

If the FDA determines that a psychedelic product requires a REMS or other restricted-distribution strategy, pharmacists would enter particularly familiar territory.

Esketamine (Spravato; Janssen Pharmaceuticals) provides an existing psychiatric example. Its REMS requires certified health care settings, administration under direct observation, post-administration monitoring, and specific dispensing requirements for certified pharmacies.15 Pharmacists already contribute to processes involving medication distribution, documentation, monitoring requirements, patient education, and regulatory compliance. Although the requirements for future psychedelic products cannot be assumed before FDA review, this experience provides a useful model for considering pharmacy's potential contribution.

Pharmacists may also support institutional protocols addressing medication reconciliation, storage and diversion prevention, adverse-event reporting, emergency procedures, and transitions on and off concomitant psychiatric medications. These functions are extensions of established clinical pharmacy practice rather than entirely new professional responsibilities. Integrating pharmacists to assist in monitoring administrations is a natural progression of that extension.

Workforce and Access Should Be Part of the Conversation

Safe implementation must also be feasible. HRSA’s RFI specifically asked how potential psychedelic therapies could eventually be delivered in medically underserved communities.10 The PPA response cautioned that credentialing requirements must protect patients without unnecessarily limiting the workforce available in rural and underserved settings.11

Workforce demands could be substantial if these therapies are approved and widely adopted. One analysis projected that treating 1 million patients annually by 2031 could require around 55,000 to 100,000 additional psychedelic therapy clinicians, equivalent to roughly 10% to 17% of the US mental health workforce.16 These projections highlight the potential for workforce limitations to become an important barrier to equitable access.

Pharmacists could represent one component of a multidisciplinary solution. Psychiatric pharmacists may be particularly suited to direct clinical responsibilities; nonpsychiatric pharmacists may support screening, medication management, education, referral, safety monitoring, and continuity of care. The goal should not be to replace psychiatrists, psychologists, nurses, therapists, or other professionals. Rather, psychedelic care offers another opportunity to use multidisciplinary teams in which each profession practices according to its competencies to optimize patient outcomes.

FDA-Regulated Care Is Not the Only Emerging Setting

Federal approval remains the clearest pathway for incorporating psychedelic drugs into conventional medical practice, but it is not the only environment pharmacists will encounter. State-regulated programs in Oregon and Colorado established models of supervised psychedelic services outside traditional FDA drug approval pathways, while New Mexico is developing a regulated medical psilocybin program currently. Early real-world data from Oregon have begun to characterize outcomes, with a prospective cohort study reporting improvements in depression, anxiety, PTSD symptoms, mental well-being, and life satisfaction following state-regulated psilocybin services, while serious adverse reactions were uncommon.17 Pharmacists should be aware of state-run programs and be prepared to counsel patients accordingly.

Psychedelic use also occurs outside regulated medical systems. Pharmacists should acknowledge this reality and apply their medication expertise to harm reduction. A nonjudgmental approach may encourage patients to disclose psychedelic use, allowing pharmacists to identify potential interactions, contraindications, and other safety concerns. Medication-interaction screening, evidence-based education, and referral to appropriate medical care remain important patient-safety functions regardless of where exposure occurs.

Maintaining this distinction allows the profession to prioritize FDA-regulated, evidence-based care while remaining realistic about the broader environment in which pharmacists influence patient safety and provide support.

A Timely Opportunity for Pharmacy

The federal government is increasingly preparing for the potential entry of psychedelic medicines into clinical care. In 2026, federal actions have included finalized FDA guidance, an FDA public hearing and request for comments, an HRSA workforce and care-delivery RFI, and collaboration between the Department of Health and Human Services and Department of Veterans Affairs on research, workforce training, and potential future implementation.10,12,13,18 Implementation questions are no longer purely theoretical.

Pharmacy has adapted repeatedly to new therapeutic frontiers. Psychedelic medicine may present another such challenge, requiring pharmacists to apply familiar principles of medication safety, patient education, interdisciplinary collaboration, and evidence-based practice in a new context. Preparation does not require predicting which drug will be approved or when. Pharmacists can begin by following the clinical evidence, understanding emerging pharmacology and drug-interaction data, learning from existing models such as esketamine, and participating in professional discussions about training, safety, and implementation.

Preparation also requires an evidence-based approach to communication with both patients and health care professionals. Pharmacists are well positioned to evaluate these therapies with the same objectivity applied to other emerging treatments, communicate without judgment, and help patients distinguish established evidence from both historical perceptions and contemporary hype.

For much of the past decade, conversations surrounding psychedelic medicine have centered on whether these therapies are effective. As evidence matures and regulatory decisions draw closer, the conversation is evolving. An equally important question is no longer whether psychedelic medicines may become part of clinical practice, but whether the health care system—and the pharmacy profession—will be prepared if they do.

text:
Dive Brief:

Roche is padding its pipeline of obesity drugs, signing a deal with China-based Rona Therapeutics on Thursday for an experimental medicine aimed at an increasingly popular metabolic target.

Per deal terms, Roche will pay Rona $100 million for full ownership of the drug, an RNA interference medicine aimed at a protein called ALK7. The Swiss pharmaceutical giant could end up paying Rona just over $1 billion overall should the therapy hit an array of development, regulatory and commercial goals. Rona is eligible for sales royalties, too.

The deal is Roche’s fifth with a China-based drugmaker since the end of August and 10th since the beginning of 2025, the most among its pharmaceutical peers, according to BioPharma Dive data. The Rona drug will join five other experimental obesity medicines in Roche’s pipeline, three of which it gained by acquiring Carmot Therapeutics in 2023.

Dive Insight:

Despite Eli Lilly and Novo’s substantial lead in the market for obesity drugs, Roche remains committed to gaining a foothold. The Carmot purchase handed Roche the kind of “incretin” drugs made popular by Lilly’s Zepbound and Novo’s Wegovy. A licensing pact with Zealand Pharma, meanwhile, gave Roche a drug that could prove more tolerable than existing medications.

The Rona alliance is focused on a different area of obesity drug research that’s also gaining traction. The strategy involves targeting ALK7, a cell surface receptor that’s frequently expressed in fat tissue and regulates lipid metabolism. Human studies have shown that people with reduced ALK7 activity have “favorable fat distribution and metabolic phenotypes,” making silencing its expression with a drug an attractive approach, Rona said in a statement.

Several companies are already working on similar medicines, with the goal of lowering levels of “visceral,” or harmful fat. These treatments could emerge as drugs to combine with incretin therapies, though research remains early. GSK licensed an ALK7-targeting agent from a China-based SiranBio earlier this year. Alnylam Pharmaceuticals and Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals have brought prospects into Phase 1 testing. And Wave Life Sciences has a different kind of RNAi medicine for obesity that targets the same pathway.

name: OpenAI
title: Stop sending me engineers: what OpenAI, Anthropic and Microsoft misread about enterprise AI | CIO
description:
They’re not wrong about the problem The frontier labs aren’t confused, and I want to be fair before I disagree.
MIT found that about 95% of enterprise AI pilots produced no measurable profit impact, despite tens of billions spent.
Anthropic: Partnered its engineering capability into an enterprise AI services venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs, reportedly valued above $1.5 billion.
Analysts have flagged the same concern from the buyer’s side: that deep reliance on frontier labs hands those labs insight into the very industries they may later enter.
Dice reported in August that the shortage of engineers is now directly holding back enterprise AI returns.
text:
The AI industry says enterprises can’t absorb AI. Its answer is to absorb it for them.

That’s not the same thing.

The engineer across the table knew the model cold. Not vendor-deck cold. He could tell me where it would break, what it would cost, and which benchmark numbers to ignore. One of the better technical minds who has ever sat in that chair.

Forty minutes in, I asked which of our problems he would point to first. He named a minor workflow one of my directors had mentioned that morning.

The easy read is that he didn’t know my business. True, and not very interesting. Here is the real issue: the people who sent him are making the exact mistake they are being paid to fix.

They’re not wrong about the problem

The frontier labs aren’t confused, and I want to be fair before I disagree.

MIT found that about 95% of enterprise AI pilots produced no measurable profit impact, despite tens of billions spent. Winning the benchmark wasn’t winning the deal. And a customer who never gets to production never renews.

So, they did the logical thing. They sent engineers:

OpenAI: Launched the OpenAI Deployment Company in May with $4 billion of initial investment from 19 partners, starting with 150 forward-deployed engineers (FDEs) and deployment specialists.

Anthropic: Partnered its engineering capability into an enterprise AI services venture with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman, and Goldman Sachs, reportedly valued above $1.5 billion.

Microsoft: Launched Frontier Company in July with $2.5 billion and approximately 6,000 embedded engineers and industry experts.

AWS: Committed $1 billion to a forward-deployed engineering unit embedding engineers with customers.

Market surge: FDE job postings grew roughly 800% in nine months, with principal-level compensation past $1.2 million.

That is a serious response. But it answers the wrong question.

All that capital is aimed at getting customers into production and keeping them there. We have been reading it as the playbook for getting AI into the wider economy. Those are two entirely different problems, and only one of them currently has anyone working on it.

The same mistake, twice

One structural fact tells you what this really is: the forward-deployed function sits on the commercial side of these companies, not in research. OpenAI capitalized its deployment arm as a separate business with outside investors.

That’s not an accusation; the org chart is simply more honest than the positioning. What that structure measures is pilots converted to production within the quarter. Against that scoreboard, the model isn’t shallow at all. It’s optimal.

Delivery vs. Diffusion

This gets celebrated as AI reaching the real economy. In practice, it does close to the opposite:

The learning runs one way. Anthropic’s job listings are the most explicit about this, asking engineers to codify repeatable deployment patterns and contribute those insights back to product and engineering. That is honest, and it is the point. Analysts have flagged the same concern from the buyer’s side: that deep reliance on frontier labs hands those labs insight into the very industries they may later enter.

Capability is replaced instead of built. The engagement leaves behind a functioning workflow, but zero internal muscle to solve the next bottleneck. Constellation Research warned this year that FDEs are often used as a crutch for product immaturity, and as part of a broader vendor dependency play. Without Palantir’s feedback loop — where every deployment continuously enriches an integrated customer ontology — this is simply an expensive systems consultancy with a frontier brand name.

The mid-market waits. Dice reported in August that the shortage of engineers is now directly holding back enterprise AI returns. The scarcest engineering talent sits inside Fortune 50 anchor accounts, while the companies that make up most of the economy queue behind them.

In engagements structured this way, the lab learns your business. You learn their product.

So here is the test I now apply to any engagement, including the ones I sign: when it ends, are we better at finding the next problem ourselves?

text:
Grocery store chain Kroger said it will lay off 3,000 corporate employees over the next three years as it ramps up its use of artificial intelligence to streamline operations.

“Technology is reshaping what’s possible,” CEO Greg Foran wrote in a memo to employees on Monday. “The way work gets done is changing across every industry; we must adapt and take advantage of technology. We need to adopt capabilities, reduce duplicative work and look closely at where work is best fit to be done.”

Kroger last month outlined its AI strategy, meant “to improve the customer experience, make work easier for associates and produce better business outcomes.”

Cincinnati-based Kroger is the largest standalone U.S. supermarket chain with 409,000 employees and more than 2,700 stores operating under various brands, including Ralphs, King Soopers, Smith’s and Fred Meyer.

Kroger named former Walmart executive Foran CEO in February, 11 months after the abrupt resignation of its previous CEO.

Foran has a reputation for being tech-savvy and detail-oriented. He led Walmart’s U.S. division from 2014 to 2019, where he focused on cleaning up stores, ensuring items were in stock and improving the fresh produce selection. He also introduced online ordering and pickup, and accelerated Walmart’s digital capabilities.

Walmart has become a larger challenge to Kroger and other traditional grocers as Americans increasingly pick up their groceries along with other general goods that Walmart sells.

Kroger has also felt pressure from fast-growing discount chains like Aldi and Lidl and online behemoths like Amazon.

Kroger proposed a merger with Albertsons in 2022 as a way to better compete with its rivals. But the Federal Trade Commission and two states — Washington and Colorado — sued to block the merger in 2024, saying it would raise prices and lower workers’ wages by eliminating competition. Judges ultimately ruled that the merger should not proceed.

A day after their merger collapsed, Albertsons filed a lawsuit against Kroger, seeking a $600 million termination fee as well as billions of dollars in legal fees and lost shareholder value.

Kroger said the claims were “baseless” and that Albertsons was not entitled to the fee.

Kroger shares fell 1.6% in morning trading Tuesday, to $61.66.

text:
By Manya Saini and Nupur Anand Oct 13 (Reuters) - JPMorgan C…

By Svea Herbst-Bayliss, Saeed Azhar and Milana Vinn NEW YORK…



The logo of Albertsons supermarket as shoppers browse for groceries ahead of the Thanksgiving Day holiday in Redmond, Washington, U.S., November 24, 2025. REUTERS/David Ryder

By Sanskriti Shekhar

Oct 13 (Reuters) - Albertsons withdrew its fiscal 2026 forecasts on Tuesday as the grocer launched a broad review of its business aimed at cutting costs, lowering prices and reversing sluggish sales.

The company has been facing cautious consumer spending, particularly by lower-income shoppers, as food and fuel costs climb, as well as market share losses to mass retailers including Walmart, discount chains and private-label brands.

The review builds on a restructuring, announced in July, and is expected to finish during the fourth quarter ending February 2027.

Albertsons plans to provide refreshed short- and long-term financial targets alongside a "comprehensive turnaround plan" by its fourth-quarter earnings call.

Executive Chair Meg Whitman said Albertsons' market-share trends had lagged and that despite individual successes across the business, the company was not delivering results consistent with the quality of its assets.

"We must turn things around," Whitman said on a post-earnings call, adding that the grocer needed to move faster to cut costs and reinvest much of those savings to lower prices and improve store experience.

Whitman, the former eBay and Hewlett-Packard CEO, was named Albertsons' executive chair last month in a newly created role aimed at helping the grocer "sharpen its strategy and strengthen execution."

CEO Susan Morris said Albertsons had accumulated too many initiatives, processes and layers of complexity over time, slowing the organization and increasing costs.

"Simply put, we're not satisfied with the results and the current trajectory of our business," she said.

The expanded turnaround effort comes nearly two years after Albertsons' proposed $24.6 billion merger with Kroger collapsed after a federal court blockedthe deal in December 2024 on antitrust grounds. Albertsons subsequently terminated the agreement.

Shares rose 2% on Tuesday, reversing premarket losses. They had fallen 27% this year as of last close.

In July, Albertsons outlined plans to expand private-label offerings and improve e-commerce, while restructuring its 11 divisions into four regions and centralizing merchandising. Albertsons now describes those changes as the first step in its broader turnaround.

"We'll exit areas that are underperforming," Morris said on Tuesday.

Albertsons had slashed its annual target prior quarter, forecast fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings per share in the range of $1.75 to $1.85 and said it expected annual identical sales to decline in the range of 0.5% to 1.5%.

Michael Gunther, an analyst at Consumer Edge, said that the research firm's credit and debit card data shows that "traditional supermarkets, including Albertsons, have continued losing grocery market share to specialty and discount format."

The grocer on Tuesday reported that its same-store sales in the second quarter ended September 12 fell 0.8%.

But it posted second-quarter adjusted profit of 36 cents per share, beating estimates of 33 cents per share, according to data compiled by LSEG.

(Reporting by Sanskriti Shekhar in Bengaluru; Editing by Sahal Muhammed)

You mentioned um Icotide, which has been one of your areas of strength uh to treat psoriasis. Um prescriptions I believe for that just about doubled. Now, we also have a drug for Trumfia, it's a biologic for psoriasis, uh known as Trumfia, I should say.

Separately, tech-ish reported employee accounts⁠ that staff had been told their roles would end. The publication also obtained a company response acknowledging changes affecting engineering in Kenya.

BI Africa

Kenya seeks to retain engineering talent

Kenya’s technology minister, William Kabogo, met a Microsoft delegation on 12 October and raised the importance of protecting engineering jobs and maintaining investor confidence.

ADVERTISEMENT

"We discussed the adoption of artificial intelligence in Government, the digitisation of government services, cybersecurity, digital infrastructure, and digital skills delivered through universities and other institutions. African engineers building global products

Microsoft established its Africa Development Centre with initial locations in Nairobi and Lagos. Its original plan envisaged a combined $100 million investment over five years and recruitment expanding to 500 engineers across both locations by 2023.

text:
watch now

Johnson & Johnson reported sales in its medical devices business on Tuesday that fell short of Wall Street expectations, citing geopolitical issues, including the Middle East conflict, and its shares fell more than 6%.

The results marked the second successive quarter that its MedTech unit missed analysts’ estimates.

Chief Financial Officer Joe Wolk said in an interview that the Middle East conflict, austerity measures in Europe, and pricing in China continued to weigh on international results in the third quarter, “but maybe in a little bit more pronounced way.”

The Middle East conflict, which has driven up fuel costs, has not yet affected the company’s costs, he said, but it has hurt sales in the region.

“These are countries that still value and actually want premium healthcare systems, think Kuwait, UAE, Saudi Arabia. They pride themselves on having solid healthcare, very good healthcare,” Wolk said. “But their budgets now are being resourced and allocated towards defense.”

MedTech soft spot

Medical technology division sales rose 2.5% to $8.6 billion overall, missing analysts’ estimates of $8.71 billion, according to LSEG data. Outside the U.S., the division’s sales were essentially flat.

“Our performance is below the standard we have set internally and below the expectations we previously communicated to investors,” said Tim Schmid, J&J’s medical technology chief.

“Simply put, we can do better,” he said, adding that the company was focused on improving fourth-quarter performance. He said the environment for medical procedures remains stable in key markets.

Shares of other medical device makers were also lower, with Boston Scientific down nearly 3% and Intuitive Surgical shares off about 2%.

But J.P. Morgan analyst Robbie Marcus said it’s hard to generalize J&J’s results to the rest of the medtech sector, given company-specific disruption from China supply, the pending orthopedics unit spin-off, and likely greater exposure to disruption in the Middle East.

Hips and knee spinoff

The company said late last year it intended to spin off its orthopedics unit, DePuy Synthes, into a standalone company, marking its second major spinoff as it sharpens its focus on higher-growth healthcare segments.

Wolk, on a conference call to discuss company results, said J&J remains on track for a mid-2027 separation.

“Given the way DePuy Synthes is performing... we are leaning towards a spin as being the best option to create long-term value for Johnson & Johnson shareholders. That has always been our base plan, and we are confident that it can be successfully executed,” he said.

Daniel Barasa, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, said depressed medtech valuations “probably made it harder to complete a sale of the orthopedic business, which may also be weighing on the stock.”

J&J raised its full-year forecast for reported sales to about $101.2 billion at the midpoint, up from $101.1 billion. It increased its adjusted earnings forecast range with a new midpoint of $11.10 per share, up from $11.04.

Quarterly pharmaceutical sales jumped 7.7% to $16.76 billion.

Sales of Tremfya for Crohn’s disease and other autoimmune conditions rose 68% to $2.4 billion, exceeding analyst estimates of about $2.2 billion, while sales of Stelara, which is facing generic competition, fell 54% to $716 million, still well above diminished Wall Street expectations of $591 million. Tremfya has increasingly replaced lost Stelara revenue following recent approvals in inflammatory bowel diseases.

Sales of blood cancer treatment Darzalex rose about 16% to $4.24 billion, short of analyst expectations of $4.4 billion.

J&J posted third-quarter revenue of $25.4 billion, above estimates of $25.28 billion, and adjusted earnings of $2.

name: Barclays
title: Barclays offers a golden lesson in how not to handle a return-to-office mandate
description:
Barclays’ public retreat over its return-to-office policy reveals how even well-intentioned management decisions can backfire when employees are told what to do without understanding why.
Over the summer and September, Barclays has run through a sequence familiar to anyone who has watched a change programme stall.
Barclays had cited collaboration and working together; banks including JP Morgan and Revolut have argued that remote working harms the training of younger staff.
Asked why senior staff should attend four days rather than three, Barclays said the extra day would “support collaboration, decision-making and leadership visibility“.
Marcus Iles is a business strategy and organisational behaviour expert specialising in strategy activation, leadership alignment, organisational storytelling and people engagement.
text:
Barclays’ public retreat over its return-to-office policy reveals how even well-intentioned management decisions can backfire when employees are told what to do without understanding why. Marcus Iles says that if leaders want lasting change rather than reluctant compliance, they must build a shared sense of purpose

In the summer, Barclays told its UK staff that from October 5 most staff coming into the office two days a week would need to come in at least three, and that managing directors and above would need four. On September 29, with six days to go, the bank’s executive committee wrote to staff that it was “extending the implementation period for UK colleagues to ensure colleagues have the right support as we move through the transition”, and that it was “also reviewing our flexible working policy”. Employees could defer compliance until 2027 if their line manager agreed by the end of the week. On the same day a spokesperson told the press: “Our updated onsite working arrangements will take effect as planned.” Barclays’ public statement also acknowledged transitional measures for staff whose personal circumstances prevented them from meeting the requirements.

It would be easy to read the episode as one more skirmish in the long war over remote working. I think, however, it’s more useful as a case study of a wider and considerably more expensive issue: what happens to a strategic decision when it’s issued as an instruction rather than built as a shared understanding.

Over the summer and September, Barclays has run through a sequence familiar to anyone who has watched a change programme stall. First instruction, then revolt, then renewed justification and finally the retreat-presented-as-continuity. Each stage followed from the one before, and all of it was avoidable from the beginning.

The approach I use with leadership teams starts from a simple observation. For people to act together on a strategy, three things have to be held in common. The first is attention: what we are looking at. The second is interpretation: what we think it means. The third is expectation: what we believe will happen next and what is now expected of us. A strategy that settles the first and neglects the other two is a demand that people lack the shared understanding to execute.

Consider the instruction. The policy specified days more clearly than it explained why those days were necessary. Barclays had cited collaboration and working together; banks including JP Morgan and Revolut have argued that remote working harms the training of younger staff. But citing those benefits did not explain why they required this particular number of days. And when an organisation supplies a number without a meaning, its people supply the meaning themselves. On Reddit, one commenter suggested that the bank wanted to justify money spent on refurbished buildings. Although that may be unfair, it’s a clear example of what a gap in shared interpretation produces: the most cynical account available fills any space that leadership leaves empty.

Then came the revolt. Thousands of staff signed an open letter drafted by Unite, which represents around 36,000 of the bank’s employees. It asks for a one-off payment before March 2027, childcare vouchers, subsidised meals, travel allowances and exemptions for anyone commuting more than 40 minutes. The letter described the effects of the policy as “material and foreseeable”. The union also asks for guaranteed weekly time for meaningful in-person work or team-building. The financial demands are the language of a transaction. When people have not accepted the reason for a decision, the conversation turns to what it will cost them and what they should be paid to bear it. The demands put a price on compliance without establishing a shared purpose. The letter recognises the value of face-to-face collaboration but disputes whether that requires a blanket increase in attendance.

The justification repeated during the dispute is the most informative step for us observers. Asked why senior staff should attend four days rather than three, Barclays said the extra day would “support collaboration, decision-making and leadership visibility“. Collaboration and decision-making are purposes, but visibility is not – it’s a condition. To be visible is to be seen, which is not the same as being available, being useful or teaching anyone anything. Anniken Grønstad, an associate professor of organisational psychology at Oslo New University College, drew the distinction precisely in a recent interview with Science Norway: if an experienced employee “sits behind a closed door or spends large parts of the day in meetings,” she said, “the main thing the younger employees have gained is a shorter physical distance to a potential mentor. They don’t necessarily have better access to the mentor’s expertise.” Her conclusion belongs in front of any board weighing a mandate: “the office itself is not the training model”.

‘Leadership visibility’ is what an organisation says when it has confused the observable with the consequential. I suspect it is also what many staff believed the policy was about all along. Gallup research published last month bears on this directly. Among surveyed workers in the United States, 59 per cent believe their employer collects activity data such as hours worked and badge swipes. Only 19 per cent say someone at work has spoken to them about the data or metrics collected about their work. Among employees who regularly work on a computer or another device, only 20 per cent trust their leaders “a great deal” to use that data responsibly. Being counted without being told why is a reliable way to persuade people that the counting is the point.

Which brings us to the retreat. The concession is real, if partial: deferral to 2027 for those whose managers allow it, and a review of flexible working. The public insistence that the arrangements would take effect as planned sits uneasily with the extension offered to colleagues. Barclays is, in effect, telling two audiences two stories and trusting that neither will compare notes. Yet they already have. One self-identified Barclays employee asked why they were still being told to return three days a week from Monday. Others read the delay as postponing the inevitable, or speculated that resignations had forced the bank’s hand.

There is a further, quieter consequence. By routing deferrals through individual line managers, Barclays has turned one leadership decision into thousands of local ones. Each will be made a little differently. Each will be read by the person on the receiving end as a verdict on how far their manager trusts them. A policy meant to bring people together now risks sorting them, team by team, into the accommodated and the refused. It is a lottery, and lotteries do not build cohesion.

None of this means Barclays is wrong to want its people together more often. There are serious arguments for in-person work, especially early in a career, and the bank’s own statements acknowledge “the benefits of balancing flexibility for colleagues with the importance of working together”. But stating the argument did not establish a shared understanding with the people expected to act on it. Grønstad notes that managers’ claims about learning, creativity and knowledge transfer in the office are empirical claims, and should therefore be backed up with evidence. I’d go further. Even well-evidenced claims do nothing until people share an understanding of what they require.

What would that have looked like? Not, I would argue, a better communications plan. The work starts earlier, and it follows a sequence. First, leaders must listen to the stories that will already be circulating in and about the organisation, before a decision is announced. The story about expensive refurbished buildings was presumably not invented in September. Then, leaders must shape a reason that people can understand and act on. That reason should then be shared and opened to challenge, so that “material and foreseeable” costs surface as design problems rather than grievances. The next step is to check whether leaders’ own behaviour fits the account they are giving. This is where ‘leadership visibility’ was always going to fail, because visibility is something done to others, not with them. When leaders’ behaviours are aligned to an authentic, meaningful story they’ve developed with colleagues, a real shift in behaviour follows. Returning to the story as circumstances change then enables leaders to sustain the strategy, rather than defending the original number.

The cost of skipping this work rarely shows up in the policy itself but, instead, later as compliance that does not deliver the intended outcome. Barclays may well get its people into the building three days a week by 2027. But what it certainly won’t get, without a shared account of why, is whatever it wanted those days for.

It’s an important reminder that while proximity can be mandated, meaning cannot.

Marcus Iles is a business strategy and organisational behaviour expert specialising in strategy activation, leadership alignment, organisational storytelling and people engagement. With 25 years’ experience spanning advertising, creative strategy, organisational storytelling and consultancy, Marcus – a former Chief Storytelling Officer at The Storytellers and an award-winning advertising creative and strategist – examines why strategies that appear clear at leadership level can fragment when they are interpreted and acted upon across an organisation.

text:
By Sanskriti Shekhar

Oct 13 (Reuters) – Albertsons withdrew its fiscal 2026 forecasts on Tuesday and launched a review of its business aimed at cutting costs, lowering prices and reversing sluggish sales.

The US grocer has battled cautious consumer spending, particularly ​by lower-income shoppers, as food and fuel costs climb, alongside market share ‌loss to mass retailers such as Walmart, discount chains and private-label brands.

The review builds on a restructuring, announced in July, and is expected to be completed in the fourth quarter ending February 2027.

By then, Albertsons also aims to provide fresh short- and long-term financial targets alongside a “comprehensive turnaround plan”.

“We must turn ‌things ​around,” Meg Whitman, the former eBay and Hewlett-Packard CEO ⁠who was named executive chair last ⁠month in a newly created role to help the grocer “sharpen its strategy and strengthen execution”, said on a post-earnings call.

The company needs to move faster to cut costs and reinvest much of those savings to lower prices and improve store ​experience, she said.

CEO Susan Morris said Albertsons had accumulated too many initiatives, processes and layers of complexity over time, slowing the organization and increasing costs.

“We’re not satisfied with ⁠the results and the current trajectory of our ⁠business,” she said.

The expanded turnaround effort comes nearly two years after ​Albertsons’ proposed $24.6 billion merger with Kroger collapsed after a federal court blocked the deal on ​antitrust grounds. Albertsons subsequently terminated the agreement.

The company’s shares rose 2% on ‌Tuesday, reversing premarket losses. They had fallen 27% so far this year.

“They have hard time remaining competitive on price as some mass merchants such as Walmart have used grocery as a traffic driver and have other high margin categories such as fashion to offset ⁠food’s low margins,” said Bruce Winder, an independent retail consultant.

In July, Albertsons outlined plans to expand private-label offerings and improve e-commerce, while restructuring its 11 divisions into four regions and ⁠centralizing merchandising.

Albertsons on Tuesday described ‌those changes as the first step in its broader turnaround.

“We’ll ⁠exit areas that are underperforming,” Morris said on Tuesday.

Albertsons in July ​forecast fiscal ‌2026 adjusted earnings per share in the range of $1.75 to $1.85 ​and projected ⁠annual identical sales to decline in the range of 0.5% to 1.5% after trimming its annual target.

The grocer on Tuesday reported that its same-store sales in the second quarter ended September 12 fell 0.8%.

But adjusted profit of 36 cents per share beat estimate of 33 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG.

(Reporting by Sanskriti Shekhar in Bengaluru; Editing by Sahal ​Muhammed and Sriraj Kalluvila)

What Happened?

Meta (META:NASDAQ) launched Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full on Monday. The company calls them its most capable AI models yet. Meta stock rose about 4% in afternoon trading.

Muse Wonder will soon power Meta's Muse personal AI agent, starting with subscribers. Muse Wonder Full is more powerful and is available to subscribers of Muse Code, Meta's AI coding tool.

The launch is a direct push at OpenAI and Anthropic. Mark Zuckerberg has pledged billions of dollars and hired top researchers over the past year to catch up.

In a blog post, Meta said it started overhauling its AI efforts 14 months ago. It says it has gone from rebuilding its foundations to pushing the frontier.

Meta also rolled out its Muse agent last month.

The agent can access other apps, send emails, and make payments. Reuters notes that this success could turn Meta's heavy AI spending into new subscription revenue.

What the Market Is Telling Us About Meta Stock

Investors are rewarding Meta stock because the launch shows progress on a big bet. AI spending is huge and the market wants proof that it can pay off.

Meta's July earnings call helps explain the mood. Q2 revenue was $60.8 billion, up 28%, and the social media giant expects Q3 revenue of $61 billion to $64 billion.

Meta now expects 2026 capital expenditures of $130 billion to $145 billion. Notably, free cash flow was only $784 million last quarter.

On that call, Zuckerberg said Meta wants to sell new AI products to businesses and consumers. Those include personal agents, business agents and a model API.

He also said Meta plans subscriptions through its new Meta One offering. The new models fit right into that plan.

Susan Li also warned about legal risk. She said youth-related trials scheduled for this year could result in a material loss.

So the picture is mixed. Better models give Meta stock a clearer path to new revenue.

But costs are high, and the payoff isn't proven yet. Today's 4% jump shows investors like what they see, though one launch won't settle the debate over Meta stock.

text:
Advances Agilent's position as a leading pathology solutions provider, with a unique and differentiated combination of instruments, reagents, and software

Acquisition seamlessly builds on Agilent's pathology portfolio expansion efforts and widens strategic moat in high-growth market

SANTA CLARA, Calif. & PHILADELPHIA, October 13, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Agilent Technologies Inc. (NYSE: A) today announced it has entered into a definitive agreement to acquire Proscia®, a provider of digital pathology software for clinical and life-sciences customers, in an all-cash transaction valued at $240 million in cash at closing and up to an additional $30 million based on achieving future performance milestones.

Proscia is a leading independent provider of enterprise digital pathology software, serving as a key enabler to address emerging trends in the $5 billion Pathology market. Proscia's software platform serves as a central operating layer for digital pathology, supporting clinical and life-sciences customers across the U.S. and Europe. By connecting slide scanners, laboratory information systems, image-analysis applications, AI tools, people, and data, Proscia's innovative technology enables customers to manage images, data, and workflows in one unified environment. Proscia serves more than 4,000 laboratories, hospitals, and clinics today as well as 16 of the top 20 pharmaceutical companies, with trailing twelve months revenue exceeding $18 million. Proscia was named 2026 Best in KLAS for Digital Pathology and earned the highest performance score across both U.S. and European markets.

Agilent and Proscia entered into a multi-year distribution agreement in September 2022 to offer a comprehensive digital diagnostic-pathology system. Today's announcement builds on Agilent's established pathology solutions and its partnership with Proscia.

"Digital pathology is quickly becoming the foundation for pathology data generation, analysis, and application across biopharmaceutical research, clinical development, and diagnostics, and our acquisition of Proscia meaningfully expands our presence in this fast-growing market," said Agilent President and CEO Padraig McDonnell. "The acquisition establishes an Agilent platform for scientific intelligence in tissue-based precision medicine, connecting data generation with AI-based interpretation in a workflow that supports biomarker research through routine clinical use. With Proscia's leading platform and talented team, we will be better equipped to help laboratories and biopharma customers manage and derive insights from pathology data. We look forward to welcoming the Proscia team to Agilent and working together to accelerate adoption of AI-enabled pathology workflows to advance drug discovery and companion-diagnostics solutions and create long-term value for customers and shareholders."

"This agreement with Agilent marks an exciting milestone for Proscia and reflects the strength of the platform our team has built," said David West, Co-Founder and CEO of Proscia. "Agilent shares our vision for advancing pathology through open, digital, and AI-enabled solutions. Together, we can accelerate innovation while continuing to provide customers with the flexibility they need across clinical and life-sciences workflows. I am grateful to the entire Proscia team, whose dedication made this milestone possible, and look forward to building on our work as part of Agilent."

Strategic and Financial Benefits of the Acquisition

The combination builds on the successful completion of Agilent's recent transaction with Biocare Medical, and offers meaningful strategic and financial benefits, including:

Strengthens Pathology Portfolio with a Leading Digital Pathology Platform. This acquisition strengthens Agilent's existing leadership in pathology instrumentation and reagents, combining industry-leading diagnostic capabilities with Proscia's vendor-agnostic digital pathology platform and established customer base. Proscia's platform holds FDA 510(k) clearance for primary diagnosis. The transaction builds on Agilent's position as a leader in pathology, well-positioning the Company to address evolving customer needs as the market embraces digitalization and AI.

Enhances Companion Diagnostics and Biopharma Drug Discovery Offerings. By leveraging a growing repository of real-world data, Proscia offers additional AI-enabled synergies with Agilent's companion diagnostics (CDx) business, enhancing value to biopharma partners as well as clinical and translational research customers.

Supports Agilent's Long-Term Growth Profile. Proscia's recurring-revenue model will add a high-growth, high-margin software business to Agilent's pathology portfolio.

description:
OpenAI has announced a $1 billion commitment to help cyber defenders protect essential services, including water systems, electricity networks, local government services and community banks.
The commitment addresses a practical problem for many essential-service providers: small security teams are responsible for protecting complex, aging systems against increasingly capable attackers.
OpenAI says the initiative builds on support offered following recent attacks on US water systems.
Affected states and utilities were offered up to $1 million in no-cost application programming interface credits, Daybreak access and technical assistance.
Daybreak Blue supports common defensive tasks using OpenAI’s mainline models, while Daybreak Red gives approved organizations access to specialized models for more sensitive and technically demanding work.
text:
OpenAI has announced a $1 billion commitment to help cyber defenders protect essential services, including water systems, electricity networks, local government services and community banks.

The initiative, Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, will give organizations with limited security resources subsidized access to OpenAI’s advanced cybersecurity tools, alongside training, technical assistance and partnerships. OpenAI is targeting the subsidized access to be consumed over the next six months, beginning in the United States before expanding to partner countries.

The commitment addresses a practical problem for many essential-service providers: small security teams are responsible for protecting complex, aging systems against increasingly capable attackers.

OpenAI says its tools can help those teams review older software, analyze suspicious activity, identify vulnerabilities, prioritize risks and develop and test fixes.

In a LinkedIn announcement, OpenAI for Government wrote: “We depend on cyber defenders to protect the systems that keep communities running: the water coming from the tap, the electricity powering homes and businesses, the local government systems that deliver public services, and the financial institutions people trust with their money.”

Subsidized access for teams with limited resources

The US element, Daybreak for America, will prioritize water and wastewater systems, electricity grid operators, state and local governments, community and regional banks, nonprofits and open-source software maintainers.

The $1 billion commitment is for subsidized access to Daybreak, rather than a cash grant fund distributed to participating organizations.

OpenAI says the initiative builds on support offered following recent attacks on US water systems. Affected states and utilities were offered up to $1 million in no-cost application programming interface credits, Daybreak access and technical assistance.

According to the company, participating teams used that support to review software and system settings, validate security findings, develop patches and confirm fixes while water services remained operational.

Daybreak provides different levels of access for verified defenders carrying out authorized security work. Daybreak Blue supports common defensive tasks using OpenAI’s mainline models, while Daybreak Red gives approved organizations access to specialized models for more sensitive and technically demanding work.

OpenAI reports that thousands of defenders across 2,000 approved organizations and workspaces already use the program.

Training and a public-sector pilot

A new pilot with the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center, known as MS-ISAC, will pair Daybreak access with guided training and hands-on assistance for an initial group of public-sector and water-system defenders.

The work will help participating teams check and prioritize findings, coordinate fixes and develop an approach that can be repeated across other organizations.

MS-ISAC provides threat intelligence, incident-response support and shared security services to public-sector organizations. Its wider membership includes utilities, public hospitals, schools and law-enforcement agencies.

The initial announcement focuses on public-sector and water-system defenders. It does not confirm a separate rollout for schools.

OpenAI is also holding meetings with frontline teams to understand how they can use its tools. The company says its second gathering of utility providers included participants representing 40 states and the District of Columbia, collectively serving more than half the US population.

Moving from finding weaknesses to fixing them

More than 35 partner products and partner-operated services are being announced through the Daybreak Defense Network, bringing OpenAI’s cybersecurity models into tools and services that security teams already use.

The company has also published its approach to a “Defense Factory,” an operation that uses AI agents alongside existing security and engineering tools to find and validate vulnerabilities and prepare tested fixes for human review.

The emphasis is on helping organizations act on security findings. Access to a capable model still needs to be accompanied by the expertise, processes and support required to deploy fixes safely.

OpenAI says it intends to expand the subsidized-access model to partner countries in the coming weeks. Eligible governments, critical infrastructure operators, nonprofits, open-source maintainers and supporting organizations can find information about access, training and technical assistance through the Daybreak website.
