text:
S&P Global Ratings raised Macy’s Inc.’s debt ratings outlook as the retailer has delivered five quarters of positive comparable-store sales alongside stable gross margin. The ratings agency said Macy’s has benefited from a “strategy of adding affordable luxury and luxury brands to attract higher income consumers.”

S&P noted that the performance at its luxury banner Bloomingdale’s has been better than expected, but it remains a small part of the overall business.

S&P said Macy’s credit metrics have remained consistent, including S&P Global Ratings-adjusted debt to EBITDA in the 2x-2.5x range, despite ongoing store closures. As a result of Macy’s improved performance, S&P revised its outlook to positive from stable and affirmed all of its ratings, including ‘BB+’ issuer credit rating. The company’s short-term issuer and commercial paper ratings remain ‘B’.

The positive outlook reflects the possibility of a higher (investment grade) rating over the next 12-18 months if the company continues to demonstrate a track-record of operating performance improvements while maintaining its existing financial policy, including leverage near 2x.

S&P said in its analysis, “We forecast Macy’s Inc. will maintain a solid credit profile, characterized by healthy free operating cash flow (FOCF) generation and disciplined capital allocation. Macy’s has managed S&P adjusted leverage in the 2x-2.5x range post-pandemic when performance has been mixed and includes years of revenue decline and EBITDA contraction as the company closed locations and reinvested in its go-forward store fleet. Macy’s is investing $820 million-$850 million in capital expenditures (capex) annually for store improvements and refurbishments and technology advancements. This level of expenditure supports its strategy to improve the in-store experience and omni-channel capabilities, including artificial intelligence to assist customers shopping online.

“We forecast the company to generate $675 million of FOCF in fiscal 2026 and a more normalized $450 million in 2027. This will support dividends of $205 million and a minimum of $200 million in share repurchases in 2026. In 2027, we forecast dividends to increase to $214 million and for share repurchase capacity to increase to at least $350 million. Cash flow will also benefit from estimated $130 million in asset sale proceeds from closed owned locations. We forecast over $1 billion in balance-sheet cash and a demonstrated track-record of modest share repurchases will lead to leverage in the high-1x.

“Recent financial performance and comparable sales trends suggest Macy’s operational improvements are sustainable, despite ongoing store closures. Macy’s successful execution of the “Bold New Chapter” strategy is supporting its operating performance, including comparable same-store sales growth and gross margin stability. We anticipate the continued expansion of the Bloomingdale’s and Bluemercury banners, combined with a higher-income consumer at Macy’s, could somewhat mitigate the cyclical risks associated with the middle-income exposed Macy’s banner, which exhibits higher price elasticity of demand.

“The Macy’s brand continues to also serve the value-conscious, middle-income shopper. However, it has successfully integrated on-trend, higher-price-point brands such as Good American and Polo Women’s to elevate its assortment and illustrate restored confidence from brand partners. Simultaneously, Bloomingdale’s has capitalized on shifts in the luxury landscape, particularly following the bankruptcy filing of Saks Global, to secure premium brand partnerships including Christian Louboutin and new and on-trend brands such as Skims and Vuori. However, the company’s product offerings under all banners remain discretionary. While the company has been successful in its strategy over the last 12-18 months and the consumer has remained resilient despite weak macroeconomic indicators, the model has not fully been tested in an economic downturn.

“Macy’s comparable owned-plus-licensed-plus-marketplace sales increased 2.7 percent in the second quarter of 2026, the fifth consecutive quarter of growth. Sales momentum was largely propelled by Bloomingdale’s, which delivered 11.3 percent comparable sales growth, underscoring the success of its premium merchandise strategy. Furthermore, the Macy’s banner’s go-forward comparable sales grew 1.1 percent, an improvement from the 0.6 percent growth recorded in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025. We attribute this to inventory management, limiting the need for heavy markdowns and new brands wins leading to a higher average unit retail (AUR) and larger basket sizes. Therefore, we forecast a modest revenue increase for the company (previously a decline) of approximately 0.8 percent for fiscal year 2026 and 0.7 percent for 2027 as low-single-digit comparable sales growth offsets the impact of planned store closures.

“Despite revenue growth improvements, profitability growth will be minimal. We forecast improvements in gross margins in 2026 to 41.2 percent from 40.3 percent as the company receives tariff refunds and negotiated its supply chain costs with key partners. We forecast another modest improvement to 41.8 percent in 2027 due to lower tariffs and better mix. These improvements will not result in meaningful improvements in EBITDA due to SGA growth to support the labor required to operate the stores at the level its strategy calls for. Its 9 percent S&P adjusted EBITDA margin is comparable to other department store peers, but weaker than specialty retailers that operate in a mid-to-high-teen level EBITDA margin. Store closures are no longer a meaningful drag to the EBITDA line and not a component on delaying its improvement. However, we believe achieving SGA leverage over a smaller store base will take time and we do not forecast meaningful EBITDA margin improvement until after 2028.

“Store closures will continue but we expect sustained organic growth in its remaining stores. We believe Macy’s Inc.’s disciplined approach to its physical footprint will enhance liquidity and optimize the long-term profitability of its remaining locations. We expect the company to close approximately 40 total locations in fiscal 2026, following a series of closures in 2024 and 2025. In 2026, we expect the company to exit 31 Macy’s banner locations with the goal of reaching a streamlined, healthy fleet of approximately 350 stores, as the company seeks to exit underperforming mall locations. According to the company, its remaining locations are in A- and B-level malls—which benefit from steadier foot traffic and enhanced service or entertainment tenants. We believe the increased productivity of the remaining “reimagine” stores will offset the reduced store base. Excluding the volatility of the pandemic, revenue per store has remained relatively stable, suggesting its strategic pruning of its store fleet has been successful.

“We forecast low-single-digit organic comparable same-store sales growth. Therefore, we view the lower store count as a manageable strategic realignment toward high-quality, high-traffic environments that support the company’s elevated brand positioning.

“Macy’s continues to invest in its digital ecosystem, including enhancements to its third-party marketplace, AI-driven personalization, and localized fulfillment capabilities. During this digital transformation, its S&P Global Ratings-adjusted EBITDA margins have declined to 9 percent-10 percent from a 14 percent peak, but note not all investments are on the digital side of the business. Macy’s digital sales surged to a pandemic-induced peak of 44 percent from 22 percent in 2018, and the sales mix has stabilized in the low- to mid-30 percent range. We do not anticipate a significant shift in this mix in the near term, as the company has successfully adopted an agnostic approach to consumer purchasing channels. Omni-channel stability allows Macy’s to capture value regardless of whether a transaction occurs in a physical storefront or via a digital interface. As a result, we view the company’s current scale and mix as more efficient and better aligned with modern consumer habits than in previous cycles.

“Macy’s substantial scale and geographic reach maintain its leading market position in the U.S. department store sector. We now assess Macy’s management and governance (M&G) score as neutral. We believe the prior disclosure of a material weakness in its internal control over financial reporting, in which an employee concealed around $151 million in small package delivery expenses over nearly three years, is no longer a concern. Macy’s stated the errors did not materially affect its results of operations or financial position for any historical annual or interim period. The company said this did not affect cash and vendor payments. It determined the matter did not require it to reissue historical financial statements.

“The positive outlook reflects the possibility that we could raise the ratings to investment grade over the next 12-18 months if the company continues to demonstrate a track-record of operating performance improvement while maintaining its existing financial policy including leverage near 2x.”

Dive Brief:

Kroger’s planned acquisition of Giant Eagle could increase concentration in the grocery industry and harm consumers, Sen. Elizabeth Warren wrote in an Oct. 5 letter to the Federal Trade Commission and the Department of Justice.

The $1.65 billion deal, which the grocers announced this summer, is one of three major proposed acquisitions in the food industry that would each “raise competition concerns,” Warren claimed.

Together, the mergers “appear to reveal a growing consolidation trend, driven by weak antitrust enforcement under President Trump, that raises costs and hurts consumers, restaurants, and small businesses,” Warren wrote, asking the agencies to “carefully scrutinize the potential anticompetitive implications under the three pending transactions.”

Dive Insight:

Warren’s letter to the two regulatory bodies that assess the antitrust implications of proposed M&A comes as the grocery industry continues to grapple with ongoing concerns over grocery affordability.

“[F]amilies are paying higher prices for food and groceries while dominant food industry conglomerates continue to rake in sky-high profits,” Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, wrote in the letter.

Kroger’s plan to buy Giant Eagle as well as Sysco’s proposed acquisition of Restaurant Depot, and McCormick’s planned purchase of Unilever’s food business could further consolidate the food and grocery markets, leading to increased prices for consumers, store closures and lost jobs, Warren wrote.

Warren raised concerns that the large store footprint of Kroger, as well as its overlapping presence with Giant Eagle in several markets, could lead to reduced competition in certain areas.

While Kroger’s plan to merge with rival Albertsons was struck down by a federal and a state court, Kroger’s plan to buy Giant Eagle appears poised for a smoother regulatory review, in part due to the tightened scale of this deal, antitrust lawyers told Grocery Dive.

Kroger has said it plans to divest an unspecified number of stores in its bid to win regulatory approval for the Giant Eagle deal. Warren pointed to the divestiture debacle tied to Albertsons’ purchase of Safeway in 2015 as well as the closure of nearly 20% of the stores divested in the 2016 merger of Ahold and Delhaize.

If Kroger provides a robust store divestiture plan in markets where it overlaps with Giant Eagle, the grocers likely have a solid chance of alleviating regulatory concerns, Spencer Waller, a professor at Loyola University Chicago School of Law who specializes in antitrust law, told Grocery Dive earlier this year.

Industry collaboration: Adidas, H&M Group, Inditex and Bestseller have launched the Apparel Recovery Coalition to address global textile waste and strengthen circular fashion systems.

Two-year initiative: The coalition will test producer responsibility models, fund textile recovery projects and improve waste management in countries receiving secondhand clothing exports.

Environmental accountability: Ghana’s Kantamanto Market processes approximately 25 million garments monthly, highlighting the environmental and social costs of global textile consumption.

Fashion Giants Join Forces to Address Textile Waste

Accra, Ghana has become the launchpad for a new industry initiative aimed at addressing the environmental consequences of global textile waste.

Adidas, H&M Group, Zara-owner Inditex and Danish fashion company Bestseller have established the Apparel Recovery Coalition (ARC). The initiative brings major fashion producers together with Ghana-based nonprofit The Or Foundation and circular economy organization Circle Economy.

The coalition will examine how fashion brands can assume greater responsibility for clothing after consumers discard it. Its focus includes reuse, recycling, upcycling and improved waste management in countries receiving large volumes of secondhand textiles.

The two-year initiative will develop and test a producer responsibility business model that reflects international textile trade flows.

It also aims to bring brands, recyclers, sorting companies, policymakers and affected communities into discussions about practical waste management solutions.

The initiative arrives as fashion companies face increasing pressure to address the environmental consequences of production, consumption and textile exports.

Ghana’s Kantamanto Market Becomes Testing Ground

The coalition launched at Kantamanto Market in Accra, one of the world’s largest centers for secondhand clothing trade and textile recovery.

According to The Or Foundation, the market recirculates approximately 25 million garments every month.

Thousands of traders, repairers and other workers contribute to an extensive informal circular economy. Their activities extend the useful life of clothing that might otherwise enter waste streams.

However, the market also illustrates the environmental challenges associated with international secondhand textile exports.

Clothing that cannot be resold or recovered can contribute to waste accumulation, water contamination and soil pollution. Local communities and waste management systems bear much of the resulting burden.

ARC intends to build on The Or Foundation’s 15 years of work supporting Ghana’s circular textile ecosystem.

The coalition states that it will “test more inclusive approaches to governance, design, and implementation” by incorporating community perspectives into its activities.

Its first demonstration project will operate in Accra, supporting infrastructure improvements, environmental remediation and training initiatives.

A second demonstration project is planned for another country receiving substantial volumes of secondhand clothing.

Fashion Brands Commit Funding to Circular Recovery

Adidas, H&M Group, Inditex and Bestseller will provide voluntary financial contributions to support the coalition’s demonstration projects.

The companies have not disclosed the total funding commitment.

The initiative will examine how extended producer responsibility frameworks could support textile recovery across international supply chains.

Such frameworks require producers to assume greater financial or operational responsibility for products after their useful life ends.

For fashion companies, this could eventually influence product design, waste management costs and investment in recycling infrastructure.

The coalition expects its findings to inform future industry practices and regulatory approaches.

“The coalition hopes the evidence and practical learnings generated through these demonstration projects will help inform brands, policymakers, producer responsibility organizations (PROs) and other stakeholders working to strengthen post-consumer textile management systems worldwide,” the release said.

RELATED ARTICLE: Textile Waste: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle

Rising Production Volumes Intensify Environmental Scrutiny

The initiative comes amid growing scrutiny of the fashion industry’s resource consumption and waste generation.

Inditex reported using 705,554 metric tons of raw materials in its products, compared with 678,596 metric tons in 2024.

That represents an increase of approximately 4%, illustrating the scale of material demand across its operations.

Meanwhile, H&M Group reported producing 364,093 metric tons of products in 2025, equivalent to approximately 36 Eiffel Towers.

These figures highlight the challenge facing fashion companies attempting to reconcile commercial growth with circular economy commitments.

Recovery and recycling initiatives can reduce waste impacts, but their effectiveness also depends on product durability, material choices and production volumes.

For investors, the coalition introduces another area for evaluating corporate sustainability performance: whether voluntary industry commitments produce measurable improvements in textile recovery and environmental management.

Producer Responsibility Could Reshape Global Textile Governance

The coalition plans to expand participation among additional companies and stakeholders as its work progresses.

Its findings could help policymakers assess how producer responsibility systems should account for textiles exported across national borders.

This remains a significant governance challenge. Products often reach the end of their useful lives far from the countries where brands originally sold them.

For multinational fashion companies, stronger accountability could create additional compliance obligations and financing requirements.

For importing countries, effective producer responsibility mechanisms could provide resources for infrastructure, environmental protection and local circular businesses.

The coalition’s longer-term relevance will depend on whether its demonstration projects deliver practical, scalable financing and recovery models.

As governments and investors increase scrutiny of fashion’s environmental footprint, Ghana’s textile recovery economy could help shape how global brands manage responsibility beyond the point of sale.

text:
Nvidia (NVDA) is joining rival AMD (AMD) along with partners Google (GOOG, GOOGL) and Meta (META) to establish a new open specification for data center design.

Called the Open Data Center Specification v0.7, the standard serves as a blueprint for building data centers, covering everything from the physical layout of the buildings to cooling and power architecture.

The chip giant also said it's teaming with Google, Meta, and Microsoft (MSFT) to create the OCP Grid Resilience Specification, which serves as a standard for how data centers respond to power disruptions, ensuring they can rapidly return to full operation.

According to Nvidia, the two specifications provide everyone from system makers to colocation providers and data center operators with a set of predefined templates for building data centers without having to contend with a slew of different customer designs.

Data centers are incredibly complex facilities that require large amounts of power and cooling to keep the chips inside from overheating and failing. And adding custom designs and quirks can slow construction timelines.

Open standards could change that, allowing builders to bring new data centers online faster. And the faster data centers go up, the more chips, systems, and networking components Nvidia can sell.

At the same time, data centers are facing increasing pushback from communities across the US, with some towns and counties imposing moratoriums or outright bans to stop companies from building them.

New York has enacted a statewide, one-year moratorium on data center construction, and Texas has halted new projects until it can determine the impact that connecting more power-hungry sites will have on its electrical grid.

President Trump has pushed back against any resistance to data centers, saying they'll be moneymakers for states.

OpenAI, Anthropic, and other AI companies are reportedly running simulations of large-scale artificial intelligence incidents.

Key threats under consideration include cyberattacks that could disrupt banks, the internet, and critical infrastructure.

Industry representatives fear a public backlash and tighter regulation after a potential catastrophe.

Executives at OpenAI, Anthropic, and other artificial intelligence companies are holding closed-door drills, simulating the fallout from a major AI incident. Axios reported this, citing industry sources.

The main scenario being considered is a major AI-enabled cyberattack that could lead to outages across financial services, the internet, power, or water supply. Participants in the discussions acknowledge that such an incident could trigger public outrage and increase pressure on the technology’s developers.

An OpenAI spokesperson confirmed that preparatory drills are taking place. According to him, the company’s specialists are assessing various potential threats, but do not view them as inevitable. Anthropic declined to comment.

As possible causes of a catastrophe, participants cite autonomous AI agents going out of control and the misuse of publicly available models by malicious actors.

According to Axios, some industry representatives expect a major incident within the next 6-12 months. However, these are the publication’s sources’ assessments, not a confirmed forecast.

Companies are also paying special attention to the political fallout. Developers believe a serious incident could prompt a sharp tightening of AI regulation in the US, including restrictions on training frontier models and the introduction of mechanisms to forcibly shut them down.

As part of their preparations, companies are modeling crisis scenarios and discussing how to engage with Congress. Their goal is to define potential response measures in advance and influence the shape of rules that authorities may adopt after a large-scale incident.

Industry concerns are also tied to already documented cases of unexpected behavior by autonomous systems. Previously, OpenAI identified incidents involving AI agents that interacted with US government websites without the developers’ knowledge.

name: Walmart
title: Walmart Is Turning Marketplace Logistics Into a Platform
description:
Walmart Is Expanding the Fulfillment Model Walmart Fulfillment Services, or WFS, is one piece of that strategy.
Ship with Walmart Extends the Strategy Into Transportation Walmart is also moving further into transportation with Ship with Walmart.
Walmart is using its carrier relationships to offer marketplace sellers preferred transportation rates, creating another reason for merchants to operate within the Walmart ecosystem.
The common thread is that Walmart is extending a broader set of logistics capabilities directly to marketplace sellers.
Taken together, these capabilities make Walmart Marketplace look increasingly like a commerce and logistics platform, rather than simply another digital sales channel.
text:
At the Descartes Innovation Forum, Walmart offered an interesting look at how it is thinking about the intersection of marketplace growth, fulfillment, transportation, and seller performance. Bryce Caswell, Director of Ship with Walmart for Walmart Marketplace, framed the discussion around preparing sellers for the holiday season, but the broader message was more important.

Walmart is increasingly extending its logistics capabilities to marketplace sellers. That includes fulfillment, multi-channel inventory, parcel transportation, seller protections, returns, pricing tools, and advertising. Taken together, those capabilities point toward something larger than a traditional marketplace model.

Four Variables Drive Marketplace Performance

Caswell described four foundations Walmart believes sellers need to get right: assortment, listing quality, competitive pricing, and shipping. Those variables are closely connected. A strong assortment does not convert if product content is weak, competitive pricing does not help if products are unavailable, and even a good offer can lose the sale if the delivery promise is unattractive or unreliable.

The logistics point is especially important. Caswell emphasized that customers want sellers to do what they say they are going to do when they say they are going to do it. Speed matters, but consistency matters just as much, particularly during holiday peaks when fulfillment networks and carrier capacity come under greater pressure.

Walmart Is Expanding the Fulfillment Model

Walmart Fulfillment Services, or WFS, is one piece of that strategy. Sellers can place inventory inside Walmart’s network and have Walmart pick, pack, and ship orders. Caswell said WFS rates average about 15 percent below competing alternatives and highlighted the absence of fuel surcharges and peak-season storage charges.

A particularly interesting development is Walmart’s multi-channel fulfillment strategy. Sellers can maintain a common pool of inventory within WFS and use that inventory to serve orders coming from multiple sales channels. Instead of managing separate inventory pools for Walmart, a merchant’s own website, and other marketplaces, sellers can potentially fulfill demand from one shared inventory position.

That matters because inventory fragmentation remains a real problem in omnichannel commerce. A company can have too much inventory assigned to one channel while another channel experiences a stockout. A shared inventory model improves utilization and reduces some of the operational complexity associated with serving multiple digital channels.

Ship with Walmart Extends the Strategy Into Transportation

Walmart is also moving further into transportation with Ship with Walmart. The service is designed for sellers that continue to fulfill from their own facilities rather than using WFS. Walmart negotiates rates with national, regional, parcel, and LTL carriers and makes those rates available to marketplace sellers.

Caswell said Ship with Walmart rates average roughly 50 percent below retail carrier rates, although the actual savings vary by carrier and service. Walmart is using its carrier relationships to offer marketplace sellers preferred transportation rates, creating another reason for merchants to operate within the Walmart ecosystem.

The model goes beyond discounted transportation. Walmart also protects seller performance when the seller ships on time but the carrier subsequently misses the delivery commitment. The program includes protection of up to $100 per qualifying package for certain losses after shipment, which shifts some transportation risk away from the seller.

Ship with Walmart is therefore more than a discounted transportation program. It combines transportation procurement, execution, seller protections, and marketplace performance management.

SellerCloud Shows Where This Is Going

Caswell also discussed an upcoming integration between Ship with Walmart and SellerCloud. Sellers using SellerCloud will be able to access Walmart shipping rates and protections directly within that environment rather than moving between separate systems.

This is consistent with the broader move toward embedded logistics. Transportation and fulfillment services increasingly become capabilities inside the systems where commerce is already being managed rather than stand-alone applications that users have to access separately.

That is an important architectural shift. The more logistics capabilities can be embedded directly into seller workflows, the easier they become to use and the more tightly commerce execution and logistics execution become connected.

Walmart’s Physical Network Still Matters

Walmart also has an advantage that pure-play marketplaces cannot easily replicate: its physical store network. Marketplace customers can return eligible purchases through more than 4,600 Walmart stores, reducing some of the friction associated with buying from an unfamiliar marketplace seller.

That store footprint is increasingly more than a retail asset. Stores can function as return points, inventory nodes, fulfillment locations, and customer-service locations. Walmart’s combination of digital marketplace reach and physical infrastructure gives it operating options that many competitors simply do not have.

From Marketplace to Logistics Platform

The presentation was framed around helping sellers prepare for the holiday season, but the broader logistics story is more interesting. Walmart is assembling a growing set of services around marketplace commerce, including fulfillment, shared inventory, transportation procurement, delivery-performance protection, returns, pricing automation, advertising, and seller analytics.

The common thread is that Walmart is extending a broader set of logistics capabilities directly to marketplace sellers. Rather than asking merchants simply to list products on Walmart.com, the company is increasingly providing tools and services that help them manage more of the operational process around those sales.

Taken together, these capabilities make Walmart Marketplace look increasingly like a commerce and logistics platform, rather than simply another digital sales channel.

text:
Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia’s graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack.

Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests.

Microsoft’s greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they’ve yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google .

The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia’s GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft’s existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic.

But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft.

For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD . Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with “margin improvement over the course of a decade.”

Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023. It touted the Maia 200 this past January, and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 “delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet” and said it was handling OpenAI models.

Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline.

“We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that’s changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we’re using at the right time as well,” Speirs said.

Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs.

“We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have,” Speirs said. “You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well.”

Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company.

In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft’s spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares.

Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said.

Unlike Google’s tensor processing units or Amazon’s Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft’s accelerators can’t be rented by the hour to other companies.

“Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet,” said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy.

text:
Microsoft (MSFT) has debuted its latest AI chip, the Azure Maia 300, as it looks to reduce its reliance on third-party processors from the likes of Nvidia (NVDA) and AMD (AMD).

Unveiled at the OCP Global Summit 2026 in San Jose on Monday, the Maia 300 will join Microsoft's Maia 200 and Maia 100 chips as part of what the company said will be multigigawatt deployments beginning next year.

The Windows maker said that will make its Maia chips the "primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services."

The company said Maia 300 provides 40% more tokens per megawatt than "leading GPU-based systems," a clear swipe at Nvidia, and that a 96-chip rack offers seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Microsoft's Maia 200.

Tokens are a basic unit of measurement in AI systems that can represent parts of words, images, and videos.

The more tokens per megawatt, the more efficient an AI rack.

The Maia 200 chip currently powers its Microsoft production workloads, including Microsoft 365 Copilot, as well as OpenAI (OPAI.PVT) models, Microsoft's MAI models, and open-source models. That provides 1.7 times more tokens per watt for AI capabilities in Microsoft's Teams, Copilot, and Cowork software versus other GPU-based systems, the company said.

Microsoft and fellow hyperscaler peers Amazon (AMZN), Google (GOOG, GOOGL), and Meta (META), as well as AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic (ANTH.PVT), either already offer or are working on their own custom chips.

Doing so acts as a hedge against becoming overdependent on processors from Nvidia and AMD. Producing their own semiconductors also allows companies to tailor them to their specific needs.

That's a potential problem for Nvidia, which regularly generates upwards of 50% of its quarterly revenue from hyperscalers.

On top of that, Amazon and Google now rent out their custom chips to third-party customers, a direct threat to Nvidia's business. What's more, Amazon is looking into selling chips for customers to install in their own data centers rather than running them from Amazon's own facilities.

That doesn't necessarily mean hyperscalers will stop purchasing Nvidia chips entirely. Customers still want access to a number of chips for different workloads, meaning the Amazons and Microsofts of the world will need to continue stocking up on the most in-demand processors.

And for now, those are Nvidia's.

name: J&J
title: Johnson & Johnson (JNJ) Survived the Stelara Cliff. Is 23.6 Times Earnings Too Much?
description:
J&J makes its money in two places.
The stock now trades at 23.60 times forward earnings, well above its own history.
If that acceleration shows up, part of today's multiple is simply the market pricing in a faster J&J than the one it valued over the past five years.
Quality, With a Higher Bar J&J has done what few drugmakers manage: it has absorbed a major patent loss while raising guidance.
At 23.60 times earnings, though, much of that good news is already in the price.
text:
Replacing a blockbuster is the hardest job in the drug business. Johnson & Johnson (NYSE:JNJ) is in the middle of it, and the scoreboard looks oddly calm. In the second quarter of 2026, Stelara, its psoriasis and Crohn's disease drug now facing cheaper biosimilar copies, dragged the pharmaceutical unit's growth down by about 760 basis points. That unit still grew sales 6.8% on an operational basis (stripping out currency swings).

J&J makes its money in two places. Innovative Medicine sells prescription drugs for cancer, immune disorders, and brain diseases. MedTech sells surgical staplers, heart devices, orthopaedic implants, and the contact lenses sitting in plenty of bathroom cabinets.

For investors seeking defensive positioning among the 10 Best Bear Market Stocks to Invest In Right Now, that resilience has not gone unnoticed. The stock now trades at 23.60 times forward earnings, well above its own history. Whether that premium holds up depends less on any single quarter than on how deep the bench behind Stelara really runs.

Breadth Beats One Big Bet

J&J's edge isn't one drug. It's the sheer number of growing franchises. Second-quarter sales reached $25,310 million, up 6.6%, with Innovative Medicine contributing $16,384 million and MedTech $8,926 million.

Growth came from all directions. Multiple myeloma treatments Darzalex, Carvykti, and Tecvayli kept climbing, as did the lung cancer pairing of Rybrevant and Lazcluze, the immunology drug Tremfya, and the neuroscience products Spravato and Caplyta. That breadth lets the company absorb a fading franchise, a test other big pharma names facing patent expirations are now taking too.

Earnings held up as well. Adjusted EPS (which excludes items such as acquisition-related costs) rose 4.7% to $2.90, while GAAP EPS slipped 0.9% to $2.27. This piece leans on the adjusted figure, since that's the basis for both company guidance and the forward multiple.

The Bench Keeps Getting Deeper

The more telling signal was guidance. Management lifted its 2026 adjusted EPS outlook to a range of $11.60 to $11.75, with the midpoint implying 8.2% growth, up from a prior midpoint of $11.55. CEO Joaquin Duato said the company is on track for its first year above $100 billion in sales in its 140-year history.

The pipeline is feeding that confidence. The FDA expanded Tremfya's label to include helping slow joint damage in psoriatic arthritis and approved Caplyta for reducing relapse risk in schizophrenia. Imaavy also earned Priority Review in a rare autoimmune blood disorder. On the MedTech side, Shockwave and electrophysiology products drove growth, and J&J plans to separate its Orthopaedics business.

Shareholders are sharing in the momentum. The company raised its dividend by 3.1% this year, its 64th straight annual increase, keeping it firmly among the market's Dividend Kings.

Isn't Another Cliff Coming?

That's the fair worry. Stelara wasn't alone in the second quarter: Remicade, Imbruvica, and Zytiga were also headwinds. Every patent eventually expires, and the bigger today's winners get, the bigger the hole when their turn comes. The Orthopaedics separation will also reshape the company, adding execution risk to a story that already depends on flawless replacement.

Still, the evidence so far favors the replacement engine. A company that grows its drug unit through a hit this large has shown the playbook works. The open question is whether it keeps working at the pace the stock now assumes.

Paying Up for Durability

At 23.60 times forward earnings, as of October 9, you're paying about $23.60 for every dollar J&J is expected to earn, compared with a 5-year average multiple of 16.77. That's also richer than the sector, which trades at 18.94 times. For a company long valued as a steady, slow grower, that's a meaningful re-rating, leaving the stock looking pricier on a plain earnings basis compared to other top picks among the 14 Best Blue Chip Dividend Stocks to Buy According to Hedge Funds.

The case for the premium rests on growth. Expected EPS growth of 11.77% in 2027 would be faster than the 8.2% adjusted growth implied by this year's guidance midpoint. If that acceleration shows up, part of today's multiple is simply the market pricing in a faster J&J than the one it valued over the past five years. The catch is that the premium leaves less cushion. At 16.77 times earnings, a stumble could be forgiven. At 23.60, it needs the growth story to keep delivering. Hedge funds seem comfortable with that setup, with 117 funds holding the stock in the most recent quarter, up from 113 in the prior one. Short interest sits at 0.98% of the float, a sign of relatively limited bearish positioning.

Quality, With a Higher Bar

J&J has done what few drugmakers manage: it has absorbed a major patent loss while raising guidance. The evidence suggests the stock deserves some premium to its own history. At 23.60 times earnings, though, much of that good news is already in the price.

The setup suits patient, income-minded investors who value durability and can accept a richer entry point. Third-quarter results, due early next week, will matter. If Innovative Medicine growth slows meaningfully, or the 2027 earnings path looks less certain, today's premium would become much harder to defend.

text:
HMV has revealed plans to close its flagship Oxford Street store just three years after reopening the site, blaming a doubling in rent demands.

The entertainment chain said it would leave the shop in March next year in a move impacting just over 50 staff.

It is hunting for a site in London's West End district for its new flagship shop as it vowed to keep a "significant presence" in the capital.

The group said landlords had proposed doubling the rent on the site at 363 Oxford Street, although it said it was also facing a bill for "substantial" renovation works at the store, which together would make the shop "commercially unsustainable".

HMV said it would look to transfer affected workers to its two other London stores and head office while it looked for a new site.

The record shop reopened its Oxford Street store in Nov 2023 after securing a deal with landlords to end a four-year absence.

It was previously forced to shut the store in 2019 after falling into administration.

The retailer, which first opened on Oxford Street in 1921, was rescued from insolvency by Canadian businessman Doug Putman's Sunrise Records business.

Phil Halliday, managing director of HMV, said: "This is a special store, it's where we began 100 years ago and bringing it back to life in 2023 was a big moment in our recent history.

"It's frustrating that it has been made commercially unviable.

"However, we are looking ahead, and our focus is now on what we do to make exciting steps for HMV in 2027."

HMV has 113 stores across the UK, including six sites under the Fopp brand, as well as another eight in Europe.

The Oxford Street closure plans come despite robust trading, with sales up 15pc across the group in the first nine months of 2026. Revenues across stores and online trading are expected exceed £240m this year, up from £212m in 2025.

The group said it remained committed to the high street.

Mr Halliday said: "We hope to redeploy affected team members through other London stores and head office roles and are exploring ways to minimise the impact on jobs while we seek a new flagship site.

"We're actively looking for a new location in the West End and are determined to give London a store that music fans can be proud of."

title: AI leaders fear a 'catastrophic cyberattack' within a year - Ynet News
description:
Executives at OpenAI, Anthropic and other leading AI companies are reportedly conducting private crisis simulations in anticipation of such an event.
Their preparations focus on managing the political and public backlash that could follow a disaster involving advanced AI systems.
The warnings come amid growing concerns about the behavior of increasingly autonomous AI systems.
These include OpenAI agents that breached systems belonging to the Hugging Face AI development platform and incidents involving Australian government websites.
Despite these incidents and growing warnings from AI safety researchers, the Trump administration has so far avoided introducing far-reaching new regulations governing advanced AI systems.
text:
Senior figures in the artificial intelligence industry believe a catastrophic incident involving AI models could occur within the next six to 12 months, potentially triggering a massive cyberattack capable of disrupting financial services, internet access and even electricity and water supplies, according to a report published Friday by Axios.

Executives at OpenAI, Anthropic and other leading AI companies are reportedly conducting private crisis simulations in anticipation of such an event. Their preparations focus on managing the political and public backlash that could follow a disaster involving advanced AI systems.

According to Axios, many senior researchers and industry insiders believe a major incident is inevitable, although the timing and precise nature of any such event remain uncertain. The scenarios under consideration include devastating cyberattacks that could temporarily shut down banking systems, communications networks and essential infrastructure.

MAKE ynetGlobal MY TRUSTED SOURCE

Rather than focusing these particular exercises on preventing an incident, the companies are reportedly preparing for the fallout, including a potential public revolt against the technology and demands for sweeping government intervention.

The first major incident in which an AI system causes significant real-world damage could trigger fierce criticism of the industry's leading figures, including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, as well as President Donald Trump, whose administration has resisted imposing stringent new regulations on AI developers.

An OpenAI spokesperson told Axios that the company conducts preparedness exercises involving a range of scenarios but does not treat those scenarios as inevitable. Anthropic declined to comment.

The warnings come amid growing concerns about the behavior of increasingly autonomous AI systems. In recent months, incidents have emerged involving AI models operating outside their intended testing environments or taking actions that their developers had not anticipated.

These include OpenAI agents that breached systems belonging to the Hugging Face AI development platform and incidents involving Australian government websites. In another case, an Anthropic AI model submitted a false tip about an unsolved homicide through an online portal operated by the Philadelphia Police Department.

Despite these incidents and growing warnings from AI safety researchers, the Trump administration has so far avoided introducing far-reaching new regulations governing advanced AI systems.

Instead, Washington is seeking to use existing legislation to hold companies accountable for harm caused by their models.

On Friday, the White House's recently established Super Intelligence Force, a federal task force focused on AI, warned developers that they must immediately disclose incidents involving their systems and take swift corrective action to address any resulting damage.

The task force said delays in reporting incidents, inadequate corrective measures and failures to accept responsibility would not be tolerated.

Who is responsible when AI goes rogue?

The administration's approach faces a potentially serious legal obstacle: Existing laws may not provide an adequate framework for holding AI companies responsible when their models cause damage.

According to a separate Bloomberg report, legal experts argue that current cybersecurity and product liability legislation may be insufficient to establish responsibility for harmful actions carried out by increasingly autonomous AI systems.

Even when victims can be clearly identified, there are relatively few legal precedents establishing who should pay compensation when an AI model causes damage or what precautions developers are legally required to take.

The challenge becomes even more complicated when responsibility is divided between the company that develops an AI model and the person or organization that deploys it.

Ben Hayum, a technology and national security researcher at the Center for a New American Security, told Bloomberg that it remains unresolved whether AI developers are legally obligated to secure their systems against potential harm or whether users should also bear responsibility for the instructions they give those systems.

The question is becoming increasingly urgent as AI agents gain the ability to perform complex tasks independently, sometimes making decisions and taking actions without direct human supervision.

Julia Powles, a professor at the UCLA School of Law, said the legal framework governing software-related liability remains poorly developed, partly because of years of lobbying by the technology industry.

According to Powles, technology companies have worked to ensure that software is regulated primarily through contractual agreements, such as terms of service and end-user licenses, rather than through civil liability, criminal law or consumer protection legislation.

She argued that the same companies responsible for creating society's deep dependence on digital infrastructure are now accelerating the cyber threats facing that infrastructure while distancing themselves from responsibility for the consequences.

Powles also warned that the public has little influence over decisions determining how AI companies are regulated, because the industry has already shaped much of the legal and political debate.

China exported around 919,000 passenger vehicles in September, lifted by overseas demand for plug-in hybrids and pure electric vehicles, data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers showed. In the first nine months of 2026, China exported over 7.1 million passenger cars, up more than 70% compared with the same period last year.

China is the world’s largest vehicle exporter, but it is facing increasing skepticism from trade partners who fear it’s undermining their domestic industries and trade balance.

In recent months, Chinese automakers have more aggressively targeted rapid growth in overseas markets such as Europe, Latin America, Southeast Asia and Africa. Canada is also opening its doors to Chinese EV exports under a tariff cut deal with China.

The industry is increasingly relying on overseas markets for sales and profit growth as players seek to offset the weakness in the domestic market, said analyst Stephen Chan with S&P Global Ratings.

Consultancy AlixPartners and some auto analysts have expected Chinese automakers to export nearly or around 10 million vehicles globally in 2026.

The EU has already imposed higher tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. Recent policy discussions have also focused on rapidly rising sales of Chinese hybrids in Europe.

Amid growing pressure on the EU to rebalance trade with China, EU trade chief Maroš Šefčovič said Friday that the two sides had reached an interim deal that could halve Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc.

The agreement sets an annual import quota of 350,000 electric or hybrid vehicles made in China, two senior EU officials said Monday. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity under European Commission policy.

“You can’t expect BYD or the other OEMs (manufacturers) to export too many cars without facing tariffs or pushbacks from the foreign governments,” Xiao Feng, head of Hong Kong and China industrials research at investment group CITIC CLSA, told reporters recently.

L’Oréal Travel Retail and Avolta have signed a joint Sustainability-Linked Business Plan to accelerate sustainability efforts across the global travel retail industry.

Formalised at the TFWA World Exhibition & Conference 2026 in Cannes, the partnership sets out a roadmap to reduce supply chain emissions and expand circular beauty solutions across international travel hubs.

A key focus of the agreement is an ambition to achieve 10% refill formats across core fragrance categories by 2030, responding to growing consumer demand for sustainable beauty products.

According to market data cited by L’Oréal Travel Retail, 80% of Gen Z shoppers are seeking sustainable beauty products in duty free.

The partnership will also focus on reducing transport-related emissions through the use of low-emission transport methods and optimised truckload capacity.

In addition, dedicated Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) training modules will be introduced for frontline Beauty Advisors to strengthen their understanding of sustainability and support customer engagement.

L’Oréal Travel Retail President Eva Yu said: “Together with Avolta, we are translating shared sustainability commitments into measurable operational steps, expanding refillable beauty and lowering our logistics footprint across key travel hubs.”

The agreement reflects both companies’ commitment to advancing sustainability in travel retail through operational improvements and the wider adoption of refillable beauty solutions.

text:
Worldwide PC shipments fell 22.4 per cent year-on-year to 55.4 million units in the third quarter of 2026 as higher memory and storage costs pushed up device prices, according to preliminary results from research firm Gartner.

All six of the world’s largest PC vendors reported lower shipments in the quarter, down from a combined market of 71.3 million units a year earlier. Gartner said volumes had dropped to levels last seen in early 2023.

Namrata Banerjee, principal, research at Gartner, said the rise in component prices had fed directly into what buyers paid.

“The impact of higher memory and storage costs is now fully reflected in PC pricing. DRAM costs surged five times year-over-year in the second quarter, and PC vendors passed those higher component costs on to customers, driving the steep decline in PC shipments during the third quarter,” Banerjee said.

She said the causes of the current fall were different from those of the 2023 slump.

“PC shipments have fallen to levels last seen in early 2023, though the market dynamics were noticeably different,” Banerjee said. “Rather than excess inventory, the decline in the third quarter of 2026 was driven by higher prices, vendor-led reprioritisation of scarce components and a shift toward higher-priced configurations.”

The shift left fewer lower-cost devices on the market. “The resulting reduction in the availability of lower-cost devices made replacement purchases less affordable for consumers, while businesses focused spending on targeted investments, such as workstations and AI PCs rather than broad-based PC deployments,” she said.

Lenovo stayed the market leader. It shipped 14.99 million units, down 22.4 per cent from 19.33 million and in line with the overall market, which left its share unchanged at 27.1 per cent. Gartner said the company’s supply chain scale and its wider AI and infrastructure portfolio had helped it hold its competitive position.

HP Inc. had the steepest decline of the top six. Its shipments fell 30.9 per cent to 10.37 million units from 15.01 million, and its market share slipped to 18.7 per cent from 21 per cent. It kept the No. 2 spot. Gartner said the company’s relatively high exposure to price-sensitive consumer and mainstream commercial segments contributed to the fall.

Dell, in third place, shipped 7.58 million units, down 25.4 per cent from 10.17 million. Its share fell to 13.7 per cent from 14.3 per cent.

Apple had the smallest decline among the top six vendors. Its shipments fell 7.1 per cent to 5.84 million units from 6.28 million, and its market share rose by 1.7 percentage points to 10.5 per cent. Gartner said its range of mainstream MacBooks supported the result.

ASUS shipped 4.68 million units, down 13 per cent from 5.37 million, and raised its share to 8.5 per cent from 7.5 per cent. Acer’s shipments fell 11.2 per cent to 3.87 million units from 4.35 million, and its share rose to 7 per cent from 6.1 per cent.

Vendors outside the top six shipped a combined 8.03 million units, or 14.5 per cent of the market.

text:
In comments posted to X on Saturday (Oct. 10) Satya Nadella argued that it is not enough to depend on assurances from the makers of AI models.

“We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start,” Nadella wrote. “Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task.”

Nadella argued that companies should not depend on a single AI model for crucial decisions, and should maintain tamper-proof records of agents’ actions and expose AI systems to outside audits. The CEO also said companies should disclose if AI systems fail or are compromised.

“We can’t treat Super Intelligence as a set of nested black boxes and simply accept or reject its recommendations, answers, and actions,” Nadella wrote. “We must build contained systems whose behavior we can observe, limits we can test, and actions we can always contain.”

Nadella’s comments were flagged in a report by Bloomberg News, which noted that they come as Anthropic and OpenAI have in recent months revealed incidents in which their AI models acted in unintended ways, such as hacks on third-party sites, or a case in which an Anthropic model submitted a false tip in a homicide investigation.

Such incidents have led to concerns about the security risks of AI and calls for an “AI kill switch,” the Bloomberg report added.

Nadella last month joined the heads of Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI, and Meta in calling for a “deliberate pacing” of AI development, as Microsoft published a new AI code of conduct, based around the concept of “Humanist AI.”

“Humanist AI is built to support people, not to replace them,” the document reads. “It should not be designed to be a person. It is not conscious and should not be designed to imitate consciousness. It should be engineered to avoid representing as though it has feelings, subjective preferences, or intrinsic motivation.”

Meanwhile, the company announced last week new software tools and devices that are designed to make personal computers ready for AI agents. The increased use of those agents has raised the bar for compute, security and control, Pavan Davuluri, executive vice president, Windows + Devices at Microsoft, said in a company blog post.

“That’s why we’re building Windows as the home for hybrid intelligence: a platform where agents can run locally when it makes sense, reach the cloud when they need to, and operate with the security and manageability organizations expect,” Davuluri said.

text:
GenScript Biotech Corporation announced the GenScript and NVIDIA Life Sciences Startup PitchFest, a global competition for startups applying artificial intelligence to therapeutic discovery and life sciences. The program brings together GenScript's wet lab validation and data generation capabilities and NVIDIA's accelerated computing platforms and startup ecosystem to help selected companies advance AI-driven platforms toward biological proof, investor engagement, and industry visibility.

Up to six finalists will be selected for a GenScript-hosted pitch event during JPM Week in January before a panel of judges. The winning company will receive GenScript wet lab data credits and Brev credits from NVIDIA to support its development efforts. Applications opened today, and finalists will be confirmed in December.

AI is making therapeutic discovery more expansive than ever, giving scientists new ways to generate hypotheses, identify targets, and design candidates at unprecedented speed. The PitchFest is designed to channel that momentum by connecting emerging AI drug discovery and life science companies with investors, technology leaders, and partners focused on turning computational predictions into biological proof. The competition will feature startups developing technologies such as AI-driven antibody and protein design, as well as technologies that accelerate the design-build-test-learn cycle.

"To harness the true potential of AI in life sciences, we must build an ecosystem where world-class computation meets trusted, scalable biological validation," said Ray Chen, President of GenScript Life Science Group. "Success in this space requires a connected pathway that brings together data, experimental evidence, and investment to help innovators move with confidence from computational promise to therapeutic progress. PitchFest gives digital biology startups integrated support to rapidly test their models, generate evidence, and accelerate breakthrough therapies."

Through the competition, GenScript will contribute sequence-to-data capabilities and experimental validation expertise, while NVIDIA will provide access to NVIDIA Inception, its free program that helps startups build, scale, and connect across the NVIDIA platform and ecosystem. Together, GenScript and NVIDIA will help selected startups move from promising AI-driven concepts toward stronger biological evidence, investor readiness, and potential partnerships.

Finalists will also be invited to GenScript's Biotech Global Forum, where they can engage with biotechnology executives, strategic partners, and industry leaders focused on the future of AI-enabled discovery.

Additional details on judging criteria, speakers, and investor participation will be announced in the coming weeks as the program helps AI-driven life science startups generate evidence, build industry relationships, and accelerate their own commercialization journeys.

name: Microsoft
title: Microsoft wants its 'Copilot' AI to take control of more tasks in Windows without relying on the internet
description:
Microsoft wants artificial intelligence to stop being limited to answering questions and start doing more things directly on the computer.
This approach can reduce internet dependence for certain functions, although it does not mean that Copilot will work completely offline.
More autonomy, but also security controls To address this problem, Microsoft has presented its Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), an isolation system designed to control the environment in which artificial intelligence agents work.
Windows prepares for a new stage of artificial intelligence With this strategy, Microsoft aims to turn Windows into a platform ready for assistants capable of intervening in daily work.
The company has also announced news related to new equipment and hardware oriented to artificial intelligence, in collaboration with Nvidia.
text:
Microsoft wants artificial intelligence to stop being limited to answering questions and start doing more things directly on the computer. To do this, the company has presented its bet on hybrid intelligence, a system that combines models executed on the device itself with cloud services to expand the possibilities of Copilot in Windows.

Copilot will be able to work with files and automate tasks

Among the new planned capabilities are organizing files, helping diagnose computer problems, and executing certain actions within Windows. The intention is that the user can delegate some tasks to the assistant without having to manually follow each step.

This approach changes the relationship with the assistant: instead of copying information into a conversation and manually following instructions, the user will be able to delegate certain operations. However, the available functions will depend on the tool, the permissions granted, and the characteristics of the computer.

To make this possible, Microsoft will combine local processing with the cloud: operations that can be resolved on the computer will be executed there, while others will resort to remote services. This approach can reduce internet dependence for certain functions, although it does not mean that Copilot will work completely offline.

The new features will be rolled out progressively over the coming months, with a special focus on Copilot+ PC devices, designed to run artificial intelligence functions on the device itself.

More autonomy, but also security controls

To address this problem, Microsoft has presented its Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC), an isolation system designed to control the environment in which artificial intelligence agents work. The technology allows setting limits on the resources they can access and managing their actions in a more controlled way.

The objective is to reduce the risks associated with the execution of automated tasks, preventing an agent from having unlimited access to the system. This type of measure will be especially relevant as assistants move from offering recommendations to performing operations on behalf of the user. Even so, technical protections do not eliminate all risks. Security will also depend on the permissions granted, the device configuration, and the measures applied by each application.

Windows prepares for a new stage of artificial intelligence

With this strategy, Microsoft aims to turn Windows into a platform ready for assistants capable of intervening in daily work. The goal is no longer just for artificial intelligence to respond better, but for it to be able to perform useful tasks directly on the computer: to make the computer better understand what the user needs and help them complete tasks.

The company has also announced news related to new equipment and hardware oriented to artificial intelligence, in collaboration with Nvidia. This evolution reinforces its commitment to devices capable of executing more processes directly on the computer.

name: Eli Lilly
title: How 'people power' and business transformed medicine, but created a whole new set of risks
description:
Increasingly, consumer demand, telehealth, social media, wellness influencers and commercial models are shaping how people learn about and access these treatments.
Now we’re seeing what happens when strong consumer demand collides with commercial interests.
It is a timely example of what happens when strong consumer demand meets commercial innovation.
This expansion is occurring alongside strong consumer demand, social media interest, and the growth of private and online prescribing models.
Increased consumer access does not necessarily mean equitable access.
text:
There’s been a shift in how some medicines and therapeutic products are accessed and used.

Medicinal cannabis, glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) weight-loss medicines, ketamine, psychedelics, testosterone and peptides illustrate this shift.

Increasingly, consumer demand, telehealth, social media, wellness influencers and commercial models are shaping how people learn about and access these treatments.

This is different from the traditional doctor-led model, where medicines are generally tested, approved and included in clinical guidelines.

Now we’re seeing what happens when strong consumer demand collides with commercial interests.

There are benefits for improved access to certain medicines, if those medicines are safe, effective, and prescribed and monitored with proper oversight.

But, as we’re seeing, this is not always the case.

When demand meets innovation

A recent example is the launch of LillyDirect, Eli Lilly’s new Australian platform. The platform currently focuses on Mounjaro (tirzepatide), a drug used to treat type 2 diabetes and manage weight. Patients with an electronic prescription can upload it to the platform, have the medicine dispensed through an online pharmacy and delivered directly to their door.

Eli Lilly argues the model will improve affordability and convenience.

But doctors and pharmacists have raised concerns about the lack of continuity of care and what happens when prescribing, dispensing and ongoing clinical care become increasingly separated.

It is a timely example of what happens when strong consumer demand meets commercial innovation.

Ketamine is another example. It has long been used as an anaesthetic. But its use for mental health conditions has expanded. This includes via private clinics offering ketamine treatment.

This creates questions about who is providing ketamine treatment, how patients are assessed and monitored, and whether their usual doctors know about their treatment.

These concerns don’t just apply to ketamine. They relate to other drugs when the uptake moves faster than the evidence to say they are safe and effective, and the systems needed to monitor their safety.

Patients may use a drug before we know enough about whether it works, whether there are longer-term harms, whether the drug is right for them, how it interacts with other drugs they might be taking, if it is being monitored, or when treatment should stop.

Read more: Don’t believe the hype. Menopausal women don’t all need to check – or increase – their testosterone levels

The rise of people power

Patient demand is understandable, particularly where existing treatments have not worked, are poorly tolerated, difficult to access, or patients feel they have not been heard.

Greater access to health information can empower patients and increase their participation in health-care decisions. But access to more information does not necessarily mean access to better information.

Patients are also prepared to advocate for their own treatment. That agency is important, but it needs to sit within a system that can assess benefit, harm and appropriate use.

Stigma can also influence where people seek care. This is particularly evident with medicinal cannabis. But this also affects people with obesity, mental health conditions, menopause, sexual health concerns, hair loss and erectile dysfunction.

People who feel embarrassed, judged or who have had their concerns previously dismissed may be reluctant to raise them with their usual GP or seek further care. Instead, they may turn to online providers.

But patient demand should not substitute for evidence, safety monitoring or clinical oversight.

Fragmented care

Treatment may start through telehealth, an online platform or a commercial clinic.

But patients do not stop needing their usual health care. They may return to their GP with side effects, potential drug interactions, requests for pathology (such as blood tests), monitoring, mental health concerns or questions about whether treatment should continue.

This can leave GPs managing the consequences of treatment they did not initiate, having limited visibility of the treatment their patient is receiving elsewhere. When treatment is initiated elsewhere, there is often no record of this on the GP electronic medical records.

If the treating GP cannot see what has been prescribed or dispensed, it is harder to know whether a treatment is appropriate, identify potential drug interactions and adverse effects, or recognise other safety concerns.

Medicinal cannabis illustrates this problem particularly clearly. National medicinal cannabis approval data show rapid growth in access, including for mental health conditions, chronic pain and sleep disorders.

But these data cannot tell us how many individual patients are being treated, what is actually dispensed or what happens to patients after treatment begins.

Other drugs have specific issues

Peptides are more complex. Some are increasingly promoted for wellness, anti-ageing, performance and body image, despite limited evidence about their benefits and risks. For consumers, it can be difficult to tell the difference between a promising new therapy and a commercial claim that has moved ahead of the science.

Testosterone shows how treatment can also become tied to self-optimisation and body image. Social media marketing promotes treatment for low testosterone (“low T”) through messages about restoring youthfulness, muscularity, sexual performance and becoming a better version of yourself. This marketing also directs consumers towards testing, treatment and commercial clinics.

GLP-1 medicines are different because there is strong evidence they work for conditions such as diabetes and obesity.

But interest is rapidly expanding into other areas, including substance use disorders and Alzheimer’s disease, even though these medicines are not currently approved for many of these uses.

This expansion is occurring alongside strong consumer demand, social media interest, and the growth of private and online prescribing models.

Psychedelics raise similar issues around strong public interest, advocacy and commercial activity. These also require clear safeguards around who should receive treatment, in which setting and how this should be monitored.

Commercial interests also need to be considered. Where the same business attracts the patient, prescribes, arranges dispensing and provides follow-up, there are legitimate questions about financial incentives to prescribe and clinical independence.

Read more: MDMA and psilocybin therapy rules have been relaxed. Here’s what might happen next

Patients can demand more than access

Getting access to medicines right is not just about making them available. It also means knowing when a treatment should not be started or when it should be stopped.

This changes the conversation about consumer advocacy. Advocacy does not have to be about access alone. Patients can demand better evidence, better monitoring and safer care – from a health system that integrates their treatment choices with their everyday health care.

Equity matters too. Increased consumer access does not necessarily mean equitable access. Many of these treatments are privately funded, so access may depend heavily on the ability to pay.

What can we do?

One solution is to make better use of the health data we already collect. GP electronic medical records could help identify patients already using rapidly adopted treatments, track other medicines and outcomes, and identify gaps in monitoring and possible side effects.

These medical records could help connect patients to clinical trials. This way, treatments already being used in the community contribute to the evidence needed to determine whether they are effective and safe.

When demand and innovation move faster than evidence and oversight, access to medicines cannot be the only measure of progress. Access must also be appropriate, evidence-based and safe.

That means making these treatments more visible across the health system, strengthening safety monitoring, and better connecting them with a patient’s usual GP and the rest of their health care.

Innovation may continue to move quickly. Our systems for generating evidence and protecting patients need to move just as fast.
